body:
## Problem

A workflow that filters on a date read from person properties fails for every event once one person is missing that property. Not "does not match", fails. The error comes out of the date library, so it reads as our failure rather than as absent data.

Here is the whole thing:

```
today() >= toDate('')           ->  Error: Invalid unit value NaN
today() >= toDate('2026-01-02') ->  true
```

`toDate` of an empty or unparseable value does not fail. It returns a date whose year, month and day are all NaN. Comparing that against today builds a date out of NaN inside the library, and that throws.

The obvious defence does not work. A filter that checks the property is not null before comparing it still fails, because Hog compiles `AND` as one operation over operands it has already evaluated. There is no short-circuit, so the comparison runs anyway. `false AND (today() >= toDate(''))` throws.

This is live. One workflow in EU is failing about 120 times an hour on exactly this, filtering on a trial window written as `person.properties.trial_start IS NOT NULL AND ... AND today() >= toDate(person.properties.trial_start)`. Every person without a trial date breaks the filter for that event.

## Changes

- **`toDate` and `toDateTime` return null when the value cannot be parsed**, instead of a date made of NaN. The ordering rule that already treats a null operand as no match then applies, so the filter simply does not fire for a person with no date. That is what the author meant to write.
- The return types become nullable, which is the whole type-level change. No production caller needed a null check, which says this value was never usefully consumed before.

**Before:** a person with no `trial_start` makes the filter throw, the event is counted as a filter error, and the workflow does not run for anybody in that batch.

**After:** the comparison is false, the filter does not match that person, and everybody else is unaffected.

> [!NOTE]
> This also changes what a failure of this kind is classified as. The error carried no Hog VM error, so the new classification reads it as `platform`, which is one of the classes we intend to park. Parking a person's missing property would fill the dead letter queue with data that no replay can fix.

### VM parity

Rust already returns null here, so this brings Node in line with it. Python still raises on the same input, which is a real divergence and a separate change: the Python VM does not evaluate these filters, and converging it has its own blast radius.

## How did you test this code?

Tests first. All five fail without the change and pass with it.

- `date.test.ts`: `toDate` and `toDateTime` are null for an empty string, a word, and an out-of-range date. Catches the NaN date coming back.
- `date.test.ts`: two existing tests pinned the NaN behaviour as a known-bad failure mode, with a comment saying converging the VMs was a separate change. This is that change, so they now pin null.
- `execute.test.ts`: comparing `today()` against an unparseable date is false rather than an error, for both `<=` and `>=`. This is the case the live workflow hits, and it is the one that would have caught this before it shipped.

Ran the full Hog VM suite, 191 tests, and the frontend typecheck. The runtime contract hash does not move, because the function signatures are unchanged, so nothing reclassifies as drift on deploy.

Not run: the Python and Rust VM suites, since neither is touched.

body:
## Problem

An operator looking at a V3 queue backlog cannot tell whether a schema is slow because it has a lot of data, or because its run keeps restarting and re-doing work it already did.

Today the second case is invisible. Every Temporal attempt of a run stages a fresh set of batches under its own `run_uuid` (`pipeline.py`), and the load idempotency key is `{team_id}:{schema_id}:{run_uuid}:{batch_index}`, so a retried attempt re-extracts and re-loads what earlier attempts already staged. Batches drain strictly serially per `(team_id, schema_id)`, so a run that keeps restarting enqueues faster than its group can drain and holds the queue head for hours.

A real example on master today: one schema's run reached attempt 16. Attempts 5-9 had fully succeeded (about 2,300 batches), attempts 10-16 held 403 more still pending, and the group was the single largest contributor to fleet-wide oldest-batch age. Nothing in Prometheus said so. `warehouse_pg_consumer_batch_retry_total` counts *batch* retries, not workflow attempts, so it stays flat while this happens.

## Changes

- New histogram `warehouse_pipeline_run_attempt` records the Temporal activity attempt number once per attempt, at the point extraction begins. A p99 above a handful now says runs are restarting and paying for the same extraction each time.
- Labelled by `source_type` only. Attempts are a per-run property, so `team_id` / `schema_id` labels would add cardinality without telling a reader anything the distribution does not.

Recorded where extraction starts rather than in the constructor, so one observation is one attempt that actually did work.

No behaviour changes: this only emits a metric.

## How did you test this code?

Automated and static only. I did not run this against a Temporal worker, and the metric has not been observed in a live environment.

- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` clean on both changed files.
- The pre-commit hook ran `uv run --no-sync ty check` over the staged files and passed.
- Verified the API against existing callers rather than assuming: `MetricHistogram` is imported from `temporalio.common` the same way as `products/batch_exports/backend/temporal/queue.py`, and `meter.create_histogram(name, description)` matches the call in `products/tasks/backend/temporal/metrics.py`.

No tests added. The change records one value that the surrounding code already computes and uses for `run_uuid`; a test asserting that the meter was called would pin the mock, not a regression. The behaviour worth testing is whether the metric is useful, which only production can answer.

Not checked: that `activity.metric_meter()` is available at this call site in every execution path. It sits a few lines after `current_activity_attempt()`, which requires the same activity context, so an environment where one works and the other does not is not reachable — but I verified that by reading, not by running.

## Problem

The per-part `trace_id` and `span_id` bloom filters on `trace_spans` use `bloom_filter(0.00001)`. Most of the cost of a lookup with these filters is the time to load the filter. The extra false positives have a much smaller effect. A 0.05 false positive rate makes the filter approx. 70% smaller.

## Changes

- Adds `idx_trace_bloom_part_v2` (`trace_id`) and `idx_span_id_bloom_part_v2` (`span_id`) with `bloom_filter(0.05)`, `GRANULARITY 99999`, next to the old indices.
- Migration `0334` runs only `ADD INDEX IF NOT EXISTS` on the LOGS nodes. It does **not** materialize the new indices. The HCL codegen added `MATERIALIZE INDEX` operations, and these were removed by hand. Parts written before the migration do not get the new indices, and they age out with retention.
- Mechanical: HCL layer edit, regenerated goldens and `sql/`, `spans.py` and the schema snapshot.
- A stacked follow-up PR removes the old `0.00001` indices.

## Problem

- The image-scrub sidecar sizes the text detector's input from its canvas budget alone, so on most frames it reads far more pixels than the redaction rule needs.
- The rule only asks each detector to see a subject `ratio` times larger than the stored image keeps it. On a 1080p frame the stored image is 161x90, so text needs 638x357 at the model, but the budget gives it 928x551.
- Faces and the stored-size cap already make the stored image that small, so the extra text pixels protect nothing.

## Changes

- The text stage costs 36% less on the production image-size mix, and 47% less than PP-OCRv3 before #106797.
- Readable words left fully visible move from 18 to 22 of 7,155. That is still below the 27 before #106797.
- `planScales` cuts the text input down to `ratio` times the stored size, per axis, once the stored size is known. The stored size and every other detector stay the same.
- The cut only applies when it makes the padded canvas smaller, because a cut inside the same canvas saves no inference and only adds a resample.
- The characterisation snapshot records the new text sizes. A 1080p frame goes from a 928x576 canvas to 640x384. Small frames keep their input.
- The bench's `prod` point is now what its `fitted-global` point measured, so that point is gone, and its `fitted` point uses the same function.
- The bench's box-for-box check keeps production's kernels under `--no-kleidiai`. Before, kernel rounding flipped one borderline box and reported a drift that was not there.

| Text stage, PP-OCRv6 tiny | Budget canvas (#106797) | Stored-size canvas |
|---|---|---|
| Readable words fully visible (`dev/text-det-bench.ts`) | 18 of 7,155 | 22 of 7,155 |
| Readable words covered at least 90% | 99.5% | 99.4% |
| Mean ms per image, M4 Pro, 1 thread, NEON only, production size mix | 40.3 | 25.8 (−36%) |

- The two timings come from back-to-back runs. #106797 quotes 39.5 ms for the budget canvas from an earlier run.

body:
## Problem

One data warehouse schema has blocked its worker pod for tens of minutes at a time, every retry, for three days. Every other team's sync sharing that pod loses its heartbeat and retries with it.

- The schema is a Knock `users` table. Knock merges each user's custom traits into the user object as top-level keys, so the key set grows with the rows.
- `table_from_py_list` unions every key in a batch into columns and builds a dense column per key. Its cost follows rows x distinct keys, not rows.
- Measured on this repo's own conversion, cost per cell is flat at about 2.8 us and 9 bytes whatever the shape: 5M cells costs ~15 s and ~45 MB as 250k rows x 20 columns, as 50k x 100, and as 10k x 500.
- So a sparse-key source is quadratic in batch size. 3,000 such rows take 38.6 s and 79 MB. 59,353 of them extrapolate to roughly 4 hours and tens of gigabytes for a single conversion.
- The row cap (500,000) and the byte cap (200 MiB) both miss it. A Knock user is about 220 bytes on the wire, so 59k of them sit far under 200 MiB while the key union reaches five figures.
- The conversion runs on the event loop, so the activity stops heartbeating. Temporal times the activity out and the retry repeats the whole thing.

`_serialize_dict_columns` already covers the nested-dict form of this, added for MongoDB documents. Rows that flatten their custom keys to the top level slip past it.

## Changes

- A sparse-key source now yields small batches steadily instead of stalling its pod, so co-tenant syncs keep their heartbeats.
- `Batcher` caps its row buffer on `rows x distinct keys` as well as on rows and bytes.
- `DEFAULT_MAX_BUFFER_CELLS` is 10M, which is what a 20-column source already reaches at `DEFAULT_CHUNK_SIZE`. An ordinary batch flushes exactly where it did before.
- A flush that the cell cap triggers logs `batcher_flush_on_cell_cap` with the row and column counts. Nothing else in a run identifies which source has this row shape.
- The buffer's key set resets with the buffer, so the cap measures one batch at a time.

Measured end to end through `Batcher` on 3,000 sparse-key rows, with the cap lowered to 250k cells to keep the harness quick:

| | time | peak heap | batches |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | 38.6 s | 79 MB | 1 |
| after | 7.4 s | 2 MB | 6 |

The gap widens with row count, because only the uncapped side is quadratic.

> [!NOTE]
> This bounds the damage, it does not make the resulting table sensible. Knock's `users` table still resolves to tens of thousands of columns, now spread over many batches whose schemas the Delta write unions back together. Folding unknown Knock keys into a single JSON property column is the durable fix, and it changes the shape of a table a customer already queries, so it needs a separate decision. Worth watching `warehouse-sources-load` after this ships, in case the cost moves downstream rather than disappearing.

The alternative was to fix the Knock source alone. The cap sits in the batcher instead because the batcher is what bounds batch size, and because the next source with this row shape gets the same protection without anyone noticing it first.

## How did you test this code?

Five new unit tests in `test_batcher.py`, each naming a regression no existing test caught:

- Sparse-key rows never flush until the row or byte cap, which no test could see because both caps are blind to column growth. `test_batcher_flushes_sparse_key_rows_before_the_row_and_byte_caps` pins the flush at the exact row where the product crosses the cap.
- The new cap shrinks ordinary batches. `test_batcher_keeps_dense_rows_on_the_row_cap` holds a dense source on the row cap.
- The key set leaks across flushes, which would trip the cap on every later row forever. `test_batcher_cell_cap_resets_between_batches` drains twice and asserts the second batch matches the first.
- The cap fires silently, leaving no way to find the source responsible. `test_batcher_logs_the_shape_when_the_cell_cap_flushes` asserts the log and its counts.
- A source that yields pages rather than single rows takes the list branch, which is separate code. `test_batcher_cell_cap_applies_to_list_items` covers it.

> [!NOTE]
> Not run locally: this checkout cannot boot the Django test suite, so the tests were not executed through pytest here. CI is the first pytest run. They were executed by importing `test_batcher.py` directly and calling every zero-argument test: 36 passed, 0 failed, including all 33 that predate this change. The 21 parameterized cases in the file need pytest's generator and were not run; none touch the buffer path this changes.

The timing and memory figures above come from the harness described in Changes, run against this repo's `Batcher` and `table_from_py_list`. No manual test against a live Knock account.

- [ ] This change makes a previously flagged feature available to everyone <!-- release-status: fully-available -->

## 🤖 Agent context

**Agent:** Claude Code, Opus 5 (1M context)

Follow-up to #105434, which fixed the same class of failure in Bing Ads by streaming its report instead of materializing it. That one was a source holding a whole report in memory. This one is the pipeline's own conversion turning a small stream into a huge table, so the fix sits a layer down.

The quadratic cost was measured rather than reasoned about: the first harness compared JSON bytes per row against Arrow bytes per row and found the Arrow cost doubling with every doubling of rows while the JSON cost stayed flat. A second harness then showed cost tracks cells across three different shapes, which is what justifies a cell cap rather than a column cap.

## Problem

- The broadcast detail page is one stacked column: eleven metric cards of equal weight, then a large trend chart.
- It shows the raw workflow status ("Active") and "Sends immediately" for a broadcast that already went out.
- There is no way to see the email that was sent, or to send it again.

## Changes

- **Header:** a status tag that matches the list (Scheduled, Sending, Sent), and an **Actions** menu with "Stop and edit" and "Send again as a new broadcast".
- **Tabs:** Overview, Content and Runs.
- **Overview:** audience, schedule and subject on one row. The schedule shows the next send, or when the last one went out.
- **Performance:** a headline row (sent, then delivered, bounced, spam and failed as rates with counts), an engagement funnel (opened, clicked, clicked to opened), and top clicked links. The big chart is gone.
- **Content:** the email preview, with "Send test email".
- **Send again:** creates a draft copy with the same audience and email and opens it in the wizard, so a resend goes through review and launch like any send. The original is not touched.
- **Reuse, not new code:**
  - The link table is extracted from `WorkflowMetricsSummary` into a shared `EmailLinksTable`.
  - Link data comes from the existing per-link metric and `parseEmailLinkTotals`.
  - Totals load through `loadAppMetricsTotals` in a small `broadcastPerformanceLogic`, because the full workflow metrics logic depends on the workflow editor logic.
- **Status on a recurring broadcast:** between runs it now reads "Scheduled" rather than "Sent".

![real-compare-overview](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PostHog/pr-assets/969e5ddc832135597090ed2417f40a9d605f925f/2026/09/57c28c4a-0fb6-4859-a1c6-2005dc6f6575.png)

## Problem

Operators cannot request fresh research followed by a new implementation run when a report already has an implementation task. The normal pipeline skips another task unless automated replacement qualifies.

## Changes

- Operators can preview an inactive report with signals using `rerun_signal_report`, then use `--execute` to start a fresh summary workflow, including when its previous report status is `failed`.
- Operator invocation: `python manage.py rerun_signal_report --team-id <team-id> --report-id <report-uuid> --user-id <user-id> [--task-id <task-uuid>]`. Omit `--execute` for the dry run; include it to start research. Specify `--task-id` when the report has multiple linked implementation tasks. A retry of a `candidate` report requires no running summary workflow.
- Actionable research resumes the selected implementation task on its existing PR branch. A report without a task, or with a changed repository, gets a new linked task.
- The command checks project access, task control, credit and daily limits, free trials, pending replacements, and running workflows before starting work. A stranded `candidate` report can be retried when its workflow is no longer running.
- A server-only rerun flag creates a fresh TaskRun with the protected implementation stage from the verified report-task link, including after a manual run with no stage. Ordinary manual reruns keep their existing behavior. The free trial verdict is resolved before the report row lock is taken.
- The command leaves older PRs open for review. It does not override safety or actionability decisions. Signals billing charges once per report with a PR, so another run of an already billable report does not add a second Signals charge; a first PR for an unbilled report is chargeable.

Before:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Report already implemented] --> B[Normal research] --> C[Second implementation skipped]
    classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
    classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
    classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
    class A phGray;
    class B phBlue;
    class C phYellow;
```

After:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Operator command] --> B[Fresh research] --> C{Actionable?}
    C -->|Yes| D[New implementation run]
    C -->|No| E[Stop]
    classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
    classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
    classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
    class A,E phYellow;
    class B,D phBlue;
    class C phGray;
```

## How did you test this code?

- Ran the command, requested implementation, summary settle, and existing auto-start suites. The new cases cover dry-run safety, duplicate prevention, actionable reruns, and changed repositories.
- Ran focused Tasks facade tests for protected stage attribution from the verified report-task link, including a manual predecessor without a stage. Ordinary manual reruns remain unstamped.
- Exercised dry-run and execute paths against the local stack with the workflow start mocked and database changes rolled back. Verified the free-trial guard, previously failed report status, and stranded `candidate` retry.

## Problem

- The image-scrub sidecar runs zxing over every pixel of the decoded frame, so the code stage costs more CPU than the redaction rule needs.
- Every other detector reads the frame at the scale plan's ratio: large enough that anything still readable in the stored image was found.
- A code only leaks when a reader can decode it from the stored image, which is several times smaller than the frame.
- `CODE_FLOOR` pairs a size at the frame with a size in the stored image (96 against 280 source px), so no ratio for zxing's input follows from it.

## Changes

- The code stage costs 38% less on the production image-size mix. Every code still decodable from the stored image stays covered.
- `planScales` gives zxing the ratio times the stored scale, per axis as kept, capped at 1.
- From a scale of 0.85 up, zxing reads the frame as it is, because a resize that small costs more than zxing saves.
- `detectCodes` resizes the shared frame to that scale and maps each box back to frame coordinates, rounding outward.
- `CODE_FLOOR` becomes 3 against 1, in multiples of a code's size in the stored image, as `dev/code-bench.ts` measures it.
- Codes now take part in `bindingRatio()`. Faces still bind at 3.05, so no stored size changes.
- `dev/floors.ts` and the `plan` point of `dev/code-bench.ts` read codes at the plan's scale, so both measure what ships.

| Code stage | Full frame | Plan scale |
|---|---|---|
| Mean ms per image, M4 Pro, 1 thread, production size mix, resize included | 13.0 | 8.0 (−38%) |
| Codes still decodable from the stored image and left unredacted (`dev/code-bench.ts`) | 0 of 118 | 0 of 118 |

- On a c6g.4xlarge (Graviton2), the #106612 run measured −37% for zxing alone at this ratio.

## How did you test this code?

- `scale-plan.test.ts`: the rule 4 test also checks the code detector. It fails when the code scale drops to half the ratio.
- `qr.test.ts`: the detector test also reads at 0.75 of the frame. It fails when boxes stay in zxing's coordinates.
- The characterisation snapshot pins the code scale for each shape class. Its frame, text and stored rows do not change.
- A script outside the diff timed the code stage on the 248 labelled images of the text benchmark, at both scales.
- Not run: the Graviton bench on this exact plan. The 0.85 cut-off only makes zxing read more than the ratio needs.

## Problem

A BigQuery source keeps retrying and failing when the table or view it reads is guarded by a deprecation check the customer's own BigQuery team added to it. Error tracking surfaced one such [issue](https://us.posthog.com/project/2/error_tracking/01a0d8ec-8ea8-77b0-9334-f1529c4a1db2): a `BadRequest` from the query-job status poll, with a message telling the customer to migrate to a replacement table/view.

The same table fails identically on every retry, since the check the customer added is deterministic, not transient.

## Changes

- Added a `get_non_retryable_errors` entry matching BigQuery's stable "Deprecated legacy table/view" wording. Retrying can't recover it, so the sync now stops with a message pointing the customer at updating their source's table/view.
- Matched on the stable phrase only, not the volatile project name or job id that surround it in the real message.

This mirrors the existing entries for other deterministic table/view problems in the same file (`failed to parse view`, `is ambiguous`, `Unrecognized name:`).

## How did you test this code?

Added `test_bigquery_deprecated_legacy_table_is_non_retryable`, parameterized over two messages with different project names and job ids, to `products/warehouse_sources/backend/temporal/data_imports/sources/bigquery/tests/test_source.py`. It catches the regression this PR fixes: the error is recognized as non-retryable regardless of the volatile ids around the stable wording.

Ran the full `test_source.py` suite locally. All non-retryable-error tests (56) pass. 7 unrelated tests error on a database connection unavailable in this sandbox; not run.

<!-- /posthog-self-driving-origin:01a0d8e1-4d55-7618-95c7-35809924ee62 -->

## Changes

- **One scoring function.** `score_reports(team_id, report_ids, persist=..., now=...)` scores reports with every model in the manifest. With `persist=True` it writes one `ranking_score` artefact per report and one `inbox_ranking_report_scored` event per report and model.
- **Train/serve parity.** Each model's matrix comes from its own `FeatureSet.build_matrix`, the same code the dag trains and grades with. A test holds the served score equal to the dag's `score_pool` value for the same booster and vector.
- **Model store.** It reads `manifest.json` and each model from the app object store, never the dataset bucket. It checks the metadata contract and every loaded booster's `feature_names`. It caches loaded models by immutable key.
- **Failure rules:**

| Case | Result |
| --- | --- |
| No manifest yet | Empty result, nothing written |
| Served model fails to load (missing file, unknown `model_kind`, feature mismatch) | Raises |
| Other model fails to load | `skipped` result with the reason |
| No served vector for a report | No row, `reason="no_vector"` |
| No challenger vector | `skipped` result, `no_vector` |
| Tabular model | `skipped`, "feature set tabular is not served yet" |

- **Vector reader.** One parameterized ClickHouse point read per rendering, scoped by `team_id` and `document_id IN`. It drops a report whose newest row is a tombstone. It pages at the new `INBOX_RANKING_SCORING_BATCH_SIZE` setting (default 500).
- **Sink.** It writes only for reports of the given team, after the whole batch is scored. Events go through `ph_scoped_capture`.
- **Model contract move (mechanical).** `model_mismatch`, `model_feature_set`, `readable_head_names` and `trained_head_files` move from the dag's `unseen.py` to `backend/ranking/model_contract.py`. The dag imports them from there. `trained_head_files` now takes the known head names as an argument, so the backend does not import the dag's `heads.py`. The dag passes `HEADS_BY_NAME`, so its behavior does not change.
- The copied `metadata.json` on each result leaves out `feature_names`, which is 1536 names for an embedding model. `feature_set` and `feature_schema_version` identify them.
- A model that did not load has `feature_schema_version` 0 on its skipped result, because the schema requires an integer and no contract was read.

## How did you test this code?

New `products/signals/backend/test/test_ranking_scoring.py`, run locally against Postgres and ClickHouse:

- Parity: fails if feature order, dtype or feature set drift between the dag and the scorer. A reversed column order made it fail.
- Store: a served load failure raises; a challenger load failure is skipped while the served model loads; a cached key is not read again but takes the new roles.
- Vector reader (ClickHouse): a tombstone hides an older live row, another team's row and another rendering never return, and the read pages at the batch size.
- Scorer: one read per rendering whatever the number of models, `no_vector` for a missing served vector, skipped results for challengers, and valid rows with the manifest's `served_key`. `persist=False` writes and captures nothing, and a report of another team is not written.
- The dag suite under `products/signals/dags/inbox_ranking/tests/` passes after the move.

Not run: semgrep (not installed in the sandbox). Repo-wide mypy was started but had not finished when this PR opened.

## Problem

- The CDC delete-enrichment alarm fires on correct loads, so it no longer tells a real data loss apart from normal traffic.
- A buffered load reads several minutes of changes as one batch. An `UPDATE` that sets a column to NULL and the `DELETE` of that row often land in the same batch.
- Enrichment correctly fills the `DELETE` row from that `UPDATE`, so the column stays NULL.
- `verify_delete_enrichment` then compares the row with the target's state before the batch and counts the NULL as a nulled column (`warehouse_load_cdc_delete_enrichment_violations_total`).
- A related bug: `enrich_delete_rows` took the last non-DELETE row for the key anywhere in the batch, including a re-insert after the delete.
  On the history lane, the delete row then carries the re-inserted values instead of the values it removed.

## Changes

- `verify_delete_enrichment` skips a `DELETE` that follows another change to the same key in the batch. Its previous state is that change, not the target.
- `enrich_delete_rows` fills a `DELETE` only from the last change **before** it, as its docstring already says. A later re-insert no longer leaks into it.
- A `DELETE` with no earlier change in the batch is still filled from the target and still verified, so a real enrichment gap still fires the alarm.

## How did you test this code?

- `test_ignores_a_null_the_source_set` gains an `UPDATE` then `DELETE` case. It fails without the verifier change.
- `test_unenriched_delete_is_reported` gains a `DELETE` then re-insert case, which checks the verifier still reports a delete that has no earlier change.
- `test_delete_uses_the_last_change_before_it` adds a re-insert after the delete. It fails without the enrichment change.
- Not run: a load against a real Delta table with a production-shaped batch.

## Problem

- Code that asks Jev a System One question can reach only TypeSafe, a third-party service approved for experiments without customer data.
- The Go ai-gateway already serves `posthog/hogference/jevk5-fp8-0.2`, a Jev build PostHog hosts, on `POST /v1/systemone`.
- No shared client reaches it, the way `build_openai_client` reaches the gateway for chat models.
- The next layer, #106432, needs one for the turn suggestion judge.

## Changes

- `build_system_one_client` returns a client for the ai-gateway where `AI_GATEWAY_URL` and `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` are set.
- TypeSafe is opt-in. A caller that passes a `TypeSafeFallback` gets TypeSafe where no gateway is configured, through the existing egress budget.
- A caller that passes no fallback never reaches TypeSafe. Without a gateway it gets `SystemOneNotConfigured`, so customer data cannot reach a third party by accident.
- The fallback names its own model, because TypeSafe runs a different Jev build with different calibration.
- The gateway client sends the gateway key as a bearer and the usual `X-PostHog-*` attribution headers, and bills the key owner's wallet.
- The gateway client refuses a choice question with more than 16 options before it sends, because JevK5 answers one letter per option.
- It refuses a non-https gateway URL unless it points at this machine, so the key never travels in clear.
- Mechanical: the System One request and answer types move from `posthog/egress/typesafe/` to `posthog/llm/system_one.py`, so both servers share them. The TypeSafe errors now subclass the shared ones.
- No behavior change for users: nothing calls the builder until #106432.
- Not moved: `products/ml_inference` keeps its own gateway client for now. It could move to this builder once its owners agree.

## How did you test this code?

- New `posthog/llm/test_system_one_client.py` catches these regressions:
  - picking TypeSafe while the gateway is configured, or the wrong model for a server;
  - reaching TypeSafe for a caller that passed no fallback;

body:
## Problem

- A resumed incremental ClickHouse sync on a datetime cursor starts from the wrong point.
- On a column typed with a timezone west of the server, the sync silently skips rows. East of the server, and on every sub-second cursor, it reads rows again.
- The cause is the cursor parameter. clickhouse-connect renders a Python datetime as a whole-second string, and ClickHouse parses that string in the column's timezone.

Resuming at `00:00:00.000004` UTC on a table where 3 rows are newer, against a local ClickHouse:

| Column type | Rows read before | Rows read after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DateTime64(9, 'UTC')` | 27 | 3 |
| `DateTime64(9)` | 27 | 3 |
| `DateTime64(9, 'America/New_York')` | 0 | 3 |

## Changes

- Incremental syncs on `DateTime` / `DateTime64` columns now resume exactly after the saved cursor, whatever the column's timezone.
- The cursor binds as integer epoch microseconds through `fromUnixTimestamp64Micro`, which names one instant with no timezone to interpret.
- A naive cursor is UTC, like the naive Arrow timestamps it comes from. A numeric cursor keeps its old meaning of epoch seconds.
- The same binding applies to the incremental row count, so progress reporting counts the same rows the query reads.
- `Date` cursors and integer cursors do not change.

> [!NOTE]
> Precision stops at microseconds. The shared cursor model parses the saved value with dateutil, which truncates `DateTime64(7..9)` values to microseconds before the source sees them. The truncation goes down, so rows in the same microsecond as the cursor are read again and never skipped. Keeping nanoseconds needs a change to cursor storage for every source.

Not changed here: row filters on timestamp columns bind through the same clickhouse-connect path and have the same whole-second and timezone behavior. The shared row-filter renderer needs a per-source hook to fix that.

## How did you test this code?

- A new test runs `clickhouse_source` against a real ClickHouse and resumes from a cursor 4 µs into the data, for three cases: sub-second on a UTC column, a column with a timezone, and a naive cursor. It checks the rows read and `rows_to_sync`.
- All three cases fail on master and pass with this change.
- Not yet run in CI: the test needs ClickHouse's HTTP port 8123 in the test environment.

## Release status

- [ ] This change is behind a feature flag and is not available to users <!-- release-status: behind-feature-flag -->
- [ ] This change makes a previously flagged feature available to everyone <!-- release-status: fully-available -->

**Autonomy:** Human-driven (agent-assisted)

**Agent:** Claude Code, Claude Opus 5.5

- Found while building #106716 (paged reads past host query limits), and split out from it on a fresh master branch. #106716 merged first; master is merged in, and the paged read binds the cursor through the same `_last_value_param`.
- Skills invoked: `/writing-tests`, `/reviewing-with-coderabbit`, `/writing-pr-descriptions`.
- CodeRabbit CLI with `--deep`: 1 finding, rejected. It asked for nanosecond binding on `DateTime64(9)`. The saved cursor reaches the source already truncated to microseconds (see the note above), so the source has no nanoseconds to bind.
- CodeRabbit PR review, fractional epoch cursors: rejected. It showed `0.000249 * 1_000_000` truncating to 248. At real epoch sizes (for example `1767225600.000000` to `.999999`) every microsecond value converts exactly, and near 1970 the error only re-reads a row, never skips one.

## Problem

- The broadcast wizard ([#105625](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/105625)) needs the same save behavior as the workflow editor: saves one at a time, and "edited elsewhere" events held back while a save is in flight.
- That behavior lives inline in `workflowLogic`, so #105625 re-implemented it with its own in-flight counter, wait loops and deferred-event cache.
- This PR moves the generic part into one helper so the wizard can use it instead of a second copy.

## Changes

- New `ResourceSaveQueue` (`Workflows/resourceSaveQueue.ts`), a plain class kept in the logic's cache:
  - `run(save)` queues saves one at a time, so a queued save fences on the stamp the save before it wrote.
  - `classify(event)` sorts a resource-edited event into `ignore` (another resource, or the echo of our own save), `defer` (a save or load is in flight), or `external`.
  - `takeDeferred()` hands back the event held while busy, once.
- `workflowLogic` now uses it for its save chain, its event sorting and its deferred event. The `deferredResourceEdited` reducer and its action are gone.
- No behavior change. Payload routing, staging, the 409 policy and the conflict banner stay in `workflowLogic`. Its busy check still counts saves whose success work hasn't run yet, as before.
- It's a plain class rather than a kea builder, because kea-typegen can't see actions a custom builder injects.

## How did you test this code?

- The existing workflow editor suites pass unchanged: `workflowLogic.autosave.test.ts` (queued saves) and `workflowLogic.externalEdits.test.ts` (deferral, own echo, Keep mine, 409 cases), 92 tests.
- New `resourceSaveQueue.test.ts`: saves run in order even when one fails, each event case, and a held event is handed over once.
- In the browser, on a local workflow:

  - Renaming it from another client through the API: the open editor received the event, re-fetched the workflow once and showed the new name, with no banner. Master behaves the same.
- Not tested in the browser: an external edit landing exactly mid-save. The deferral path is covered by the external-edit suite.

body:
## Problem

- ClickHouse syncs from hosts with per-query caps fail on every run once a table outgrows the cap, and the user cannot raise it.
- Tinybird's ClickHouse interface is one such host. It caps each query's result at 500 MiB and each query's memory.
- The source reads a table with one unbounded `SELECT`, so the host answers `TOO_MANY_ROWS_OR_BYTES` (code 396) or `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` (code 241).
- The host rejects the query before it sends a row. No progress is saved, so every retry fails the same way.
- The only workaround today is to move a row filter forward by hand, one window per sync.

## Changes

- These tables now sync. On either error, the source reads the table again in pages instead of one query.
- A page is a range of key values, not a row count, so rows with equal keys never split across two pages:
  - one query finds the upper bound: the key of the n-th row after the lower bound (`ORDER BY key LIMIT 1 OFFSET n-1`)
  - the page query reads `key > lower AND key <= upper`
- The key is the incremental cursor for an incremental sync. A full refresh uses the sorting-key columns as a tuple.
- A full refresh with no sorting key, or with a nullable key column, raises the original error. A NULL fails every comparison, so paging would drop those rows.
- Pages start at 500k rows and halve on each rejection, down to 1k rows. Below that, the original error raises.
- A page that fails after it read rows raises instead of paging again, because a retry would read those rows twice in append-mode tables.
- Bounds travel as `toString()` output, and ClickHouse parses them back into the column type. A Python round trip truncates `DateTime64(9)` to microseconds, and paging then stalls.
- Hosts without these caps see no change: the single query stays the first attempt.
- Mechanical: `_build_query` moves its WHERE assembly into `_build_conditions`. The SQL it emits does not change.

> [!NOTE]
> Where to look first: the `read_batches` loop in `clickhouse_source`. Each page runs one extra bound query that reads the key column from the lower bound onward. That is cheap when the key leads the sorting key, and a column scan per page otherwise.

Related: #106050 makes code 396 non-retryable. With this PR, that error reaches the rule only when paging cannot fit under the cap.

## How did you test this code?

- New tests run `clickhouse_source` against a real ClickHouse. `max_result_rows` with `http_wait_end_of_query=1` makes the server reject a query before it sends a row, the same shape Tinybird returns.
  - Incremental first sync and resume: every row exactly once, in cursor order. The data has equal cursor values on page bounds and values 500 ns apart, which catches a split tie group and a truncated bound.
  - Full refresh on a two-column sorting key: every row exactly once.
  - The original error raises when a tie group exceeds the cap at the minimum page size, and for a full refresh with no sorting key. These catch an endless retry loop.
- A mock test checks that a limit error after rows were read raises and does not page. This catches duplicate rows in append-mode tables.
- Checked by hand: with bounds read back as Python values instead of `toString()`, the tests hang, which is the stall described above.
- Not checked: Tinybird itself (whether its interface accepts `OFFSET`, and whether a per-query time limit hits a single page). Not yet run in CI: the new tests need ClickHouse's HTTP port 8123 in the test environment.

## Release status

- [x] No feature flag controls this change <!-- release-status: no-feature-flag -->
- [ ] This change is behind a feature flag and is not available to users <!-- release-status: behind-feature-flag -->
- [ ] This change makes a previously flagged feature available to everyone <!-- release-status: fully-available -->

## Automatic notifications

- [ ] Publish to changelog?

## Docs update

None.

## 🤖 Agent context

**Autonomy:** Human-driven (agent-assisted)

**Agent:** Claude Code, Claude Opus 5.5

- Skills invoked: `/writing-tests`, `/writing-dataclasses` (the paging state stayed in a local generator, no dataclass), `/reviewing-with-coderabbit`, `/writing-pr-descriptions`.
- CodeRabbit CLI with `--deep`: 0 findings. It ran before the last commit, which only changes test typing.
- Duplicate search: found #106050, which complements this change (see above). Nothing else.

- Session decision: the same work found that datetime incremental cursors lose sub-second precision and shift by the column's timezone. That fix ships separately in #106727.

## Problem

- In a space's Activity list, a person can act on only one session at a time.
- The sidebar session list already supports multi-select and bulk actions. The Activity list does not.
- Why: the author of this change asked for the same multi-select and bulk actions in this view.

## Changes

- Cmd/Ctrl-click adds or removes one session. Shift-click selects a range. Esc clears the selection.
- A drag selects every session it passes. In this list, the drag can start on a row, because the rows are not draggable here.
- A click at the end of a drag does not open the row under the pointer.
- A bar under the list and the right-click menu act on the whole selection: Pin, File to… and Archive. Archive asks first.
- This list does not offer "Add to Command Center". The sidebar keeps it.
- The Activity list keeps its own selection store (`TaskSelectionScope`). The shared store made the sidebar prune the feed's selection to its own rows, and it showed two bulk bars.
- Mechanical: the sidebar hooks read the store from the scope, and the default is the old global store, so the sidebar does not change.
- The cards style and other feeds do not change. Only the list style of the space Activity view gets selection.

## Problem

- Most broadcast drafts never launch because they stall on the email sender. Most of those teams have no email sender set up at all.
- With no sender, the content step's only way forward is "Connect email sender", which opens the Channels page in a new tab and leaves the broadcast behind.
- A broadcast could launch with a sender whose domain was never verified, so every email in the send failed.

## Changes

- With no email sender, the content step shows a banner with "Set up email sender". It opens the existing workflows email setup modal inline, and "Save & finish later" selects the new sender in the broadcast.
- With an unverified sender selected, the content step warns and offers "Verify domain", which reopens the same modal on its DNS records.
- The review step blocks Launch while the chosen sender can't send: its domain is unverified, the sender was deleted, or the senders list hasn't loaded yet. Drafts can still be written and saved.
- The setup flow is the existing `EmailSetupModal`, and the sender picker is still the shared `EmailTemplater`. Only the banner and the review guard are new.

## Problem

- A shared metric attached to an experiment could share a uuid with an inline metric, so one metric showed the other's results.
- The backend result rows and the frontend both key metric results by uuid.
- #59729 closed collisions between two inline metrics. Two paths still created an inline and a shared metric with one uuid:
  - Promoting an inline metric to a shared one kept its uuid. The `configuring-experiment-analytics` skill told agents to promote "with the same query", then attach, while the inline copy stayed.
  - A PATCH that sends only `saved_metrics_ids` never re-checked the stored inline metrics.

## Changes

- Creating a shared metric always assigns a new uuid. The API ignores a `query.uuid` that the caller sends. Updates keep the stored uuid, as before.
- Attaching shared metrics re-checks the stored inline lists. A list that collides goes through the existing uuid assignment, so the inline copy gets a fresh uuid. The shared metric keeps its uuid.
- The ordering sync keeps an old inline uuid when a linked shared metric still owns it. Without this, an experiment that already stores a collision got a 400 (`primary_metrics_ordered_uuids is missing UUIDs`) on attach. On master it already gets that 400 when someone edits its inline metrics. This is the part to review most closely.
- The skill now tells agents to omit `query.uuid` when promoting, and to drop the inline metric in the same `experiment-update` that attaches the shared one.
- Mechanical: presentation API tests read the uuid the API assigns instead of posting a fixed one.
- No change needed: the frontend "Duplicate" action (the API now ignores its client uuid), the MCP create tool description (it never mentions `query.uuid`), copy-to-project (it copies rows through the ORM, not the service), and clone (it already regenerates uuids).

> [!NOTE]
> When an attach regenerates an inline uuid, the activity log and the "experiment updated" event record a metrics change and an ordering change.

## How did you test this code?

- `test_create_saved_metric_with_minimum_fields` gains a case with a client uuid. It catches a create that keeps the caller's uuid.
- `test_attaching_saved_metric_regenerates_stored_inline_uuid_that_collides` covers primary, secondary and no collision. It catches an attach that leaves the inline copy on the shared uuid.
  - The stored inline metric uses an unknown event name, which proves the re-sent list passes validation.
  - The no-collision case asserts the stored lists stay unchanged.
- `test_update_keeps_saved_metric_uuid_in_ordering_when_stored_inline_copy_collides` catches the 400 on an experiment that already stores a collision. It covers attaching another shared metric and re-sending the inline metrics.
- All five collision cases fail with the service changes reverted.
- `hogli test` ran on the service, saved-metric service, saved-metric API and presentation API test files.
- Locally, `TestExperimentCRUD::test_can_filter_experiments_by_status` and two `test_experiment_admin.py` tests fail on the unchanged base as well, because of local database state. CI is authoritative for those.
- Not checked: production data. After deploy, recheck production for inline and shared metrics that share a uuid.

body: ## Problem An MCP server owner who cares about quality mostly wants to know whether a tool got worse, for example after a deploy or a client update. The Tool quality table only compared call volume with the previous period, so a tool whose error rate or latency regressed looked the same as last week. Stacked on #106040 (which is stacked on #106038). ## Changes - Error rate and p95 show a small red or green arrow when they moved meaningfully versus the previous period, for example "39% ↑16pt" or "6s ↑596%". Hovering shows the previous value. - These columns get color because they have a clear good direction. Call volume stays neutral, since a surge can be good or bad. - "Meaningful" means: - at least 20 calls in both periods; - error rate moved 2 points or more and clears a two-proportion z-score of 2, so normal noise on a busy tool is not flagged; - p95 got 25% slower or 20% faster. - The thresholds are starting points, not tuned. - Hovering Sessions shows the previous session share, for example "84% of sessions, was 60% in the previous period". - The error rate, p95, and Sessions cells stay on one line. The session share from #106040 wrapped at laptop widths. - `MCPToolQualityRowsQuery` rows gain `previous_error_rate_pct`, `previous_p95_duration_ms` and `previous_sessions`, computed in the same scan. The response gains `previousTotalSessions`. Before (this PR's base, #106040) and after, demo data with planted regressions, 1440px window: | Before | After | |---|---| | | | ## How did you test this code? - Extended `test_tool_quality_tables.py`. The new tests catch previous-window metrics leaking into or out of the current window, a tool with no previous calls getting non-null previous values, and the previous session totals. - On a devbox with seeded regressions at 1440px: - a planted error spike and a planted slowdown are flagged; - a significant error-rate drop is flagged green; - steady tools with ±2 points of random noise are not flagged; - every row stays on one line; - the table fits its card. ## Release status - [x] No feature flag controls this change - [ ] This change is behind a feature flag and is not available to users - [ ] This change makes a previously flagged feature available to everyone ## Automatic notifications - [ ] Publish to changelog? ## Docs update None. ## 🤖 Agent context **Autonomy:** Human-driven (agent-assisted) **Agent:** Claude Code, Claude Opus 5.5 - The first version used a flat 2-point threshold. On seeded data it flagged steady tools whose error rate wobbles about ±2 points week to week, so a significance check was added. - A separate session-share trend column was considered and left out: it mostly repeats the calls trend, so the previous share went into the Sessions hover instead. - Pre-PR review: CodeRabbit CLI plus two adversarial reviewers (Claude Opus, Claude Fable). Fixed: threshold rules moved to `qualityChange.ts` with a parameterized test (all three raised it); the z-test now runs on error counts instead of rounded rates; a p95 of 0 (no timed calls) no longer reads as "100% faster"; new response fields are required; markers have an aria-label; tooltips format values like the cells; header tooltips explain the arrows; a test covers a previous period with no durations. Dismissed: switching to `@posthog/icons` arrows, since that package has no up/down arrow glyph; treating a sub-millisecond previous p95 as a regression, since 0 means no timing data here.

body:
## Problem

- Per-scout tool scoping, enforcement, and the scout settings picker are all blocked: nothing in the app can read the MCP tool definitions that already ship in the repository.
- The two definition files under `services/mcp/schema/` have exactly one server-side reader, `posthog/api/oauth/mcp_resource_scopes.py`, and its loader is private and returns required scopes only. It cannot say what tools exist, what each one does, or whether a scout could hold the scopes it needs.
- With no shared loader, a handful of tests and product modules open the JSON by path themselves.

Closes #106595

<!-- posthog-self-driving-origin:01a0d87f-9fd5-762d-b0d2-ac6a9296a0d6 -->
## Origin

- Issues: [#106595](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/issues/106595)
- First signal: 2026-09-25
- Inbox report: [open](https://us.posthog.com/project/2/inbox/reports/01a0d87f-9fd5-762d-b0d2-ac6a9296a0d6)
- Likely cause: [`df33661`](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/commit/df336612c80caf3c4350a8b09dd5f588fd155a8a)
- Task started by: auto-start, after the report was rated P2 and ready to fix
<!-- /posthog-self-driving-origin:01a0d87f-9fd5-762d-b0d2-ac6a9296a0d6 -->

## Changes

- **Shared loader** (`posthog/mcp_tool_definitions.py`): merges both definition files with the generated set winning, which is the precedence `getToolDefinitions()` in `services/mcp/src/tools/toolDefinitions.ts` and the OAuth module already use. Returns typed, frozen `McpToolDefinition` values, read once per process.
- **OAuth module reads the loader** instead of merging the files itself. The advertised consent scopes are unchanged; the keyed-merge test moved to the loader, where the merge now lives.
- **New endpoint** `GET /api/projects/:id/signals/scout/configs/tool_catalogue/`, behind `signal_scout:read`. Read-only, side effect free, and identical for every project, so the rendered body is built once per process.

Each entry answers what a picker has to know before it can offer a tool:

| Field | What it answers |
| --- | --- |
| `holdable` | Can any scout run hold every scope the tool requires? |
| `missing_scopes` | What the scout has to be granted on top of the baseline `signals_scout` preset, or what no scout can reach |
| `feature_flag`, `feature_flag_behavior`, `feature_flag_variant`, `hidden_when_flag_on` | The flag gate, so a caller can resolve it for one project |
| `required_scopes`, `read_only`, `requires_ai_consent`, `feature_entitlement` | The remaining gates the MCP server applies |

The response also returns the scout scope presets with their resolved scopes, and the write scopes a person can grant to one scout, so a surface can say why a tool is out of reach instead of only hiding it.

Two deliberate calls, both different from the tracking issue:

- **Superseded tools are dropped; flag-gated tools are not.** Dropping every flagged tool would remove about a quarter of the catalogue, including whole product areas that ship behind a rollout flag, and a project whose flag is on could then never pick those tools. The gate resolves per project, and evaluating hundreds of flags inside a read endpoint would add latency and a failure mode, so the endpoint reports the gate and the caller resolves it. Superseded tools have successors and are dropped outright.
- **The full tool `description` is not in the listing.** It runs to several kilobytes on the query tools. Entries carry `summary` instead.

## How did you test this code?

Automated only. No manual testing, and no UI consumes the endpoint yet.

- `posthog/test/test_mcp_tool_definitions.py` (new): the generated definition wins on a name both files hold, a hand-written-only tool still loads, and the real committed files parse. Catches a flipped merge order, which would describe a tool the server does not serve, and a loader that silently reads one file.
- `posthog/api/oauth/test_mcp_resource_scopes.py`: unchanged coverage, retargeted at the shared loader.
- `TestScoutHarnessToolCatalogueAPI` in `products/signals/backend/test/test_scout_harness_api.py` (new): the endpoint returns the catalogue with the scout postures, leaves superseded tools out, reports `holdable` and `missing_scopes` against the scout scope sets rather than the full MCP set, and accepts a `signal_scout:read` key. The scope case catches the "no scopes declared" rejection that a custom action falls into without explicit `required_scopes`.

`hogli build:openapi` regenerated `products/signals/frontend/generated/`; no file there was hand-edited.

## Release status

## Automatic notifications

- [ ] Publish to changelog?

## Docs update

The scout harness guide documents the catalogue source, filtering, and API path. The endpoint has no user-facing surface yet.

## 🤖 Agent context

**Autonomy:** Fully autonomous

**Agent:** Claude Code, Opus 5

- No duplicate: `gh pr list --state open --search "mcp tool catalogue scout"` found no PR against these paths.
- Public artifact: the diff carries no material from the agent session. Every value in it comes from this repository.
- Skills invoked: `/improving-drf-endpoints`, `/writing-dataclasses`, `/writing-code-comments`, `/writing-tests`, `/writing-pr-descriptions`, `/writing-simplified-technical-english`. CodeRabbit CLI was skipped: this is a cloud task run.
- Decisions along the way: the first shape read the pre-merged `tool-definitions-all.json`, which is byte-identical to the merge today. The loader merges the two source files instead, so the precedence invariant stays next to the code that depends on it rather than depending on a third artifact staying in sync. The API path uses `tool_catalogue` to satisfy the repository URL naming rule. The MCP tool name remains unchanged. The CI fix uses Codex, GPT-6.

body:
## Problem

Someone syncing E2B gets an inventory of sandboxes, templates and snapshots, but no numbers. There is no way to chart a sandbox's CPU, memory or disk usage, no team capacity figures, and no template build history. Those are the only quantitative data E2B exposes.

The gaps are long-standing entries in `COVERAGE_GAPS_APPENDIX.md`, not new vendor endpoints.

## Changes

- `sandbox_metrics` charts CPU, memory and disk over time for each sandbox. It fans out from the sandbox list, one request per sandbox, so it starts unselected.
- `sandbox_metrics_latest` shows current usage, one row per sandbox. It batches up to 100 sandbox ids per request, so a team with 1000 sandboxes costs 10 requests rather than 1000.
- `template_builds` shows each template's build history: status, timestamps and the resources each build provisioned.
- `team_metrics` charts concurrent sandboxes and sandbox start rate. It needs a new optional Team ID field, because E2B takes the team in the request path even though the API key already identifies it.
- A table that needs the Team ID starts unselected and names the missing value, rather than failing its first sync.
- Every new table syncs full refresh, like the three that already exist. The metrics endpoints do take `start` and `end` filters, but the spec documents no ordering guarantee, and a fan-out child's ascending watermark would advance past sandboxes a partial run has not reached yet.

Three audited endpoints were skipped, with the reasoning recorded in the appendix:

- `GET /teams` is the only path in the spec that does not accept `ApiKeyAuth`, so the team-scoped key this source stores cannot call it. It also returns the team's live `apiKey`, which must not reach a warehouse table. The gap's rationale does not hold either: `ListedSandbox`, `Template` and `SnapshotInfo` carry no `teamID`.
- `GET /teams/{teamID}/metrics/max` returns one `{timestamp, value}` object per metric, so it is a scalar per call rather than a table, and it is the max of the `team_metrics` series.
- `GET /templates/{templateID}/builds/{buildID}/status` is a second fan-out hop costing one request per build. Its only non-log fields already arrive in `template_builds`.

Mechanical: the regenerated config module, the `SOURCES.md` library column, and the endpoint dataclass gaining the fields the shared fan-out helper reads.

Nothing looks different in the UI beyond one extra optional text field on the E2B connection form and four extra rows in the table picker.

## How did you test this code?

Automated only. No E2B account or API key was available in this sandbox, so no request reached the live API. Every endpoint, response shape, auth scheme and query parameter came from the vendor's OpenAPI spec: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/e2b-dev/infra/main/spec/openapi.yml

New transport tests, each aimed at a regression no existing test caught:

- The fan-out child stamps the parent id onto rows (`sandbox_metrics` rows carry no sandbox id of their own, so without it every row is unattributable and the primary key collides across sandboxes).
- The child sends no `limit`, which the endpoint does not document.
- `template_builds` reads the `builds` key (the response is the template object, so a missing selector syncs the whole object as one row).
- Fan-out resume state lands in its own slot, not in `next_token`, and a resumed run skips completed parents.
- The batched iterator turns one page of sandboxes into one `sandbox_ids` request and keys rows by the map key.
- The batched iterator walks past page one and seeds from a saved cursor.
- An empty sandbox page sends no metrics request (the `sandbox_ids` parameter is required).
- The Team ID reaches the path only after validation, so a traversal-shaped value is refused before any request.
- The message `_require_team_id` raises is one the source classifies as non-retryable.

Source-level tests cover the `should_sync_default` gating and the per-schema credential check that reports the missing Team ID without probing.

Not run: the database-backed and object-store suites, because this sandbox has no Postgres and no SeaweedFS. `hogli` could not boot the stack here, so the checks on this PR are the first full run.

## Release status

- [x] No feature flag controls this change <!-- release-status: no-feature-flag -->

## Automatic notifications

- [ ] Publish to changelog?

## Docs update

The source's user-facing doc still lives in the repo at `products/warehouse_sources/backend/temporal/data_imports/sources/e2b/e2b.md`, pending a move to posthog.com. It is updated here with the new tables, the Team ID field, and the cost difference between the two metrics tables.

## 🤖 Agent context

**Autonomy:** Fully autonomous

**Agent:** Claude Code, Opus 5

Skills invoked: `/implementing-warehouse-sources`, `/writing-tests`, `/writing-pr-descriptions`.

No duplicate: `gh pr list --state open` found no open PR touching the E2B source, by branch name, title, or the maintainer's own open PRs.

Decisions worth flagging for review. The audit's note on `GET /teams` claimed it resolves a `teamID` stamped on sandboxes, templates and snapshots; the spec shows no such field on any of those schemas, which is why that endpoint is skipped rather than deferred. Incremental sync was considered for the metrics endpoints and rejected on the ordering and fan-out watermark reasoning above. The batched `sandbox_metrics_latest` iterator is hand-rolled because the declarative fan-out issues one request per parent and cannot express a 100-id batch.

Public artifact: nothing in this PR draws on non-public material. The endpoint behavior came from the vendor's public OpenAPI spec, and the test fixtures are invented from the schemas in it.

body:
## Problem

A Dynatrace user can sync the metric catalog but not a single metric value, and cannot sync synthetic monitoring at all. The endpoint-coverage audit recorded both as long-standing gaps.

- The `metrics` table lists metric descriptors only, because the source calls `GET /api/v2/metrics`. Nothing reads `GET /api/v2/metrics/query`, so no timeseries values are syncable.
- The entity inventory is hardcoded to `HOST`, `SERVICE`, `APPLICATION` and `PROCESS_GROUP`. Kubernetes, disks, queues, databases and custom devices are served by the same endpoint with a different type selector.
- No synthetic endpoint is wired up, so the availability side of Dynatrace is absent.

## Changes

Ten new tables. Four endpoints were verified against the Dynatrace API reference before building; two of the audit's claims turned out to be wrong and are corrected below.

- `metric_data_points` syncs hourly metric values for up to 10 metric keys the user names in a new optional **Metric keys** field. One row per metric, dimension tuple and timestamp, keyed on all three.
- Seven entity tables: `databases`, `disks`, `queues`, `kubernetes_clusters`, `kubernetes_nodes`, `cloud_applications`, `custom_devices`. Same request shape as the existing four, different `entitySelector` type.
- `synthetic_monitors` syncs monitor name, type and enabled state.
- `synthetic_executions` syncs on-demand executions, incrementally, merging on `executionId`.

Decisions a reviewer should check:

- `/api/v2/metrics/query` returns each series as two index-aligned arrays, `timestamps` and `values`, which no warehouse query can use. The source flattens them into data point rows. The series identity comes from the sorted `dimensionMap`, because the id has to be part of the primary key and `dimensions` is deprecated.
- The metrics query rejects a request that names no metric. The table stays in the picker either way, and `get_endpoint_permissions` reports the missing keys as the table's reason, so a user sees why before selecting it rather than after a failed sync.
- Its scope probe hits the descriptor endpoint, not the query endpoint. Both sit behind `metrics.read`, and a probe with no metric selector could never separate a missing scope from a malformed request.
- Synthetic monitors read the **v1** listing. The v2 equivalent needs the broad `settings.read` scope and its docs say only browser and multi-protocol monitors are supported today. Both listings return the same fields.
- Dynatrace serves at most 6 hours of synthetic executions, so an older watermark would ask for a window it refuses. The incremental cursor is clamped to that window, and merge accumulates history across syncs.

Corrections to the audit notes:

- `DATABASE` is not a Dynatrace entity type. The `databases` table selects `RELATIONAL_DATABASE_SERVICE`, which is the database entity in the classic topology.
- `/api/v2/synthetic/executions` returns **on-demand** executions only, not every scheduled monitor run. The schema description says so.

Nothing else is skipped. No frontend change and nothing visually different, beyond the new optional field and the new tables in the schema picker.

Mechanical: the endpoint config's `primary_key` became `primary_keys`, and the scope-probe params moved into one helper shared by `validate_credentials` and `check_endpoint_permissions`.

## How did you test this code?

Automated tests only. The sandbox has no Dynatrace environment, so nothing ran against the live API; every endpoint was verified against the vendor's published reference instead.

New transport tests, each aimed at a regression no existing test caught:

- Flattening the metrics query response: a series that drops to zero rows if the two arrays stop being zipped, a `dimensionKey` that collides across series if the map stops being sorted, and the deprecated `dimensions` fallback.
- Clamping the synthetic executions watermark: a stale cursor that would otherwise request a window Dynatrace refuses.
- Request shaping for the new endpoints: `executionFrom` rather than `from`, `metricSelector` and `resolution` sent, and no `pageSize` on endpoints that have no such param.
- The metric scope probe hitting `/api/v2/metrics`, and the missing-keys reason returned without any probe at all.
- Composite primary keys on `metric_data_points`, added as cases to the existing `test_source_response_shape` matrix.

The repo-wide `mypy` pass is clean.

## Problem

- A team analysing their Deel data cannot decode the department, team, job title, seniority, country or currency codes carried on their `people` and `contracts` rows. Nothing in the warehouse resolves them.
- Payroll cost is not available either: `invoices` and `payments` say what was billed and paid, but there is no gross-to-net breakdown of what payroll actually cost.
- Joiner and leaver funnels cannot be measured, because no table holds onboarding or offboarding state.
- These endpoints have been on Deel's REST API for a while. The source never wired them up, and the gaps are recorded in `COVERAGE_GAPS_APPENDIX.md`.

## Changes

- Twelve new selectable tables appear in the Deel schema picker: `departments`, `teams`, `groups`, `onboarding_tracker`, `offboarding_tracker`, `payroll_cycles`, `payroll_reports`, `payroll_gross_to_net`, `countries`, `currencies`, `job_titles` and `seniorities`.
- `offboarding_tracker` sends `ignore_date_range=true`. Deel otherwise returns only the last 45 days of terminations, so the table would silently drop every older leaver.
- `payroll_gross_to_net` walks legal entities, then payroll cycles, then the report. The shared fan-out helper binds one level of path params, and the report sits two hops from a top-level listing, so this endpoint uses a hand-rolled iterator like `time_off_events` already does. It asks only for cycles Deel flags with `has_g2n_report`, and checkpoints per cycle rather than per page.
- `payroll_cycles` is a table beyond what the appendix line names. The cycle listing is the only path to the gross-to-net report, and it is what dates each report, so it earns its own table rather than staying an internal walk.
- `/lookups/time-off-types` is skipped. It returns a bare array of enum strings with no object shape or row identity, and those same values already arrive on `time_offs` rows.
- The trackers and gross-to-net are added to the endpoints excluded from HTTP sample capture. They carry worker names, work emails and per-worker pay.
- Mechanical: canonical column descriptions for the new tables, three token scopes added to the connection form caption, and the appendix checkboxes ticked.

No screenshots. The only visible change is twelve extra rows in the table picker of a source that needs a live Deel account to render.

## How did you test this code?

- New transport tests cover the request shaping and walks that can break at runtime, each one a regression no existing test caught:
  - `offboarding_tracker` sends `ignore_date_range`. Without it the table loses every leaver older than 45 days, and the sync still looks healthy.
  - `payroll_gross_to_net` requests only flagged cycles, injects `cycle_id` and `legal_entity_id` into each row, resumes past cycles it already emitted, tolerates a report that 404s, and stops when a report echoes the same cursor back.

  - `job_titles` pages on `after_cursor` with no page-size param, and ends on the empty page rather than on a missing cursor.

## Problem

A Dropbox Sign user cannot tell who the account ids on their synced tables belong to, which bulk send batch produced a signature request, or how many seats their team uses.

- The source syncs four tables today: `signature_requests`, `templates`, `api_apps` and `account`.
- Those rows carry account ids and a `bulk_send_job_id`, but nothing resolves either one.
- The warehouse source coverage audit recorded four endpoints with no table, one of them ranked high.

## Changes

- `team_members` gives one row per member, with the account id, email address and team role, so account ids on the other tables resolve to a person.
- `team` gives the team record from `/team/info`: the team id, name, member count and sub-team count.
- `bulk_send_jobs` gives one row per bulk send batch. `signature_requests.bulk_send_job_id` joins to it.
- `faxes` gives sent and received fax transactions. It is off by default, because faxing is a separate Dropbox Sign product most accounts do not use.
- A team endpoint 404s for an account that belongs to no team. The source reads that as an empty table instead of failing the sync, and keeps the 404 out of the error log.
- `/team/members/{team_id}` takes a team id in the path, so the sync resolves it from `/team/info` first.

Two endpoints from the audit entry are not synced:

- `/bulk_send_job/{id}` returns the batch's signature requests. The `signature_requests` table already holds them, and every row there carries `bulk_send_job_id`, so a fan-out would spend one request per batch to re-fetch rows we have.
- `/team` has no id field to key a row on, and its `accounts` array repeats `team_members`. `/team/info` carries the id and the counts, so it is the better source for the same record.

All four tables are full refresh. No Dropbox Sign list endpoint takes a server-side timestamp filter, which matches the existing tables.

Nothing in the UI changes beyond four new rows in the table picker.

## How did you test this code?

Automated tests only. This sandbox holds no Dropbox Sign account, so no request went to the live API, and the endpoint shapes come from the vendor's OpenAPI spec at <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hellosign/hellosign-openapi/main/openapi.yaml>.

New coverage, and the regression each part catches:

- The team id resolves from `/team/info` into the `/team/members/{team_id}` path. A regression that drops the resolution sends every request to an unformatted path.
- Both team tables return no rows when the account has no team. A regression that stops translating the 404 fails the whole sync for solo accounts.
- `_fetch_page` returns `None` for a 404 only when the endpoint opts in, and raises otherwise. A regression that widens the rule turns a real 404 on any table into a silent empty sync.
- `faxes` is not selected by default, while `signature_requests` is. No previous test could catch a dropped `should_sync_default`, because every endpoint used the same value.

The existing endpoint-parameterized tests pick up the new tables for primary keys and partitioning.

## Problem

- A Dub workspace can sync links and raw events, but none of Dub's aggregate analytics, so there is no way to see clicks, leads or sales by country, device, browser or over time.
- The raw `/events` stream needs a Dub Business plan. `GET /analytics` does not, so for every workspace below that plan it is the only path to any performance numbers at all.
- The partner program syncs partners, commissions and payouts, but not the applications waiting for approval, so the partner-acquisition funnel starts at "already approved".
- These are long-standing gaps recorded in `COVERAGE_GAPS_APPENDIX.md`, not a new Dub release.

## Changes

- Ten new tables break workspace clicks, leads and sales down by time, continent, country, region, city, device, browser, OS, referer and trigger. Each one is a `groupBy` cut of `GET /analytics`.
- `partner_applications` lists the applications pending approval, with the applicant's profile and their answers to the program's application form.
- `partner_analytics_timeseries` reports each enrolled partner's clicks, leads, sales and earnings over time, one row per partner per interval. No other Dub table carries `earnings`.
- Every new table is full refresh, because `/analytics` recomputes its aggregates per request and exposes no row-level cursor.
- The requests pin `interval=all` and `event=composite`. Dub otherwise answers a 24 hour window of clicks only, which returns a well-formed but near-empty table.
- Mechanical: `DubEndpointConfig.primary_key` becomes `primary_keys`, and a `"single"` pagination mode selects `SinglePagePaginator` and drops the page-size param that the aggregate endpoints reject.
- The partner walk is a custom iterator rather than a paginated path, because each row needs the partner id stamped onto it to stay unique.

### Endpoints verified but not implemented

- `GET /bounties/{bountyId}/submissions`: the spec exposes no endpoint that lists bounties, and no other response carries a `bountyId`, so there is no way to enumerate the parent IDs to fan out over.
- The `top_links` and `top_urls` cuts of `/analytics`: `links` already carries each link's destination URL alongside its lifetime clicks, leads and sales.
- A program-wide cut of `/partners/analytics`: the handler calls `throwIfNoPartnerIdOrTenantId` before it reads anything, so the endpoint only answers for one named partner. The table walks every enrolled partner instead.

## How did you test this code?

Automated only. No Dub account was available, so nothing in this PR was run against the live API. Every endpoint path, parameter name, enum value and response shape was checked against [Dub's published OpenAPI spec](https://spec.speakeasy.com/dub/dub/dub-with-code-samples), which is the same reference the coverage audit diffed against.

Three tests added, each for a failure that stays silent:

- `test_analytics_endpoints_widen_both_dub_defaults` — leaving either Dub default in place still yields a well-formed table, just a near-empty one, so no other test would go red.
- `test_aggregate_endpoints_stop_after_one_request` — these responses carry no next-page marker, so a paginator that kept asking would re-import the same rows until the run was killed, and a leaked page-size param makes the endpoint 422.
- `test_composite_primary_keys_all_reach_the_source_response` — a geo table keyed on its leaf dimension alone merges same-named cities in different countries on every merge.
- `TestPartnerAnalyticsWalk` — a request that names no partner is rejected outright, and two partners share bucket timestamps, so unstamped rows collide on the key. Also covers resume and a workspace with no program.

Ran locally: the Dub suite and the `sources/` invariant suite (categories, versions, schema), plus `ruff` and the `.semgrep/rules/security/` set over the changed files.

Repo-wide `mypy --cache-fine-grained .` reports no issues across 21588 source files. The only type-shaped change is the `primary_key` to `primary_keys` rename, and a grep found no reference to that field outside the Dub package.

## Problem

An Easypromos customer reporting on prize stock cannot see the prizes with the most stock left. A prize type that nobody has won yet appears in no synced table, so remaining-stock and redemption reports silently omit it.

The `prizes` table syncs awarded prizes. Each row embeds the `prize_type` object carrying `qty` and `given`, so stock shows up only once at least one unit has been given away.

This closes an endpoint-coverage gap recorded in `COVERAGE_GAPS_APPENDIX.md`, not a new vendor release.

## Changes

- New `prize_inventory` table: one row per prize type per promotion, with `qty` (total units) and `given` (units awarded).
- Syncs `GET /prizes/inventory/{promotion_id}`, fanned out over `/promotions` like every other promotion-scoped Easypromos table. Full refresh, since the API exposes no updated-since filter.
- `EasypromosEndpointConfig` gains a `paginated` flag. The inventory response returns the whole catalog with no `paging` envelope, so the endpoint uses a single-page paginator rather than the shared cursor one.
- Curated canonical descriptions for the new table, so the public docs and the AI agent describe its columns without an LLM pass.

Two of the three audited endpoints were verified against the vendor reference and skipped.

- `GET /prizes/{promotion_id}/users/{user_id}` (GetUserPrizesByPromotion): the audit note claims `prizes` is only a catalog. It is not. `prizes` syncs `GET /prizes/{promotion_id}`, documented as "Get the list of all assigned prizes and their winners", and its rows already carry `user_id`, `stage_id`, `participation_id`, `created` and `code`. The per-user route returns the same award objects filtered to one user and minus the embedded `user`, so it is a strict subset that would need a second fan-out level over every participant.
- `GET /coins/{promotion_id}/users/{user_id}` (GetUserBalanceVirtualCoin): the route is keyed on a single `user_id` and the API publishes no promotion-wide balances collection. The table would cost one request per participant per sync, with no server-side filter to bound it. Each `coin_transactions` row already carries the running `balance` after the transaction, so the current balance is the latest row per user and coin.

> [!NOTE]
> Separate from this diff: the existing `coin_transactions` endpoint points at `/coins/{promotion_id}`, which the reference documents as PUT-only (UpdateVirtualCoinBalance). The GET list lives at `/coin_transactions/{promotion_id}`. Left alone here as a different root cause; worth a follow-up.

No user-visible UI changed. The new table appears in the source's table picker, which is generated from the endpoint catalog.

## How did you test this code?

Two cases added to `TestFanOut` in `test_easypromos.py`.

- `test_prize_inventory_reads_a_body_without_a_paging_envelope` catches a wrong path, a wrong `data_selector`, a missing `promotion_id` injection, or a crash on a response body that has no `paging` key. No existing test serves a body without that envelope.
- `test_unpaginated_endpoint_does_not_follow_a_cursor` catches the `paginated=False` declaration or the paginator branch being dropped. Following an echoed cursor would re-read the same catalog forever.

The existing parameterized `test_primary_keys_and_partitioning_match_settings` and the source-level schema tests pick up the new endpoint automatically.
