## Problem

Most `page_load` rows in `time to see data` from web analytics have an empty `last_tile_kind`, so you can't tell which kind of tile held the page up.

- It only happens for the web analytics chart tiles, the ones keyed `InsightViz.*`.
- `insightDataLogic` builds their data node with only a key, before `InsightViz` passes the query.
- The node registers with its collection at that point, so `kind: props.query?.kind` is still undefined.
- The load runs later with the query set, but the collection already recorded no kind.

Follows PR 104097.

## Changes

- The data node now sends its query kind with `collectionNodeLoadData`. The query is always set by the time a tile loads.
- The kind follows the query that actually runs, so a `loadData` with an `overrideQuery` reports the override's kind.
- The collection keeps that kind from the load through to the finish.
- Registration no longer carries `kind`.
- Mechanical: regenerated typegen blocks in `dataNodeCollectionLogic`, `dataNodeLogic` and `webAnalyticsLoadTimeLogic`.

Nothing looks different. No UI changed.

## How did you test this code?

- New `dataNodeLogic` test builds the node with only a key, then gives it a query, and checks the collection receives the query kind. It fails without the fix.
- The same test runs an `overrideQuery` and checks the collection receives that query's kind.
- The existing collection test now takes the kind from the load.

Not checked: production rows after this ships. The share of `page_load` rows missing `last_tile_kind` should drop to near zero.

## Problem

Developers can merge broken queries against the native JSON events table because CI tests only the legacy table. Testing both tables previously added 51 jobs and roughly doubled backend test cost. This PR restores coverage with seven extra jobs, which used 86 runner-minutes in the [measured full run](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36058659541).

#104783 introduced the full duplication. #105879 restricted it to an optional label, removing routine coverage too.

## Changes

Most tests run once. Critical event-query tests run against both tables, catching regressions before merge without repeating the entire suite.

The extra tests cover HogQL, event-query runners, and selected direct SQL readers. `.github/new-events-schema-targets.txt` defines the list. These tests also refresh their SQL snapshots for the native table.

The merge queue and full backend runs execute the whole list. Narrowed PR runs execute only relevant listed tests. GitHub Actions and Depot use the same selection.

The `test-new-events-schema` label still requests broader testing against both tables. Tests excluded from those larger suites still run separately, so the label cannot remove their coverage.

The tradeoff is maintaining the list: authors must add new event-reading tests. Scheduled testing alone would find regressions after merge and leave someone else to repair them. This PR changes CI, not which table users query.

## How did you test this code?

The measured run passed all seven native-schema jobs. An [earlier run](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36056038185) exposed a deletion-request test requiring a missing ClickHouse UDF; that test left the list. A [draft run](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36061159741) confirmed the full-run skip on drafts.

Local selector and workflow tests cover test selection and the label coverage fix. The final full CI run is [here](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36064364070).

## Problem

Cached marketing attribution reports spend memory and time grouping sessions that the shared reader already resolved to unique session/person pairs.

## Changes

- Read resolved sessions directly when calculating reach and building touchpoint arrays, removing two redundant aggregation stages.
- Preserve dimension deduplication, current event identities, exclusions and conversion bounds.
- Keep existing cache jobs reusable; this change requires no writer update or backfill.

No visual changes.

<details>
<summary>Aggregation flow</summary>

Before:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Resolved sessions] --> B[Regroup for reach] --> D[Reach]
    A --> C[Regroup for credit] --> E[Touchpoints]
    classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
    classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
    class A phGray;
    class B,C,D,E phBlue;
```

After:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Resolved sessions] --> D[Reach]
    A --> E[Touchpoints]
    classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
    classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
    class A phGray;
    class D,E phBlue;
```

</details>

## How did you test this code?

- Extended duplicate-job coverage to paths and tested unattributed exclusions against superseded dimensions.
- Compared generated table SQL with synthetic inputs on ClickHouse 26.6.2: one million sessions, 100,000 people, 50,000 converters and 16 channels.

| Median of five runs | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Query duration | 1,276 ms | 789 ms |
| Peak memory | 577,321,388 bytes | 285,516,647 bytes |
| Reported read bytes | 171,275,096 bytes | 137,275,072 bytes |
| Aggregation stages | 7 | 5 |

The benchmark uses four threads and disables the uncompressed cache.
Both versions produce matching rows and integer counts; weighted values differ only by floating-point accumulation, at most `2.91e-10` across runs.
The synthetic inputs replace session and conversion resolution, so these measurements do not include production event scans or prove production timeout avoidance.

The [legacy](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36059747426/job/107836025815) and [JSON](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36059747426/job/107836026045) marketing suites pass on `8c2a973b072`.
Their JUnit artifacts confirm all 48 parity cases ran successfully, including identity overrides, channel-rule changes and conversion ceilings.
The JSON suite skips two existing conversion-ordering tests; neither belongs to the affected suites.
[CI coverage](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36059747426/artifacts/10834193298) records execution of every added executable reader line.

<details>
<summary>Local revalidation and earlier failures</summary>

The combined reader, parity, attribution-table and paths suites pass locally: 154 tests and 9 snapshots, without snapshot updates.
The 14 targeted identity, channel and conversion-ceiling cases also pass.
The three previously failing cases pass in 20 consecutive local rounds: 60 executions, with no failures, errors or skips.

The earlier writer timeout occurred during materialization, before the modified reader executed.
The earlier local failures did not recur in this validation; their historical cause remains unconfirmed.
No production code, assertions or timeouts changed during revalidation.
The CI-generated JSON snapshots contain the expected removal of the two aggregation stages.

</details>

## Problem

- A CDC table reset by a TRUNCATE, or by slot-invalidation recovery, can lose its rows.
- The sync running at the time of the reset can still finish afterward, and its hand-over flips the table to streaming with `reset_pipeline` still set.
- The next streaming run then wipes the table and replays only the change buffer.
- The reset already cancels that sync (#105139), but a cancel only asks the workflow to stop. The loader still applies batches the sync queued, and the final one runs the hand-over.

## Changes

- The reset pauses the table's schedule, cancels its sync, and proceeds only once the workflow has closed and none of the table's batches remain in the load queue.
- Until then the table carries `cdc_reset_pending`, capture drops its changes, and each later capture run retries the reset before it reads the WAL.
  The new snapshot reads the table after the reset, so the dropped changes are not lost.
- The key stays until the schedule is unpaused, so a failed unpause is retried instead of leaving the paused table without a snapshot.
- Only queued batches count as in progress. Deferred runs flush only after a hand-over, which the paused schedule prevents, so counting them would make a legacy table wait forever.
- `cancel_running_sync` now returns a workflow id only when it asked a live workflow to stop. #105912 carries the same change for its conversion fix. The two PRs still overlap in `_reset_schema_to_snapshot`, so whichever lands second resolves that.
- Rejected: failing the capture run until the cancel lands. It stalls every table of the source and reports a failure each tick.
- Rejected: a guard in the hand-over. A resumed snapshot keeps its own `reset_pipeline` set, so the hand-over cannot tell a new reset from its own.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Before
    A1[TRUNCATE read]:::y --> B1[cancel running sync] --> C1[purge and reset now]
    C1 -.-> D1[old sync hands over]:::r --> E1[next run wipes the table]:::r
  end
  classDef y fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
  classDef r fill:#f54e00,stroke:#f54e00,color:#fff;
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph After
    A2[TRUNCATE read]:::y --> P2[pause schedule] --> B2[cancel running sync]
    B2 --> Q2{sync still stopping or batches queued?}
    Q2 -- yes --> W2[cdc_reset_pending, table left out of capture]:::g --> R2[next capture run retries]
    R2 --> P2
    Q2 -- no --> C2[purge and reset] --> U2[unpause, clear the key]:::b
  end
  classDef y fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
  classDef g fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
  classDef b fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
```

Not fixed here: the resync endpoint, the table-mode switch, re-enabling a table, the ad hoc sync, Repair CDC, and the migrate command's rollback reset a table right after a cancel request, or with none.
They run synchronously, so they cannot wait for a later capture run.
A follow-up could route them through `cdc_reset_pending` so capture finishes the reset.

## How did you test this code?

- `test_a_reset_stops_the_tables_running_sync_first` is extended with the waiting cases and written first. On master, a live sync still stopping and a closed sync with batches still loading both reset at once.
  It now also covers a closed sync with nothing queued, a table with deferred runs left, and a failed cancel.
- `test_a_pending_reset_finishes_before_the_read_once_the_sync_stopped` covers the next run. It finishes the reset before the read, or keeps the table out of capture while the slot still advances.
- Each new case fails with its fix removed.
- Not run: an end-to-end check against a real Temporal cancel and loader.

## Problem

Replay Vision users open an observation from search and hit a generic "Recording not found" player screen, because the session passed the project's recording retention period (30 days by default). Nothing warns them before the click, and search has no way to narrow results to a date range.

The observation detail page's own expired state is being reworked in #105826. This PR covers the search surfaces, which that PR does not touch.

## Changes

- Search result cards and rows show a "Recording expired" tag with a tooltip when the observed session's recording no longer exists, so users know before they open a result that playback is gone.
- Observation search gets a date range filter next to the scanner scope (the standard `DateFilter`, presets plus custom ranges). It maps to the search endpoint's existing `date_from`/`date_to` parameters, re-runs the shown search on change, and round-trips through the URL.
- Expiry is confirmed, not derived from age: a recording keeps the retention period it was captured under and the team setting can change afterwards, so age against the current setting can flag a recording that still plays. After a search lands, one batched recordings-API request checks the old results, and the tag shows only for sessions the API no longer returns. Age (older than the shortest offered period, 30 days) only decides which sessions are worth that one request, since younger recordings cannot be expired under any period.

These are real renders of the components, captured from Storybook on this branch (fixture data, not the live app). New stories drive them: `RecordingExpiredTag.stories.tsx` and `SearchResults.stories.tsx`, so the same states also render in the branch's Storybook and Chromatic runs.

**Grid result, recording expired** (the tag sits on the thumbnail where the watch caption would be, so it does not truncate the title):

![Expired grid result](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PostHog/pr-assets/main/images/pr-106265-sb-expired-grid-card-v3.png)

**Grid result, recording still plays** (for contrast: the poster keeps its play target, no tag):

![Playable grid result](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PostHog/pr-assets/main/images/pr-106265-sb-playable-grid-card.png)

**List result, recording expired** (the small thumbnail carries the clock icon, with the full text on hover):

![Expired list result](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PostHog/pr-assets/main/images/pr-106265-sb-expired-list-row-v3.png)

**The tag on its own** (its tooltip explains the retention deletion on hover):

![Recording expired tag](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PostHog/pr-assets/main/images/pr-106265-sb-expired-tag.png)

## How did you test this code?

- `pnpm jest products/replay_vision/frontend`: all 70 suites pass. New coverage: an `observationSearchLogic` case catches a tag shown without API confirmation (a still-playable old recording must not be tagged), a fresh session reaching the existence check, and the confirmed-absent session not being tagged; another case catches the date range not reaching the request, not re-running the shown search, or not syncing with the URL; `recordingRetention.test.ts` catches a wrong candidate threshold direction.
- `pnpm --filter=@posthog/frontend typescript:check` and oxlint/oxfmt pass.
- Not verified in a running browser; the tag and filter placement were not visually checked.

## Problem

Agents using the PostHog MCP can read Replay Vision scanners but cannot set up alerts, backfill history, retry failed scans, or add scouts, although the UI supports all of these.
43 of the product's 66 API operations had no MCP tool, most of them features the UI calls.

## Changes

- Enables 29 Replay Vision tools in `products/replay_vision/mcp/tools.yaml`:

| Area | Tools |
| --- | --- |
| Alerts | `vision-alerts-{list,get,create,partial-update,delete,reset,events-list}`, `vision-alerts-destinations-{create,delete}` |
| Backfills | `vision-scanners-backfills-{estimate,create,list,get,cancel,resume}` |
| Scanning | `vision-scanners-scan-sessions` (bulk), `vision-observations-retry` |
| Scouts | `vision-scanners-scouts-create`, `vision-scanners-scout-reports-{list,get}` |
| Read-only | `vision-scanners-watch-feed`, `vision-scanners-counts`, `vision-scanners-self-driving-stats`, `vision-quota-spend-series-get` |
| Authoring | `vision-scanners-draft`, `vision-scanners-suggest-tags`, `vision-scanners-duplicate` |
| Findings | `vision-observations-create-task`, `vision-observations-signal-reports-list` |

- Scopes mirror each endpoint's `required_scopes`. Tools that call an LLM or start scans set `requires_ai_consent`.
- The backfill tools tell the agent to estimate first and get the person's agreement before spending credits.
- Calibration stays off MCP on purpose: `prompt-suggestions-evaluate` and `prompt-suggestions-list`.
- Nested duplicates of session-route actions and the alert `PUT` stay disabled.

> [!WARNING]
> Three API behavior changes, each needed to make a tool safe:
> - **Alert destinations:** creating one now requires `session_recording:read` as well as `vision_alert:write`. The action-level `required_scopes` silently overrode the stricter `dangerously_get_required_scopes`. API keys without the recording scope now get 403.
> - **Backfill create:** now requires `max_total_credits` and rejects the create if the window costs more. The UI passes its estimate's `total_credits`. Other clients that omit it get 400.
> - **Alert create:** metric-only fields lost their serializer defaults (the model keeps identical ones). The MCP schema sent those defaults on every call, so every match alert through MCP got 400.

- **Scanner scouts:** accept `display_name` and derive `name` from it, like the generic Signals endpoint, through a new `display_name` path on the Signals facade. Before, a body with only `display_name` passed validation and then failed with a 500, and scanner scouts never got a label.
- **Alert destinations:** `vision-alerts-get` now lists them (type, target without secrets, and the ids that delete takes), mirroring Logs alerts. List responses skip them to avoid a query per row.
- **Tool names:** six older tools move to `-get`/`-delete`/bare-verb names and `vision-alerts-partial-update` becomes `vision-alerts-update`. Each old name stays as a deprecated alias to the same endpoint, so existing prompts and clients keep working.
- **SQL:** new `system.replay_scanners`. Access follows the scanner; inline scanners and experiment targeting stay hidden. Alerts and backfills stay off SQL, because their API checks a second scope a system table cannot enforce.
- **Evals:** `products/replay_vision/evals/eval_mcp_tools.py`, three sandboxed cases: webhook alert, backfill without a blind create, retry of a failed scan.
- The two Replay Vision skills now point at the new tools instead of saying there is no tool for retry or task creation.
- Mechanical: regenerated OpenAPI types, MCP tool code, tool-schema snapshots, and `agentScopes.generated.ts` (adds `vision_alert:read`/`write`).

## How did you test this code?

- MCP unit suite passes locally, including the 29 new tool-schema snapshots.
- Scout tests: a `display_name`-only body gets a derived name, keeps its label, and stays owned by the scanner; a body with neither is a 400.
- Extended the alert scope test: a `vision_alert:write`-only key cannot create a destination.
- Extended the backfill create test: a cap below the cost is a 400 with no row, the exact cost succeeds.
- Not run locally: the Django test suite, because the shared local test database has a persons migration from another branch. CI is the first run of the new cases, and `test_database.ambr` still needs its snapshot update.
- Called every new tool on a devbox through the agent CLI, which uses the generated MCP handlers. Alerts (including a match alert), the destination create, list and delete cycle, stats, quota under the new and old names, duplicate, draft, suggest-tags, scout create with a derived name, and create-task all worked.
- Not verified end to end: retry and bulk scan (the devbox stack has no Temporal) and backfill create (demo data has no recordings; the Django test covers the cap).
- Not run: the new eval suite, because the Braintrust and gateway keys are not configured.

## Problem

- On PostHog Cloud, the enforced app policy lets a page load a script from any PostHog subdomain, and connect to any of them.
- The ingestion hosts serve any project's remote config as a script, so an injected script tag can run code from a project an attacker controls.
- The report-only shadow policy from #104099 tested named-host lists for these two directives.
- Since #104811, the shadow policy reported no first-party host, except calls that #105501 fixed and tabs opened before #104811.

## Changes

- On Cloud, the app policy's `script-src` and `connect-src` list each PostHog host instead of `*.posthog.com` and `*.i.posthog.com`. Users see no difference.
- The lists hold these hosts:
  - the bundle host;
  - the posthog-js host's `/static/` path and our project's config;
  - live events;
  - the public webhooks host, for source-webhook tests and manual workflow triggers;
  - the `/decide/` adblock probe;
  - the agent proxy.
- The shadow policy tested every host above except the webhooks host. It never saw a request to that host, and code review found it.
- `style-src`, `font-src` and `img-src` keep the wildcard, because the shadow policy did not test them.
- Self-hosted installs, E2E runs and the dev environment keep the wildcards, because the named hosts and the token belong to Cloud.
- The shadow policy (report version 3) is removed, because it now matches the app policy.
- On Cloud, the app policy reports as version 4, so its reports stay apart from the wildcard policy's version 2. Version 3 stays unused, because the shadow's reports carry it.
- `.agents/security.md` now says that a new PostHog subdomain needs an entry in these lists.
- The test changes are mechanical and follow from the changes above.

> [!WARNING]
> A script or request to an unlisted PostHog host now fails on Cloud only. Local runs and E2E cannot show it.
> Every deployment that serves signed-in app pages must set `JS_URL` and `TASKS_AGENT_PROXY_PUBLIC_URL`. An empty value drops that host from the enforced lists.
> Rollback: revert this PR, or set `csp-enforce-app-policy` to report-only.

> [!NOTE]
> #105596 moved posthog-js to `internal-cf.posthog.com` on 2026-09-24. Merge after the shadow policy has a full day of reports for that host.

## How did you test this code?

- Ran `posthog/test/test_csp_middleware.py` on a devbox.
- `test_only_cloud_pages_swap_the_wildcards_for_named_posthog_hosts` replaces the shadow test. It reads the enforced header, because Cloud enforces the app policy for everyone. It fails if any of these happen:
  - a wildcard comes back into either directive on Cloud;
  - the bundle host or a named host goes missing;
  - the other region's host appears;
  - a self-hosted install loses the wildcards;
  - the report version is not 4 on Cloud, or an operator's configured version changes.
- `test_swaps_the_wildcards_and_keeps_every_other_source` fails if the narrowing drops any other directive or source from the enforced policy.
- Not checked: loading the app in a browser under the narrowed, enforced policy. The evidence that nothing breaks is the production shadow reports.

## Problem

The tasks golden bake's promote step hardcodes `posthog-tasks-default` — the alias every task box restores from. Combined with the pluggable-memory bake knob (`box_mem_boot_mib`, added in #105407), dispatching a hotplug bake would **overwrite the default golden and flip the whole fleet to a pluggable-memory box at once**, bypassing the `tasks-hogland-hotplug-golden` flag and its instant rollback. That is the opposite of the two-golden rollout the flag was built for.

## Changes

- Add a `target_alias` dispatch input to `cd-tasks-golden-snapshot`. Blank = `posthog-tasks-default` (today's behavior, unchanged). Set `posthog-tasks-hotplug` to publish a pluggable-memory golden **alongside** the default, which the flag then selects per team.
- The promote step repoints `$TARGET_ALIAS` instead of the hardcoded default (PUT + resolve-confirm + error text).
- Mechanical: the candidate is still smoke-tested before the alias is repointed, so a hotplug golden that can't boot never goes live.

## How did you test this code?

Agent-authored. YAML validates and `hogli lint:workflows` passes (WF001–WF010). Not run: an actual bake (needs the armed hogland tailnet/principal). The scheduled default bake is unchanged — `target_alias` defaults to `posthog-tasks-default`.

- [x] No feature flag controls this change <!-- release-status: no-feature-flag -->

Additive dispatch input; default behavior unchanged. The pluggable golden it enables is gated by the `tasks-hogland-hotplug-golden` flag (shipped in #105407).

body:
## Problem

PostHog AI takes plain text only. A screenshot of a broken dashboard, a CSV or an error log has to be pasted in as fragments, or cannot be sent at all.

Closes #62926. That issue scopes the work against the frozen LangGraph runtime. On the sandbox runtime the artifact API, its Temporal forwarding and the sandbox-side hydration already exist — Desktop has used them since cloud tasks shipped — so this is frontend-only.

## Changes

- Attach files with a button, a drop anywhere on the composer, or a paste.
- Any type is accepted: the sandbox writes the artifact to disk and the agent reads it with its own tools. 10 files per message, 30 MB each, 10 MB for a PDF.
- A sent message shows its images in a row, then a badge per other file linking to its download.
- The staged file is drawn straight away, so a send never reads as text-only. The artifact replaces it once the upload lands.
- Files upload on send, because the creation composer has no task to upload against until it submits.

Warm runs decide which endpoint holds them. With a lease, upload to that run and pass the ids on task creation — the only request that runs when creation activates a warm run. Without one, give up warm reuse by omitting `branch` and stage on the cold task. Mirrors `taskCreationSaga.ts` in Desktop.

A message still needs text. Attachment-only sends reach into the queue concatenation, the optimistic echo and the task description, so they are a separate change.

### How it flows

```
Composer (Task / TaskRun)  ── pick · drop · paste ──┐
                                                    ▼
                                    composerAttachmentsLogic
                                    File handles, keyed per composer
                                              │
                                          ══ send ══
                                              ▼
                                    artifactUpload.ts
                                    prepare → POST bytes to S3 → finalize
                                              │
                                        artifact ids
                                              │
      ┌───────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┐
 warm lease                             cold create                          live run
 tasksCreate                          tasksRunCreate               tasksRunsCommandCreate
 pending_user_artifact_ids     pending_user_artifact_ids              params.artifact_ids
      └───────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┘
                                              ▼
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
   below here already existed — Desktop has used it since cloud tasks shipped
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
                                              ▼
              products/tasks API     validates the ids against the run
                                              ▼
              Temporal               send_user_message(artifacts=…)
                                              ▼
              agent-server            downloads to
                                      .posthog/attachments/<run>/<artifact>/<name>
                                      emits { type: resource_link, uri, name }
                                              ▼
              harness                 reads the file with its own tools
                                              │
               echo: session/update user_message_chunk { resource_link }
                                              ▼
              runStreamLogic → ThreadItem.attachments → images + badges
```

The thread recovers the run and artifact ids from that sandbox path, the only place the wire carries them. A path that does not match renders as a plain name, so a layout change there degrades rather than breaks.


https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/25bcd545-05eb-4b94-b633-343a5aae7f93



## How did you test this code?

The recording above is the author's. The agent ran unit tests only — no manual click-through and no screenshots from its side.

What the new tests catch:

- **Upload** — presigned fields go out verbatim and ahead of the file, and one failed upload rejects the batch without finalizing, so a message cannot arrive with fewer files than were attached.
- **Types and limits** — content type comes from the extension, so a `.md` the browser calls `application/octet-stream` does not reach the agent as a binary. A PDF between the two ceilings is refused in the composer, not after its upload.
- **Send paths** — ids reach `user_message`; a terminal run stages on the task instead; files are released on success and kept on failure.
- **Warm reuse** — the lease-less create omits `branch` and its run gets the ids, while a create with nothing attached still offers its branch.
- **Drop** — a second drop does not re-stage the earlier files. It did, while the composer used `LemonFileInput`'s drop target: that keeps its own copy of the list and re-syncs it only when `value` changes identity, so the copy grew and each drop reported everything staged so far.
- **Rendering** — ids are recovered from the sandbox path, a non-matching path yields a plain name, a later frame fills ids onto the entry an optimistic send drew rather than adding a second, and an unfetchable image drops to the badges rather than leaving a broken frame.

Locally clean: `typescript:check`, `oxlint`, `typegen:check`, and the `products/posthog_ai` suite.

## Problem

- cohort-seeder cannot authenticate to ClickHouse with a rotating ServiceAccount token, so it can only use a static password.
- `build_client` sets the password once, on a client that lives for the whole process.
- A token read at startup stops working after the kubelet's first rotation.

REF: https://github.com/PostHog/clickhouse_team_issues/issues/84

## Changes

- Each query now authenticates with the current contents of `CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD_FILE` when that variable is set.
- A `ClickHouseClient` wrapper sets the password on a clone of the inner client before each query.
- ClickHouse authenticates every HTTP request, and the clone shares the connection pool, so no refresh task is needed.
- The fallback matches `read_password` in the Python client: an unreadable or empty file uses the static password.
- An expired token also uses the static password, but only when one is set.
- Each fallback increments `seeder_clickhouse_password_fallback_total`, labelled by `reason`: `unreadable`, `empty` or `expired`.
- Without the counter, a token mount that never works hides behind the static password.
- Each fallback warning names the token file.
- Behavior is unchanged while `CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD_FILE` is unset. A separate charts change mounts the token and sets the variable.
- Mechanical: the scanners and the two live-ClickHouse tests take the wrapper type. The query call sites are unchanged.

## How did you test this code?

- The rotation test sends real queries to a local HTTP server across a token rewrite. It fails if the password is read once at startup.
- Its first round has no token file and fails if the static password stops reaching the server.
- The table test covers each token-file state. It fails if a fallback rule drifts from the Python client or a fallback stops counting its reason.
- Its expired token encodes to `-` and `_`, so the test fails if the decoder switches to the standard base64 alphabet.
- The config test fails if the variable name stops matching the one the chart sets.
- Temporary code changes confirmed the read-once, standard-alphabet and missing-static-password failures.
- Not run locally: the Postgres- and ClickHouse-backed suites, which need the compose stack.
- Not yet tested against a real cluster. That happens when the charts change rolls out.
- No `test-new-events-schema` label: the diff touches no event ingestion or event-table SQL.

## Problem

An endpoint that is in the served OpenAPI schema becomes a public REST contract: it appears in Swagger, Redoc and the API docs at posthog.com, and people can build integrations on it. A team that wants MCP tools and frontend types for an endpoint has no way to get them without that contract.

The codegen build already runs with `OPENAPI_INCLUDE_INTERNAL=1` and the served `/api/schema/` runs without it, but the only thing that uses the split is the viewset-level `scope_object = "INTERNAL"`, which also removes API key access.

Raised in the review of #102274: the access control settings endpoints should stay private until access control v2 (aka ReBAC) replaces them.

## Changes

- An endpoint marked `@extend_schema(extensions={"x-internal": True})` is dropped from the served `/api/schema/`, Swagger, Redoc and the API docs, and kept in the codegen build, so its MCP tools and frontend types are still generated.
- `PostHogAutoSchema.is_excluded()` applies the marker before the operation is built, the same path `@extend_schema(exclude=True)` takes, so no serializer components leak into the served schema.
- No product endpoint carries the marker in this PR. The access control settings actions get it in #102274.

> [!NOTE]
> The marker only controls schema inclusion. The endpoints stay reachable, and auth and scopes still apply.

## How did you test this code?

- `test_x_internal_operations_are_only_in_the_codegen_schema` in `test_api_docs.py` runs the schema generator over a test-only marked view. The view is absent from the served schema and present in the codegen schema. It catches a change that leaks a marked operation into Swagger, and one that drops it from codegen.
## Release status

## Automatic notifications

- [ ] Publish to changelog?

## Docs update

`docs/published/handbook/engineering/ai/implementing-mcp-tools.md` gains a section on MCP-only endpoints.

body:
## Problem

A GPU smoke test of the serving command (the `docker run` in the package README) found four problems in the entrypoint. Each one costs an operator time, or lets a box stay down:

- Every start hashed the 8.4 GB of weights twice, which added about 30 s to each restart.
- When vLLM or Caddy stopped cleanly on its own, the container exited 0. Both exit 0 on SIGTERM. `--restart always` still restarted the box, but under `--restart on-failure` it would have stayed down.
- Caddy saved its running config, bearer included, to disk inside the container.
- The vLLM and Triton compile caches lived in the container, so every new container paid the full cold start. That was about 9 minutes on a T4.

## Changes

- `bin/serve.sh` verifies the weights once when they are already on the volume. It verifies again only after a fetch.
- A child that exits on its own now makes the container exit 1, even when the child exited 0. A `docker stop` still exits 0.
- The Caddyfile sets `persist_config off`.
- The compile caches move to `/models/cache` on the named volume (`VLLM_CACHE_ROOT`, `TRITON_CACHE_DIR`, unless the operator sets them), and the image creates that directory for the serving user. Docker seeds only a new volume from the image, so on an older volume without a writable cache directory, the entrypoint says so and keeps the caches in the container instead of failing to start.
- The README records JevK5's parity on an L4, measured 2026-09-24. Against the fp32 readout of JevK5's own runtime, this image differs by at most 0.046, with one argmax flip on a near tie. That is as close as the runtime's own default output gets. fp8 answers about 30% faster, but it moves answers by up to 0.41, so the image stays on bf16.

## How did you test this code?

- `tests/test_serve_entrypoint.py` runs `bin/serve.sh` against stub `vllm`, `caddy`, `s5cmd` and `kev-vllm-checkpoint` commands. It fails if a clean exit of a child stops failing the container, if a stop signal stops exiting 0, if weights already on the volume are verified twice, if an explicit `VLLM_CACHE_ROOT` is overridden, or if an unwritable cache directory stops falling back. Each check was seen to fail with its fix reverted.
- Not run on a GPU: a real restart that reads the compile cache back from the volume, and Caddy with `persist_config off`. Both need the next image build on a GPU box.

## Problem

The GitHub data warehouse source's merge-commit enrichment step failed with a retryable error instead of honoring GitHub's rate-limit backoff, surfaced by [this error tracking issue](https://us.posthog.com/project/2/error_tracking/01a0d4a1-59aa-76d0-a66f-48c3be832411).

GitHub's GraphQL API answers a rate limit with a 200 response whose `errors` carry an error type. The code only recognized the type `RATE_LIMITED`, but the observed error carries type `RATE_LIMIT` (with `code: graphql_rate_limit`) instead. That spelling fell through to a generic `GithubRetryableError`, whose plain exponential backoff is capped at 30 seconds — far short of GitHub's hourly GraphQL rate-limit window.

## Changes

- `_raise_if_graphql_rate_limited` now matches both `RATE_LIMITED` and `RATE_LIMIT` error types (via the existing `_graphql_error_type` helper, which already normalizes casing and checks both top-level and `extensions` fields), so either spelling raises `GitHubRateLimitError` and waits out GitHub's advertised reset instead of retrying blind.
- Mechanical: extended the rate-limit test to cover the `RATE_LIMIT` spelling alongside the existing `RATE_LIMITED` case.

## How did you test this code?

- Extended `test_graphql_rate_limit_carries_a_wait_that_outlasts_the_window` with a case using the `RATE_LIMIT` spelling seen in production — this is the regression no existing test caught, since the suite only exercised `RATE_LIMITED`.
- Ran the full file: `hogli test products/warehouse_sources/backend/temporal/data_imports/sources/github/tests/test_github_repository_endpoints.py` (56 passed).
- Ran `ruff check --fix`, `ruff format --check`, and `mypy --cache-fine-grained` on both changed files: clean.

body:
## Problem

Dashboards with many SQL insights over layered warehouse views stopped loading after #104170. The request runs for minutes, so the browser and the edge proxy give up.

Before a tile reads its cached result, `queried_access_controlled_resources` builds the cache fingerprint. Since #104170 it walks view definitions. On each nested call it read the team's whole warehouse table catalog again, and it walked a view once per path to it (`_seen_views` was per path). So a base view that many views read was parsed and fetched again for every parent. In traces, one tile repeated the table + view lookup + parse loop about 150 times.

**Why:** a large internal dashboard over layered views timed out on every load, and the traces showed this loop as the cost.

## Changes

- One `_WarehouseCatalog` is shared by a fingerprint and every nested call. It reads the table catalog once, looks up each view name once, and keeps a walked-view set. Each view is now walked once per fingerprint.
- Cache keys stay the same: a view's scopes join the top-level result the first time it is walked, a later path adds nothing, and fail-closed (`None`) still goes to the top. Views that reference each other still end.
- No other change a person can see. Dashboards over layered views only load faster.

## How did you test this code?

- `test_view_fan_out_does_not_scale_queries` is an N+1-style probe on the fingerprint itself, because every query path builds it, not only dashboards. It checks that six views over one base view cost the same Postgres queries as two. It compares the two counts, so it does not pin a fixed number. It fails on the code from #104170 (14 vs 6 queries) and passes with this change.
- Ran `test_access_controlled_resources.py`, the dataclass ratchet, `test_adding_insights_is_not_nplus1_for_gets` and `test_query_runner.py` locally. All passed.
- Not tested: a real dashboard load before and after deploy.

This PR shortens long keys in the middle and keeps the full key one hover away.

### Truncated key

Keys over 32 characters render through `midEllipsis`, the same helper the property filter buttons use, with the full key in a tooltip. A CSS `truncate` caps the width too, so a 32 character key of wide glyphs cannot push the copy and open controls out of a narrow row. Copy and the open link still use the full key. The copy icon now sits next to the text instead of wrapping it, so the key text and the copy icon each have one tooltip. An 85 character key fits the bar on one line at a 1512px viewport.

- `products/experiments/frontend/components/ExperimentMetaBar/ExperimentMetaBar.tsx`

### Reusable component

`TruncatedText` pairs `midEllipsis` with a tooltip. It also watches its own width with a `ResizeObserver`, so a short key that a CSS cap clips still shows the full key on hover. Plain text renders when nothing is cut. It lives in the product's `components/` folder for the next identifier that needs the same treatment.

- `products/experiments/frontend/components/TruncatedText.tsx`

### Story

`ExperimentWithLongFlagKey` is the funnel metric story with an 85 character key, so the snapshot locks the truncation in. Visual Review adds its hashes to `snapshots.yml` on approval.

body:
## Problem

Capture's global rate limiter started timing out writes to Redis in bursts after #104891, and the write-error ratio crossed the alert threshold in prod-us.

- Every key of one epoch shares the same deadline, so a whole generation now expires in the same instant. Redis is single-threaded, and that burst blocks it long enough to time out concurrent limiter writes.
- The error ratio went from a 0.03% baseline to **1.06%**, against a 1% warning threshold. Yesterday at the same clock time it was ~0.01/s, so this is not the daily traffic ramp.
- The bursts land exactly **120 seconds apart**, at the same point in the epoch, with **zero** errors between them.
- Redis does *less* expiry work than before (expire-cycle CPU 4.89% to 3.41%, 14,699 to 11,621 keys/s). The work is not larger, it is concentrated.

## Changes

- `epoch_expire_at` now derives a stable per-key offset inside the window, so a generation's keys expire spread out instead of together.
- The offset only ever **adds** time, so a key still outlives every read that consults it. Reads use the current and previous epoch, and the deadline stays at or after `(epoch + 2) * window`.
- The offset is salted, so it cannot correlate with `select_redis_client`, which hashes the same key. Sharing that hash would leave each shard only a fraction of the offsets whenever the shard count shares a factor with the window, bringing the burst back per shard. Harmless today at one instance, latent the moment the limiter is sharded.
- The offset is stable per key, so a repeat write cannot walk a deadline forward on every write. That was the original defect #104891 fixed, and it stays fixed: a key's lifetime is still a property of its epoch, never of when it was last written.
- Moves shard selection off `DefaultHasher`, whose algorithm the standard library does not guarantee across releases, onto SipHash-1-3. Every pod has to agree on the owner of a key, so a toolchain bump mid-rollout could otherwise split one entity's counter across two instances. `select_redis_client` returns early at one instance and never hashes, so this is **inert until the limiter is sharded**.
- Nothing user-visible changes. Limiter decisions are untouched; only the instant a key leaves Redis moves.

Keys live up to one window longer on average, so the keyspace reduction from #104891 shrinks somewhat while the over-retention fix is preserved.

## How did you test this code?

- A test asserts no key in a sample expires inside the readable window, across several key shapes including the empty string. An offset that could subtract time would expire a key that reads still consult, and the limiter would silently under-count.
- A test asserts 500 keys land on many distinct deadlines inside the window, and that the same key always resolves to the same deadline. The first catches a regression to a single shared deadline, which is the bug this fixes; the second catches a non-deterministic offset, which would re-arm a key's life on every write.
- A test shards 4000 keys the way `select_redis_client` does, at 2, 3, 4 and 8 instances, and asserts every shard still sees a wide spread of deadlines. Without the salt a 4-instance fleet sees 30 of 120 offsets per shard, and this fails.
- A golden test pins the instance each of four keys routes to at a pool of 4. A change of shard-hash algorithm splits an entity's counter across two instances and under-enforces its limit silently, so this fails instead.
- A test asserts keys spread within a factor of two of even across pools of 2, 3, 4 and 8, and that a pool of 1 skips hashing entirely.

Ran locally: `cargo test -p limiters --lib` (84 pass), `cargo check --all-targets` for `limiters` and `capture`, `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy`.

Not run: the `limiters` integration tests and benches, which need a live Redis this sandbox has no access to. The production numbers above are measured from `INFO stats` on the prod-us limiter Redis and from the limiter's own metrics.

## Automatic notifications

- [ ] Publish to changelog?

## Docs update

Updates `GLOBAL_RATE_LIMITER.md` twice.

- It stated that only 2 keys per entity exist at any time and that a key dies at the shared epoch deadline. The offset can hold the generation before the two readable ones alive for up to one more window, so up to 3 can coexist.
- Adds "Before raising the instance count" to the partitioning section: salt any new per-key derivation or it re-correlates with shard selection, and expect counters to split while a shard-count rollout is in flight. That second one fails open and clears once pods agree; a consistent-hashing scheme would shrink the window but cannot remove it.

## 🤖 Agent context

- Authored by Claude Opus 5 (1M context), model id `claude-opus-5[1m]`, running in Claude Code, supervised.
- Skills invoked: `/writing-tests`, `/writing-code-comments`, `/writing-pr-descriptions`.
- No local CodeRabbit pass: the CLI is signed out and the author chose to skip it.
- Follow-up to #104891. The periodic error pattern predates that PR, because epoch keys are wall-clock derived and key creation was always synchronized. This removes the expiry burst added on top of it, so errors should return to the prior baseline rather than to zero.

## Problem

- Node ingestion's team lookup fails for every team when its query names a column the database does not have yet.
- #105446 adds a per-team `flag_evaluations_mode` column and a Node read of it. Node pods do not wait for Django migrations, so the column and the read cannot ship in one deploy.

## Problem

- The ML mirror drops a recording message whenever its stylesheet has a colon inside a CSS custom property value, such as `--link: https://example.com/a`.
- The replay anonymizer panics on that CSS in `rewrite` at `css.rs:136` with `begin <= end ... when slicing`. The mirror fails closed on the panic and drops the message.
- Sites that use such stylesheets are therefore under-represented in the ML dataset.
- When the panic is not caught, the same records crash-loop mirror pods until the messages move on.

## Changes

- `declaration_value_ranges` now ignores a colon that falls inside the previous declaration's value.
- The cause: `css_property` accepts any trimmed segment that starts with `--`, so `--link: https` also looked like a custom property name. The scanner then started a second declaration inside the first one's value.
- A nested block in a custom property value, such as `--block: { --nested: url(…) }`, overlapped in the same way, and is fixed by the same check.
- The overlapping range was always inside the first one, so the first range already covers the whole value. The fix keeps that range and drops the nested one.
- The crate version moves from 0.7.2 to 0.7.3, as for earlier anonymizer fixes. The Node lane builds the addon from source, so no publish is needed.

## How did you test this code?

- A new unit test rewrites both CSS shapes. Against master, it panics at `css.rs:136:17` with the same message as production. With the fix, it keeps the text in order and still scrubs the inline image in each case.
- The crate's 137 unit tests and its integration suites pass locally, and clippy is clean.

## Problem

- A dashboard viewer can see an old widget while the dashboard-wide Refresh button still waits for its shared clock.
- Widgets use a 15-minute client reuse window. Insights and the manual-refresh wait use a five-minute interval.
- A failed widget request records a new fetch time, even though it did not update the data.

## Changes

- A widget with a successful result older than five minutes releases the dashboard-wide Refresh block. The widget stays under the existing feature flag.
- A normal widget refresh uses the same five-minute constant. A manual refresh still fetches every widget.
- Failed requests keep the last successful fetch time. A failed widget keeps the bulk Refresh limit; its tile has a separate retry control.
- Timers in dashboard logic update Refresh when a widget becomes stale or the dashboard limit expires.

| Case | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Widget fetched six minutes ago; shared dashboard clock is recent | Refresh blocked; normal widget request skipped | Refresh enabled; normal widget request fetches it |
| Widget request fails | New fetch time suggests fresh data | Previous successful time remains; bulk limit stays; tile retry remains available |

This is separate from [the insight-tile refresh PR](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/102793). It does not change insight refresh rules. No screenshot: the change uses the existing button states; no browser session was run.

## Problem

- Warehouse users cannot remove rows deleted at the source from an incremental table without running a full resync by hand.
- Incremental, append only, and xmin syncs read forward from a cursor, so a deleted row never leaves the table.
- Origin: https://posthog.slack.com/archives/C0A6L24BU0P/p1789497860104079

## Changes

- The Schedule section of a table gains a "Scheduled full refresh" field: every N days (1 to 90), the table is wiped and re-imported.
- The first refresh is due one interval after the setting is saved. Any full resync, manual or scheduled, restarts the wait.
- The interval cannot be shorter than the table's sync frequency, because a refresh runs on a scheduled sync.
- A warning under the field says that workflows and destinations on the table see every row again after a refresh.

![scheduled-full-refresh-v2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PostHog/pr-assets/d134bbe57fdaefb1a0b4178ce4acfa5a4f5e23a7/2026/09/ed7f3322-a2a7-4ac0-984e-2ac24b1ae81a.png)

The screenshot was replaced to show the trigger warning.

- The refresh is an ordinary scheduled sync. The create-job activity decides that a due run is a refresh, and the workflow passes that flag to the import.
- The import resets only while the schema it just loaded is still due. The first wipe moves the due time forward, so a retried attempt continues the re-import instead of wiping again.
- Nothing is stored on the schema. A run that stops before the wipe (billing limit, repartition hold) leaves no reset for later runs, and turning the setting off takes effect at once.
- There is no second schedule and no pause logic. The existing overlap policy and v3 lock already stop the refresh from racing a regular sync.
- A second schedule per table was the rejected alternative. It needs its own pause (overlap policy is per schedule) and lifecycle handling everywhere the main schedule is created, paused, or deleted.
- Only runs that the table's own schedule starts can become a refresh. The workflow reads Temporal's `TemporalScheduledById` search attribute, so admin resyncs and non-billable resumes keep their behavior.
- The due check fires up to one hour early (or half the sync interval, if shorter), so each refresh stays on the same tick instead of slipping one tick per cycle.
- The wipe restarts the clock inside the reset's locked write, from the interval on the locked row, and the v2 per-chunk cursor save now writes only `sync_type_config`. An interval edited during a run survives both.
- A scheduled full refresh skips the pre-import repartition, because the import deletes the table before extracting.
- A repartition that holds the import defers the refresh until it resolves. The deferral and the import hold share one check, so the two cannot disagree.
- `full_refresh_interval_days` (writable) and `next_full_refresh_at` (read-only) are new on the schema endpoint and the bulk update endpoint. The MCP resync tool now points agents at the setting.
- The incremental-fields action now declares no request body, so its MCP discovery tool stops advertising schema settings it ignores.
- The migration adds two nullable columns, without a `CHECK`, so it is metadata-only.
- Mechanical: regenerated OpenAPI types and MCP tools, the Schedule save moved to the generated client, the activity log skips the derived timestamp, and the create-job input dataclass is now frozen.

> [!NOTE]
> Queries keep returning the current rows until a refresh finishes, because they read the published table. Re-imported rows are billable, the same as a manual full resync. A team near its billing limit sees each due sync fail the billing check until the limit rises or the setting is turned off.

Review first: the decision in `create_job_model.py` and its use in `external_data_job.py`. The workflow reads one new activity output field (default false) and adds no command, so replay is unaffected.

## How did you test this code?

- Model tests pin the due check to the tick nearest the due time (daily and half-hourly), and assert it never fires for full refresh, CDC, or webhook tables.
- A model test edits the interval between loading the run's copy and the wipe. The wipe keeps the edit and restarts the clock from it.
- Activity tests assert only a due, schedule-started run returns the refresh flag, and nothing is written to the schema.
- A workflow test asserts the import learns about a refresh only when the create-job activity reports one.
- A resolver test asserts a retry after the wipe does not reset again.
- A model test edits the interval between loading the run's copy and a cursor save, and asserts the save keeps the edit. The workflow test also asserts a refresh skips the repartition.
- A unit test pins the schedule check: own schedule, another schedule, and a direct start.
- API tests cover the clock rules (enable, change, re-save, clear, switch sync method, reject), the sync frequency minimum in both directions, and the bulk endpoint keeping the field.
- Each new guard was removed once, and the matching test failed each time.
- A real Temporal dev server confirmed that schedule fires and manual triggers carry `TemporalScheduledById`, and direct starts do not.
- The UI was rendered in an uncommitted Storybook story: the field states, the warning, the out-of-range Save reason, the saved payload, and a 520px layout.
- Not run: a scheduled refresh against a real source. No `test-new-events-schema` label: nothing touches events.

## Release status

- [x] No feature flag controls this change <!-- release-status: no-feature-flag -->
- [ ] This change is behind a feature flag and is not available to users <!-- release-status: behind-feature-flag -->
- [ ] This change makes a previously flagged feature available to everyone <!-- release-status: fully-available -->

The setting defaults to null, so nothing changes until someone sets it.

## Automatic notifications

## Docs update

None in this repo.

## 🤖 Agent context

**Autonomy:** Human-driven (agent-assisted)

**Agent:** Claude Code, Claude Fable 5.1 (plan) and Claude Opus 5.5 (implementation)

- Daniel set the design over several planning rounds: days from 1 to 90, incremental, append, and xmin only, first refresh one interval after saving, any wipe restarts the clock, and a numeric input like the lookback window.

## Problem

- The team that trains the inbox ranking model cannot see a score on a real report, so the model stays unvalidated.
- The daily pipeline trains, calibrates and promotes a model, then discards every probability it produces, because nothing on the product side can hold one.
- `SignalReportArtefact.ArtefactType` has 28 members and none of them is a score, so the planned scoring sweep has nowhere to write.

Closes #106061

<!-- posthog-self-driving-origin:01a0d434-9470-70a4-a8a8-13ffc133caf8 -->
## Origin

- Issues: [#106061](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/issues/106061)
- First signal: 2026-09-24
- Inbox report: [open](https://us.posthog.com/project/2/inbox/reports/01a0d434-9470-70a4-a8a8-13ffc133caf8)
- Likely cause: [`b362fcf`](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/commit/b362fcf0166e92f6ea74ae65b554b39cd2ad63f3)
- Task started by: auto-start, after the report was rated P3 and ready to fix
<!-- /posthog-self-driving-origin:01a0d434-9470-70a4-a8a8-13ffc133caf8 -->

## Changes

- Nothing user-visible changes. No report carries a score until the sweep lands, and the inbox keeps its heuristic order.
- `ranking_score` joins the artefact type enum as a status artefact, so the newest row is the report's current score.
- `RankingScore` holds one scoring pass: the served model and its challengers, keyed by `<model_name>@<model_version>`.
- One row per pass, not one row per model. "The current served score" has to be answerable from a single row, and a pass that runs a different set of models would otherwise leave stale rows looking current.
- Validators keep the served entry resolvable and every score a probability.

  | Rule | Why it holds |
  | --- | --- |
  | `served_key` names a `scored` entry that carries the `served` role | A consumer reads the served score as `results[served_key]` |
  | Each key equals its entry's `model_name@model_version` | The key is the join handle back to the training partition |
  | Every score falls in `[0, 1]` | A threshold and the composite score over the heads both read it as a probability |
  | Exactly one entry carries `served` | Two make the served score ambiguous |
  | `results` holds 1 to 5 models | Bounds the row, so a grown manifest cannot make every report read expensive |

- The artefact API refuses `ranking_score`. The scoring sweep is its only writer, so an API write would let a caller fabricate model output.
- Mechanical: the generated signals API type enum picks up the new value.
- No migration. The `choices` field is callable, so growing the enum changes no schema.

> [!NOTE]
> `artefact_count` on the inbox row is a `Count("*")` over every artefact type. Once the sweep writes on a schedule, every report's activity count climbs with no human work behind it. The counter needs a decision in the sweep PR, not here, because nothing writes this type yet.

## How did you test this code?

Added cases to the existing parameterized boundary tests rather than new test functions, since each is a variation of "does this payload parse as this type".

- `test_registry_covers_every_artefact_type_exactly` already fails if the enum member and the schema land apart.
- The reject cases each name a shape a consumer would break on: a `served_key` outside `results` (KeyError on read), a served entry that is `skipped` (a served score that does not exist), a key that names another model (the join handle points at the wrong partition), a score above 1 (a raw margin stored as a probability), two served entries, an empty `results`, and a `results` past the cap.
- Folded the `code_review` write-rejection test into a parameterized one and added `ranking_score`, so a type added to the enum but left out of `NON_WRITABLE_ARTEFACT_TYPES` fails here.
- Ran locally: the three artefact suites, `ruff`, repo-wide `mypy`, and `makemigrations --check` (no changes detected).
- Not run: the frontend suites. The generated diff is one enum member, and `ARTEFACT_TYPE_LABELS` is keyed by plain string, so the activity log needs no new renderer. Nothing was checked in a browser, because the dev stack does not boot in this sandbox (the plugin-server native build fails).
- Not classified for `test-new-events-schema`: the diff touches no event ingestion, event or property read, or generated event-table SQL.

Latest-row-wins is the status semantic, and the key lets a SQL reader over the `content` column pluck the served model without scanning roles.

## Problem

- An ML image-fetch pod exits when one crawl-history DynamoDB command runs past its command timeout.
- The timeout aborts the command, and the AWS SDK does not retry an aborted command, so the whole fetch batch fails.
- consumer-v2 latches the failed batch and exits its loop. The pod then exits on the unhandled rejection.
- The restart repeats every fetch in flight and replays the pod's partitions from the last commit.
- If a partition's committed offset is older than the topic retention, the restart also resets that offset past messages that retention deleted.

## Changes

- A crawl-history command that times out now backs off and retries, like a batch with unprocessed items.
- The retries use the existing limit of 5 attempts and the existing batch budget. A timeout on the last attempt still fails the batch.
- Other failures still fail the batch at once.
- Retrying is safe because a batch get or batch write of the same items is idempotent.
- A retried write can land after a newer write of the same key from an overlapping fetch pass. The aborted request can do that too, because DynamoDB may still apply it.
- The retry therefore adds no new kind of reordering. The worst case is a history record a few seconds older.
- Conditional writes would prevent the reordering, but `BatchWriteItem` does not support them. Most timeouts in production come from writes, so retrying only reads would not stop the crashes.
- `withTimeout` turns our own abort into a `CommandTimeoutError`, so the retry loops can tell a timeout from other failures.
- The ML mirror's URL precheck uses the same class, with a budget equal to its timeout. A timed-out precheck read still fails there, now with the budget error, and the precheck already catches any failure.
- `IMPLEMENTATION_NOTES.md` states the retry. The worst-case timing note stays true: the batch budget plus one command timeout.

## How did you test this code?

- A new parameterized test makes the first batch get or batch write hang until the command timeout aborts it. Against master, it fails with `AbortError: Request aborted`, which is the error that the pods log. With the fix, the retry completes.
- A second test makes every attempt time out. The operation fails with the timeout error after exactly 5 sends. The test also fails if the attempt cap is removed.
- The existing tests for request failures and exhausted retries still pass, so other failures still fail at once.
- Not checked: a timeout in a deployed pod.

## Problem

- Failed Depot CI jobs have no logs in PostHog, so `run_failure_logs`, broken tests and `hogli ci:insights view --logs` show nothing for Depot-routed PRs.
- [Read depot ci runs and jobs](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/106074) added their runs and jobs, not their logs.

## Changes

- The job-logs coordinator now also fetches failed Depot CI job attempts and emits their thinned logs to Logs, like failed GitHub jobs.
- Discovery reads failed attempts from each Depot source's `job_attempts` table, oldest first.
- A backlog over the 2,000-attempt cap pages forward across ticks. The coordinator returns a per-source cursor, and the schedule hands it to the next run as its [last completion result](https://docs.temporal.io/schedule).
- A page that does not fill the cap clears the cursor, so the next tick rereads the 24-hour window and finds rows that landed late.
- Logs carry the same integer `run_id` and `job_id` the runs and jobs views give Depot rows, so every log read joins them. The rule lives once in `depot_ci.py`.
- The fetch pages Depot's `GetJobAttemptLogs` with the team's own Depot token, under a head-and-tail byte cap shared with the GitHub fetcher.
- Each page streams, and a page over the byte cap or the remaining read budget is dropped before JSON decoding.
- A Depot 429 hands `Retry-After` to the Temporal retry. No PostHog egress budget applies, because the token is the team's own.
- The Depot child workflow has no execution timeout, so its retry policy bounds it. While it waits out `Retry-After`, its id stays taken and a later tick cannot fetch early.
- The coordinator change sits behind `workflow.patched("depot-job-logs-2026-09")`, so in-flight executions replay unchanged.
- Child workflows use `depot-logs-{team}-{attempt}` ids, apart from GitHub's `gh-logs-…`.
- Not covered: retried-then-passed Depot jobs. That recovery path matches GitHub runner names.

## How did you test this code?

- ClickHouse test: discovery picks only recent failed attempts, skips push runs, and keys multi-workflow runs by workflow id.
- The same test, with the cap at 2: the second tick returns the attempt the first tick left out. The old newest-first query fails it.
- Fetcher tests: pagination, byte cap, 404, and 401 and 429 handling, with no token in error text.
- Fetcher test: a page over the read budget is never decoded, and the pages read before it are kept.
- Activity tests: Depot ids reach the emitter as integers.
- A time-skipping Temporal run started the Depot child workflow. A replay of a pre-change coordinator history found no nondeterminism.
- A second time-skipping run (not committed) checked that the cursors serialize into the run result and that the child starts with no execution timeout.
- Not run: a live schedule passing the cursor between two runs.
- Not run: a call against the live Depot API. Shapes come from the Depot CLI's generated protobuf code.

## Problem

A MySQL/MariaDB sync backed by Vitess or PlanetScale can fail mid-sync with `OperationalError (1105, ... code = Canceled desc = grpc: the client connection is closing)`, surfaced by [error tracking](https://us.posthog.com/project/2/error_tracking/01a0d439-5a42-75b0-b22a-56da3163e280).

This fires while streaming rows, when vtgate's own gRPC client to the backend vttablet was already closing as the query's RPC went out — a tablet swap during a failover, reparent, or pool recycle. It is the same self-healing class as the `code = Unavailable` and "reparent operation in progress" Vitess conditions already handled, but it was missing its own classification, so every occurrence logged at `exception` level and paged as if it were a bug.

## Changes

- Classify `grpc: the client connection is closing` as retryable in `MySQLSource.get_retryable_errors`, matching the existing sibling Vitess 1105 entries.
- No behavior change to retries themselves: Temporal's own activity retry already recovers this once vtgate reconnects. This only stops the noise reaching error tracking.

## How did you test this code?

Added a parameterized case to `TestMySQLSourceNonRetryableErrors`, mirroring the existing `test_vitess_reparent_is_classified_retryable` test, asserting the new message is recognised as retryable. Ran the full `test_mysql.py` suite locally: 318 passed.

Not run: a live sync against a real Vitess/PlanetScale backend, because this sandbox has no such database.

## Problem

- `event_names` and `excluded_properties` are documented as JSON-encoded, but nothing validated them.

body:
## Problem

Evaluation scripts need an authenticated API to store results in Postgres.
[The model PR](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/105418) added the tables; this adds ingestion and experiment lifecycle operations.

## Changes

Callers can create an experiment, upload results against existing scorer versions, and explicitly complete or fail the experiment.
The base path is `/api/projects/{project_id}/ai_observability/offline_experiments/`.

| POST operation | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `/` | Create an experiment; an identical retry returns the existing record. |
| `/{experiment_id}/upload/` | Atomically accept one or many results and their shared items. |
| `/{experiment_id}/complete/` | Check declared counts and close the experiment. |
| `/{experiment_id}/fail/` | Close an interrupted experiment while preserving accepted data. |

- Exact retries preserve identities and acceptance times, including after closure or payload deletion; changed content returns a conflict.
- Uploads and closure lock the same experiment, preventing completion from racing with new writes.
- Invalid batches return all detected validation failures with indexed field paths; every upload remains atomic.
- Numeric scores tolerate bounded floating-point rounding at minimum and maximum values.
- Sessions, personal keys, and project secret keys use the separate `offline_evaluation_ingestion:write` scope.
- Pinned scorer versions share configuration validation with manual reviews; hosted dataset references must belong to the pinned revision.
- Request, payload, and rate limits bound ingestion work; payload deadlines prepare for later retention cleanup.

Thin viewsets handle HTTP concerns; typed submissions and product services own validation, transactions, and lifecycle rules.
Scope-picker registration and generated API/Kea/MCP types accompany the new permission and endpoint schemas.
Read APIs, SDK integration, billing, and retention workers remain separate changes.

**Before**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Script[Evaluation script] --> Capture[Event capture API] --> CH[ClickHouse events]
    Models[Postgres evaluation tables]
    classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
    classDef phRed fill:#f54e00,stroke:#f54e00,color:#fff;
    classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
    class Script phYellow;
    class Capture phRed;
    class CH,Models phGray;
```

**After** — the existing event reporter remains unchanged.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Script[Evaluation script] --> API[Create / upload / close API] --> Service[Experiment services] --> PG[Postgres evaluation tables]
    Script --> Capture[Existing event capture] --> CH[ClickHouse events]
    classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
    classDef phRed fill:#f54e00,stroke:#f54e00,color:#fff;
    classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
    classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
    class Script phYellow;
    class API,Capture phRed;
    class Service phBlue;
    class PG,CH phGray;
```

## How did you test this code?

- PostgreSQL service/API tests cover atomic rollback, immutable retries, ownership, dataset membership/deletion, counts, and concurrent upload/closure orderings.
- Authentication tests exercise real personal/project-secret credentials, session access, scopes, rollout gating, and throttling.
- Parser, serializer, fingerprint, and shared scorer tests cover malformed input and normalization; existing manual-review tests protect that extraction.
- Numeric regression tests cover rounded boundaries, reject meaningful overshoots and off-step scores, and prevent Decimal crashes with tiny steps.
- Batch tests report multiple invalid scores, dataset references, and field errors together, while preserving atomic rejection.
- Action-schema tests check upload and closure request/response contracts; conflict tests preserve count fields in HTTP 409 responses.
- Local probes accepted and replayed 1,000-result, 4.7 MB batches with either one or 1,000 distinct scorer versions.
- Repository-wide mypy, frontend TypeScript, OpenAPI generation, scoped security rules, preflight, and commit hooks passed.

Native JSON event-table coverage: not applicable; this adds Postgres ingestion and does not change event-table reads or capture.

Browser QA used the existing Storybook personal-key modal: the new scope renders correctly, disables Read, and allows Write.
No API key was created.

## Problem

- Engineering analytics cannot see backend CI runs that PostHog/posthog routes to Depot CI.
- On those PRs, cost, job durations, retries and flaky-test setup checks miss the Depot jobs.

## Changes

- Runs, jobs and cost now include Depot CI runs when a Depot source syncs the same repository.
- `logic/views/depot_ci.py` reshapes Depot attempts into the GitHub runs and jobs contracts and unions them onto those tables. No builder changes.
- Each Depot workflow is one runs row. A single-workflow run decodes its id to the numeric `GITHUB_RUN_ID` Depot CI stamps on its per-test traces, so traces join these jobs.
- A run with several workflows keys each workflow by its own decoded id, so no join fans out.
- The PR number comes from `refs/pull/<n>/merge`, and the branch from that PR's snapshot, so branch filters include Depot rows.
- Cost assumes the default `depot-ubuntu-24.04` sandbox, because the Depot API reports no `runs-on`.
- Endpoint reads look up the Depot table lazily, like the Trunk tables. The team views attach it once per repository.
- A Depot load re-syncs the managed views.
- Not in scope: failure logs of Depot jobs.

## How did you test this code?

- ClickHouse test: Depot attempts come out of the runs, jobs and cost builders with decoded ids, per-workflow keys, PR number, branch and Depot pricing.
- Resolver test: a Depot table joins only the repository it syncs, once.
- View sync test: a Depot load re-syncs the views.
- The decode rule matched the trace run ids of two real Depot runs.

body:
## Problem

- CI runs on Depot CI (Depot's own engine, not Depot runners under GitHub Actions) never reach the GitHub source, so PostHog has no record of them.
- The Depot source was a hidden stub with no tables.

## Changes

- The Depot source syncs one table, `job_attempts`: one row per job attempt, with its run, workflow and job fields.
- Setup takes an organization API token and one `owner/name` repository. Released as alpha.
- Each run is read with `GetRunStatus`, then `GetWorkflow` per workflow. `GetRunMetrics` would be one call, but Depot refuses it for runs with many attempts.
- A sync reads only runs created before the oldest in-flight run, so each run is read once, after it finishes.
- A run stuck in `queued` for over 6 hours stops holding the sync back. A `running` run always holds it.
- Each row records `run_workflow_count`, so readers need no self-join to count a run's workflows.
- A first sync reaches back 7 days.
- Known gap: a job retried after its run synced is not picked up.
- [Read depot ci runs and jobs](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/106074) joins these rows into engineering analytics.

## How did you test this code?

- Unit tests over mocked HTTP: paging stops at the watermark, queued and running runs hold the horizon, rows come out oldest first, every workflow of a run is read, 401 and 403 map to messages.

body:
## Problem

- A Postgres batch export for a mutable model (persons, sessions) can retry for hours when another session holds row locks on the destination table.
- The final merge waits on the lock until the destination's own `statement_timeout` cancels it, if one is set. Temporal then retries the activity without limit, and each retry waits again.
- The user sees `QueryCanceled: canceling statement due to statement timeout`, which does not say that a lock can be the cause.

## Changes

- A merge blocked by a lock now fails after 5 minutes (`SET LOCAL lock_timeout`). Before, it waited until the destination's `statement_timeout`, or without limit.
- The client retries the merge up to 3 times, with backoff, on a lock timeout or a `statement_timeout` cancel. A short lock can go away between attempts.
- After the last attempt, the run fails with the non-retryable `PostgreSQLMergeTimeoutError`. The user sees the cause and how to find the blocking session with `pg_stat_activity` and `pg_blocking_pids()`.
- Other `QueryCanceled` errors (for example, an administrator cancel) are not retried by this loop, and keep their current behavior.
- `lock_timeout` is set in a savepoint. A Postgres-compatible server that rejects it logs a warning, and the merge runs as before without a lock limit.
- Redshift is not affected. It uses a different merge method.
- Mechanical: `amerge_mutable_tables` is split into `_build_merge_query` (SQL only), `_amerge_once` (one attempt in one transaction) and the retry with error conversion. The unused `merge_condition` is removed. The generated SQL does not change, which was checked by comparing the old and new output.

## How did you test this code?

- New test `test_amerge_mutable_tables_raises_non_retryable_error_when_a_row_lock_blocks_it`: a second connection locks a row. The merge must raise `PostgreSQLMergeTimeoutError`, and the error name must be in `NON_RETRYABLE_ERROR_TYPES`. It catches a merge that waits on a lock until the statement timeout. With `lock_timeout` removed, an earlier version of this test failed after the full 60-second merge timeout.
- Checked with temporary tests, not committed: 2 attempts against a held lock ran both lock waits and then raised. A 1-second `statement_timeout` on the test database gave the statement timeout message.
- Ran locally: `test_postgres_client.py` and the Postgres `test_activity.py` suite. `test_insert_into_postgres_activity_merges_persons_data_in_follow_up_runs` failed once on a ClickHouse error before the merge. It also failed without this change, and passed on a second run.
- Not labeled `test-new-events-schema`: the diff does not read or write the events table.

## Problem

- A Self-driving report can show an implementation run as failed after the agent opens a pull request and finishes its turn.
- The run stays open to watch the pull request, and the wall-clock limit currently marks every such exit as failed.
- A later report revision cannot replace that pull request while predecessor selection requires a completed run.

## Changes

- A delivered implementation run now completes when its last turn succeeded, the agent is idle, and no follow-up remains pending.
- The run retains `timed_out_wall_clock` so the end of monitoring remains visible. Runs without a delivered pull request or with unfinished work still fail.
- A Temporal patch preserves replay behavior. Existing terminal run records remain unchanged.
- Later research can replace a timed-out predecessor only when the server verified its pull request and the normal automation and live GitHub checks pass.

Before:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  PR["PR opened"] --> Watch["Watch for feedback"] --> Cap["Wall-clock limit"] --> Failed["Failed run"]
  class PR,Cap phYellow;
  class Watch phBlue;
  class Failed phRed;
  classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
  classDef phRed fill:#f54e00,stroke:#f54e00,color:#fff;
  classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
```

After:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  PR["PR opened"] --> Watch["Watch for feedback"] --> Cap["Wall-clock limit"] --> Finished{"Turn finished and no work pending?"}
  Finished -->|Yes| Complete["Completed run"]
  Finished -->|No| Failed["Failed run"]
  class PR,Cap phYellow;
  class Watch phBlue;
  class Finished phGray;
  class Complete phBlue;
  class Failed phRed;
  classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
  classDef phRed fill:#f54e00,stroke:#f54e00,color:#fff;
  classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
  classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
```
