body:
## Problem

The serving image batches requests: vLLM's scheduler keeps every row in an in-memory queue and packs rows from all callers into each forward pass. But its queue has no limit. Under overload, the wait becomes longer than the gateway's 10 s timeout, and then nearly every request fails. On one L4 at twice its capacity, only 26% of its capacity came back as answers, and 86% of requests timed out.

## Changes

- `bin/serve.sh` passes `--max-num-queued-tokens` (`MAX_NUM_QUEUED_TOKENS`, default 24,000, about four seconds of an L4's prefill). vLLM then answers 503 when its prefill backlog is full. In the load test, that kept the box at full throughput at twice its capacity, rejected nothing below capacity, and kept the slowest answers at about half the gateway's wait.
- `JevK5Pooler` reads each row's last hidden state in one gather and one matmul, in place of `AllPool`. So a row that is split across steps holds no hidden states between steps.
- `PendingRequests` moves to `kev_vllm/pending.py`, and each entry expires on its own after a maximum age. Before, entries expired only after 10k had collected. A 503 comes after `pre_process`, so every rejected request left an entry behind.
- The README gets a Batching section and a dated load test on an L4.

The token budget stays at vLLM's default. On an L4, prefill is compute-bound: 2,048 tokens per step was as fast as 8,192 or 16,384, and had a shorter latency tail.

## How did you test this code?

Load test on one L4 (EC2 gr6.4xlarge) with this branch's image and JevK5 at revision `27d2d6b8`, on JevBench's public items. The README has the tables.

| Queue limit | Offered load | Answers within 10 s | 503 | Timed out |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| none | 2.0x capacity | 3.3/s | 0% | 86% |
| 23,260 | 0.9x | 11.9/s | 0% | 0% |
| 23,260 | 2.0x | 12.9/s | 49% | 0% |

- The new readout matches `AllPool`'s on 294 items to a median 0.0016 (maximum 0.022), inside JevK5's own bf16-versus-fp32 gap of 0.059, at the same throughput.
- A T4 starts with this image in fp16 and serves about 1,270 tokens/s, a fifth of an L4.
- `tests/test_pending.py` fails if an entry outlives its age, including under a reused request id. Both tests were checked red then green.

Not covered: at 2x load, 49% of requests get a 503, near the gateway breaker's 50% threshold. Beyond that load, the breaker opens the host for 5 s.

## Problem

A ClickHouse sync keeps retrying to the maximum instead of stopping, when the source server's own result-size limit rejects the extraction query for a table that is too large for it.

[Error tracking](https://us.posthog.com/project/2/error_tracking/01a0d400-3121-7e93-9ed8-3c8cf1350c0a) surfaced this as a `DatabaseError`: `TOO_MANY_ROWS_OR_BYTES` (code 396), `Limit for result exceeded, max bytes: 500.00 MiB`. The source's ClickHouse-compatible endpoint enforces a `max_result_bytes`/`max_result_rows` cap on the connecting user, and the query producing this table's result set exceeds it.

## Changes

- Add `TOO_MANY_ROWS_OR_BYTES` to `ClickHouseSource.get_non_retryable_errors()`, matching the error-code name rather than `Code: 396` because this endpoint wraps the error without the usual native `Code: NNN. DB::Exception:` wording.
- The user-facing message follows the existing `Code: 241` (memory limit) / `Code: 243` (disk space) pattern: this is a capacity/config limit on the customer's database, and retrying replays the identical failure, so we stop and tell them to raise the limit, sync fewer columns, or switch to an incremental sync.
- Mechanical: extend the existing non-retryable-error test with this message shape.

## How did you test this code?

Ran the source's full test suite locally: `pytest products/warehouse_sources/backend/temporal/data_imports/sources/clickhouse/test_clickhouse.py` — 264 passed, including the new case. One unrelated pre-existing test in that file errors in this sandbox for lack of a reachable Postgres fixture DB; not touched by this change.

Not run: CI (will run on push).

None — this only changes internal retry classification, no documented behavior changes.

## Problem

- When Salesforce routes a lead to a TAE or TAM on an account nobody has enrolled, customer analytics records nothing, so the rep still adds themselves as AE by hand. Most routed leads land on such accounts: the claim is refused as `role_not_managed`.
- Leads from EU-hosted organizations would be refused as well. The claim compared the Task's region with the instance region (US), but one project holds accounts from both clouds.
- Stacked on [#106046](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/106046), which pins the claim view.

## Changes

- An accepted claim enrolls the account under every controlled definition it lacks (AE and CSM today), the same rule as a person's edit since [#105292](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/105292). Billing then hands the customer off and writes the rep to Salesforce.
- Control starts at the claim's allocation time, not at the sweep. A later lead that Salesforce allocated before the sweep, after the first one was released, can then still claim.
- On an account not yet enrolled, the fence is the relationship's last change by any writer. A clear made while the account had no `external_id` (which enrolls nothing) still refuses an older Task.
- A sibling that a claim enrolls starts at its own last change, not at the claim's allocation time. A sibling Task allocated earlier can still claim once a second definition takes claims.
- A refused claim enrolls nothing. Every refusal returns before enrollment, inside one transaction.
- Claims accept both cloud regions, `us` and `eu`.
- `claim()` locks every controlled definition in id order before the account, the order every writer takes. `_enroll_locked` becomes the public `enroll_locked`.
- Mechanical: the `role_not_managed` reason and `ownership.region_matches` are removed, and docstrings name the claim as a second enrollment path.

> [!WARNING]
> Enrollment by a claim makes customer analytics authoritative for every controlled role on that account. The CSM, empty or not, then wins in Salesforce, as it already does after a person's edit.

## How did you test this code?

- New and extended tests in `test_ownership_claims.py`:
  - An accepted claim on an unenrolled account enrolls exactly the controlled definitions, keeps the sibling's holder, and attributes the audit rows to the claim. An account enrolled under AE only gains CSM.
  - Refused claims on an unenrolled account (occupied role, future allocation) enroll nothing.
  - An `eu` claim is accepted on a US instance, and an unknown region is refused.
  - A second Task allocated before the sweep claims the account after the first Task's release.
  - A clear made while the account was unlinked refuses an older Task, and a sibling Task allocated before an enrolling claim still claims the sibling.

## Problem

- Anyone who can edit a warehouse view in a project could make a bound claim view return any decision rows. The ownership claim sweep of [#100044](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/100044) would then apply them to account ownership.
- No definition has claims enabled yet. This pin is a gate before the first one does.

## Changes

- Binding a claim view stores the SHA-256 of its SQL and switches claims off. A person enables claims in a separate call, after checking the printed digest against the SQL they reviewed.
- Each sweep executes the pinned text as a subquery, not the view by name. It refuses the view as `misconfigured` once the view's SQL no longer matches the pin.
- The check refuses a view that reads another saved query, or a field defined outside its text (a warehouse join or a saved expression). It runs at binding and on every sweep.
- The check and every page of the read share one catalog, and a page is also refused when its execution reached a saved query. A join or a saved expression added after the check cannot shape the rows.
- Claims and releases re-check the binding (view, digest, enabled) under the definition lock, so rows read under an older binding never apply.
- `configure_account_ownership` prints `claim_view_sha256`. It refuses binding and enabling the same definition in one call, and it refuses enabling an unpinned binding.
- Migration 0058 adds one nullable column to a table that is not hot. The data_modeling facade gains one read, `get_saved_query_sql`.
- Nothing user-visible changes apart from the command output.

> [!NOTE]
> The pin covers the view's text, not the sources behind its table names. A person who can reconfigure a warehouse source can still change the rows. The claim rules limit such rows to empty roles, active organization members and allocations after the fence.

## How did you test this code?

- New and extended tests in `test_ownership_claims.py` and `test_account_ownership_commands.py`:
  - An edited view, a missing pin, an upstream saved query, a join field, a saved expression, and an execution that reached a saved query are each refused before any decision applies. The project's other definitions still run.
  - A rebind during a sweep (a moved view, or a new pin) applies nothing from the old rows, for claims and for releases.
  - The command refuses bind-and-enable in one call and enabling an unpinned binding. A rebind after an edit prints a new digest.
  - One test runs the pinned read through HogQL and ClickHouse, with paging and a Salesforce `+0000` timestamp.
- Each new guard was removed once locally, and its test failed.

body: ## Problem On the MCP analytics Tool quality tab, there is no way to spot a tool whose usage suddenly surged. The table shows each tool's calls for the selected window only, so a tool that jumps from a few hundred to thousands of calls a week looks like any other mid-sized tool. A prompt or harness change that starts calling a tool everywhere goes unnoticed until someone stumbles on it. Stacked on #106038. Origin: https://posthog.slack.com/archives/C0B3E1Y576X/p1790236415678759 ## Changes - The Tool quality table has a sortable "Trend" column after Calls. It shows the change in calls versus the previous period of the same length ("+3,043%", "-12%"), or "New" for tools with no calls in the previous period. - Sorting by Trend ranks tools by `(calls - previous) / (previous + k)`, not by raw percent. `k` is at least 10 and grows with overall volume (0.01% of all calls in the window). Without it, a tool going from 2 to 40 calls outranks one going from 200 to 5,000. - The Trend text is neutral, with no green or red, because a surge can be good or bad. - For to-date ranges such as "This month", the previous period is the same part of the previous unit, matching how other PostHog comparisons work. - `MCPToolQualityRowsQuery` rows gain `previous_calls` and `trend_score`, and `trend_score` is a new sort column. The runner scans both windows in one query with an `is_current` column. Every existing metric still covers the current window only. - `seed_mcp_sessions` gains `--surge-tool NAME`, which makes one tool spike in the most recent quarter of `--days`, for demos and local testing. The ranking was chosen by backtesting three options (raw percent, absolute change, smoothed ratio) against real tool-call history. Only the smoothed ratio put a known prompt-driven surge near the top instead of burying it under the largest tools or tiny ones. No data from that check is in this PR. Before and after on the Tool quality table, demo data, 1440px window: | Before | After | |---|---| | | | The Sessions cell wraps at this width here; #106656 keeps it on one line. ## How did you test this code? - Extended `test_tool_quality_tables.py`. The new tests catch: previous-window events leaking into current metrics, tools with only previous calls showing up or counting in the total, the ranking putting a small big-percent tool above a larger surge, and "This month" counting the whole previous month (this test fails with the earlier logic). - Not yet rendered: the Trend column has no story, and the devbox check is pending. - Labeled `test-new-events-schema` because the diff changes generated SQL over events. ## Release status - [x] No feature flag controls this change - [ ] This change is behind a feature flag and is not available to users - [ ] This change makes a previously flagged feature available to everyone ## Automatic notifications - [ ] Publish to changelog? ## Docs update None. ## 🤖 Agent context **Autonomy:** Human-driven (agent-assisted) **Agent:** Claude Code, Claude Opus 5.5 (design, backtest, review, fixes) with a Claude Sonnet 5 delegate (implementation) - CodeRabbit CLI pass found one issue, fixed: the previous period was not bounded by its own end for to-date ranges. - Review changed the delegate's first version to scan events once (it referenced a CTE twice, which ClickHouse runs twice), replaced eleven copies of the window predicate with one column, and made the Trend color neutral. - Pre-PR adversarial review (Claude Opus and Claude Fable). Fixed: the previous window overlapped the current one by a day on -7d and -14d (the default range), and after clipping it was a partial day shorter, so flat tools showed about +7%. It now has the same length as the current window, and the scan covers only the two windows. Also fixed: +0%/-0% rendering, the sort type now comes from the schema, and `--surge-tool` needs `--days`. Not changed: the smoothing constant is computed over the filtered set, so search can change scores (ordering within the results stays sensible); "All time" shows every tool as New because nothing precedes it.
title: feat(mcp-analytics): surface trending tools on tool quality

body: ## Problem On an MCP tool's detail page, you can't tell whether a tool is a rare call or one that shows up in most sessions. The page shows calls and sessions as absolute numbers only, so answering "what share of activity is this tool?" takes hand-written SQL. Call share and session share can tell opposite stories: a tool can be a tiny fraction of calls and still run in most sessions of one harness. Origin: https://posthog.slack.com/archives/C0B3E1Y576X/p1790236415678759 ## Changes - The Calls tile shows the tool's share of all calls (for example "0.041% of all calls"). - The Sessions tile shows the share of sessions the tool appears in ("In 6.6% of sessions"). - The "By harness" table has a new "Session share" column: the tool's sessions in that harness, out of all sessions in that harness. - `MCPToolStatsQuery` returns `total_calls` and `total_conversations`. `MCPHarnessBreakdownQuery`, when scoped to a tool, returns `harness_sessions`. The MCP query tools pick these up from the same schema. - Numerators and denominators come from one scan with an `is_tool` column, so both sides share the same filters and session id by construction. - Session counts use one shared conversation id (MCP session id, falling back to the PostHog session id), and calls without any session id no longer count as a session. This also applies to the daily sessions sparkline, and to the dashboard's harness breakdown, whose session counts can rise slightly for SDKs that only send an MCP session id. - At narrow widths the harness and top users tables drop their lowest-priority columns instead of clipping. - Mechanical: the conversation id expression moves to `base.py` (it had two copies), the tool predicate splits into source and tool parts, and there is a new tool detail story. Before and after on the tool detail page, demo data, 1440px window: | Before | After | |---|---| | | | | | | The "before" Top users table clips its Last seen column; the "after" drops low-priority columns instead. The Storybook screenshot this section had earlier is replaced by these live captures. ## How did you test this code? - Extended `test_tool_tables.py` and `test_harness_breakdown.py`. They catch: denominators missing other tools, shared filters not narrowing the denominators, harness share not counting sessions that only carry an MCP session id, and empty session ids inflating the session count. - Rendered the new `MCPAnalyticsToolDetail` story at full width and at 520px in a headless browser. - Not yet checked in a running app against real events. A devbox with seeded data is in progress. - Labeled `test-new-events-schema` because the diff changes generated SQL over events. ## Release status - [x] No feature flag controls this change - [ ] This change is behind a feature flag and is not available to users - [ ] This change makes a previously flagged feature available to everyone ## Automatic notifications - [ ] Publish to changelog? ## Docs update None. ## 🤖 Agent context **Autonomy:** Human-driven (agent-assisted) **Agent:** Claude Code, Claude Opus 5.5 (design, review, fixes) with Claude Sonnet 5 delegates (implementation, story) - CodeRabbit CLI pass found two issues, both fixed: the harness share used a different session id than the Sessions tile, and empty session ids counted as a session. - The ranking and share definitions were checked against real tool-call data before implementation. No data from that check is in this PR. - Pre-PR adversarial review (Claude Opus and Claude Fable). Fixed: the stats query had its own copy of the tool-call WHERE, two spellings for excluding empty conversation ids, and a wrong comment about `formatPercentage`. Review bots then raised that the harness breakdown counted sessions by `$session_id` on the overview but by conversation id on tool detail; both paths now use the conversation id.

```text
image builder run                 model = zai-org/glm-5.3-flash

```

body:
## Problem

- An `@posthog/agent` release fails to publish when a workflow file changes on master right after an agent commit merges.
- This blocked agent 2.4.221 and 2.4.223 today, and 2.4.120 on 2026-09-01.
- The tag job tags the commit that triggered it, which is often behind master by the time it pushes.
- When master changed a workflow file since that commit, GitHub checks whether the new tag changes workflows.
- The release App has no `workflows` permission. On this repo the check times out, and GitHub rejects the push with GH013.
- A rerun tags the same commit, so it cannot pass.

## Changes

- The tag job tags the master head it fetches right before the push, so the tag's workflow files match master.
- The patch number counts agent and harness commits up to that same commit.
- A rejected push refetches master, recomputes the tag, and retries up to three times. This covers a workflow change that lands between the fetch and the push.
- Rejected alternative: `workflows: write` on the release App. It would let a release bot rewrite workflows.

## Problem

- On `/home`, moving the mouse quickly over the suggestions (and the pinned dashboards and recents rail) flashes a bright orange ring on rows.
- Hover sets the same `highlight` state that arrow-key navigation uses, so every hover writes `data-highlighted` on the row.
- The global keyboard ring [`[data-highlighted]:not(:hover)`](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/blob/ef406c0c/frontend/src/styles/base.scss#L1174-L1177) draws a 2px accent outline.
- React commits the hover update a task after the browser moves `:hover`, so for one frame the old row matches that rule.

## Changes

## Problem

- Users who opened the similar issues panel with a malformed issue id got a server error instead of a 400. Ten distinct users hit it inside one short window.
- `ErrorTrackingSimilarIssuesQueryRunner` passed `query.issueId` (a plain `str` in the schema) straight into a Django ORM filter, so Django raised its own `ValidationError`. The query API maps only DRF's `ValidationError` to a 400.
- This runner was the only error tracking runner without the shared guard:

| Runner | `validate_uuid_param` before |
| --- | --- |
| `ErrorTrackingQueryRunner` | yes |
| `ErrorTrackingBreakdownsQueryRunner` | yes |
| `ErrorTrackingReleasesQueryRunner` | yes |
| `ErrorTrackingFingerprintProjectionQueryRunner` | yes |
| `ErrorTrackingSimilarIssuesQueryRunner` | **no** |

- Separately, the same runner raises DRF `NotFound` when an issue has no fingerprint rows. That is a correct 404, but `_classify_error_for_slo` did not recognise it, so every one failed the query SLO and got captured as an error tracking issue.

<!-- posthog-self-driving-origin:01a0d399-8212-70a0-818c-e23007ec5718 -->
## Origin

- Error tracking: [issue 1](https://us.posthog.com/project/2/error_tracking/01a0d398-671f-7032-88f6-22dadd281d4f), [issue 2](https://us.posthog.com/project/2/error_tracking/01a0d3a9-abdf-7551-828e-983331486acc)
- First signal: 2026-09-24
- Inbox report: [open](https://us.posthog.com/project/2/inbox/reports/01a0d399-8212-70a0-818c-e23007ec5718)
- Likely cause: [`06e5153`](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/commit/06e5153f5f60378affe85758bb141d94a2c71322)
- Task started by: auto-start, after the report was rated P2 and ready to fix
<!-- /posthog-self-driving-origin:01a0d399-8212-70a0-818c-e23007ec5718 -->

## Changes

- A bad issue id now returns a 400 with a clear message, not a 500. The runner constructor calls `validate_uuid_param(self.query.issueId, "issueId")`, matching its four siblings. The call replaces a comment that marked the missing validation.
- A 404 from a query runner no longer counts as downtime or reaches error tracking. `_classify_error_for_slo` folds DRF `NotFound` into `USER_ERROR`, the same treatment `UserAccessControlError` already gets. Users see no change from this part.

## How did you test this code?

- Added `test_similar_issues_rejects_malformed_issue_id`. It catches the reported regression: before the guard, building the runner with a non-UUID id raised nothing, and the failure surfaced later as a 500 from the ORM. Confirmed it fails on the unpatched runner and passes with the fix.

body:
## Problem

- The ML Parquet sink can lose block metadata rows on a graceful shutdown under load. Training and eval datasets then miss those blocks, and no metric shows it.
- The sink autoscales, so scale-downs and deploys run this shutdown path often.
- The shutdown hook flushes the batcher while the Kafka consumer loop still delivers batches.
- The flush awaits its S3 write, then clears its buffers and stores every pending offset.
- A batch that arrives during that write loses its rows, but the flush stores its offsets. Kafka never replays it.

## Changes

- A flush now takes the buffers and the pending offsets when it starts, and writes and stores only those.
- A batch that arrives during the write stays buffered for the next flush.
- Flushes run one at a time and in order. A later flush's offsets also cover rows that an earlier flush is still writing.
- A failed write puts its unwritten rows and offsets back in front of newer ones, and the next flush writes them together.
- A failed offset store keeps the offsets pending for the next flush. The next flush does not write the rows again.
- The batcher counts a batch's bytes after its key read. A flush that starts during the read then cannot take the bytes without the rows.
- The batcher counts bytes for each buffer. A failed flush puts back only the bytes of the buffers that it puts back.
- The obvious alternative is to stop the consumer loop before the final flush. `KafkaConsumer.disconnect()` stops the loop and disconnects the client in one step, so the sink could not store the final offsets after that.
- The server does not change. Rows that arrive after the final flush starts stay uncommitted, so Kafka replays them after the restart.

> [!NOTE]
> PostHog/posthog#105254 merged first, and this branch merges it. A flush also takes the plain v3 buffer at its start, with its own byte count, and writes it first as before.

## How did you test this code?

- A new test handles a batch while the shutdown flush's write is pending. Against master's batcher, the flush stores the late batch's offset and drops its row.
- A second new test fills the row limit while the shutdown flush's write is pending, then fails that write. Against master's batcher, the overlapping flush stores offsets before the first write settles.
- The second test also fails when the flush queue or the restore after a failed write is removed.
- Both tests run on legacy rows and on plain v3 rows. The plain v3 cases fail if a flush does not take the plain v3 buffer at its start.
- A test fails the first offset store. It fails if the flush drops those offsets, writes the rows again, or counts their bytes again.
- A test starts a flush during a key read. It fails if the bytes of that batch miss the byte limit of the next flush.
- Not checked: a real shutdown against Kafka and S3.

body:
## Problem

- DevEx cannot find the people the dev loop fails most: every author read covers one author at a time.
- This is layer 2 of a stack, on top of #105972, which adds the per-PR friction view.

## Changes

- A new endpoint, `author_friction`, lists every author's friction over the last 30 days, most first.
- The score is a multiple of the typical author, so 1.0 is typical and 2.0 is twice as much.
- Each author carries the split by group (CI, review, queue, rework) and a rank band from resampling their PRs. The band shows how settled a position is.
- An optional `github_team` lists only that team's members and keeps their repo-wide ranks, so a member reads the same on every page.
- Friction counts only what happened to the author, never how much or how fast they ship.

| Group | Weight | What counts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Queue | 40 | time in the merge queue past 30 min, kickouts |
| Review | 25 | wait for the first approval, first approval over a day |
| CI | 20 | red stretches by cause, re-runs that failed again, CI time past 10 min per push |
| Rework | 15 | own failures fixed by a push, extra pushes, pushes after approval |

- Causes the author did not create (flakes, a broken master, kickouts, failed re-runs) get 1.5x inside their group.
- Each red stretch counts once, whatever its length, because a red PR left alone hardly affects anyone.
- The weights are a choice, not a fit to this data. No data records how bad an author's experience was, so nothing can be fitted.
- In a simulation, equal weights inside judged pain groups ranked authors almost as well as the true weights. Paired comparisons of friction set the group weights.
- Authors need 3 merged PRs. Shrinkage toward the repo keeps a few PRs from putting anyone at either end.
- SPEC §6 names `author_friction` as the read that scores friction. The ranking rule itself narrows in #105972.
- The read always filters on the caller's authorized source, because the view unions every source of the team.
- The endpoint is UI-only for now (MCP `enabled: false`). Frontend layers follow in this stack.
- Mechanical: regenerated OpenAPI types, and a `FrictionGroupEnum` name override in the settings.

No user-visible UI change in this layer.

## How did you test this code?

- `test_friction.py`, scorer case: fails when the typical author drifts from 1.0, the group parts stop adding up, or the order breaks.
- `test_friction.py`, read cases: fail when a missing view raises instead of reading as unavailable, a team filter re-ranks its members, or the read drops the source filter.
- `test_presentation.py`: fails when the endpoint stops forwarding the team or serializing the group split.
- The scorer also ran on a real 30-day extract of the view. The mean score came out at 1.0, and scoring took well under a second.
- Not run: the endpoint against a materialized view, because the view needs the flag from #105972.

## Problem

- Two batch-exports API tests fail in about 4 of 10 runs of the shard that holds them, since [split product test shards by file](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/104858). Trunk quarantines both.
- The tests are `test_delete_batch_export_cancels_backfills` and, downstream of it, `test_cancelling_a_batch_export_run`.
- Backfill workflows that an earlier test started keep running after that test ends.
- When one of their activities leaves a `transaction.atomic` block while pytest-django blocks database access between tests, turning autocommit back on raises.
- Activity ORM calls share one asgiref executor thread, so its connection stays in a transaction and later activity writes never commit.
- The delete request then finds no backfill row, cancels nothing, and the backfill fails instead of ending canceled.

## Changes

- Before each test, the existing `cleanup` fixture closes the database connections on that executor thread. This discards any transaction left open between tests.
- Production already resets this state: [`database_sync_to_async`](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/blob/cbfdce81f3e/posthog/sync.py#L46-L55) calls Django's `close_old_connections()` around every call.
- `close_old_connections()` drops any connection whose autocommit was not restored. Tests skip it under `settings.TEST`, so the fixture restores it once per test.
- Test-only change. Production code does not change.

## How did you test this code?

**Before: 37 of 90 runs fail. After: 0 of 90.**

| Batch-exports shard 1, 30 runs per sample | Sample 1 | Sample 2 | Sample 3 | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Before (master) | [10 fail](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36028968901) | [8 fail](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36034966724) | [19 fail](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36035170971) | **37 / 90** |
| After (this PR) | [0 fail](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36033212972) | [0 fail](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36034979328) | [0 fail](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36035174893) | **0 / 90** |

- Both rows run master `cbfdce81f3e` with a CI change that repeats shard 1. Only this fixture differs.
- The jobs show green because Trunk quarantines both tests. A failure shows in the job log, for example [this job](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36034966724/job/107753103058) (search for `ERROR`).
- A run counts as failed when either test logs `FAILED` or `ERROR`. Fisher exact test, one-sided: p < 1e-13.
- [All 7 batch-exports shards, 5 runs each](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36033568590): no test fails, so the fixture breaks nothing else.
- [Diagnostic run J](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36018817672): at delete time the backfill row exists only on the executor connection, which Postgres lists as idle in transaction.
- [Diagnostic run K2](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/36025723562): `set_autocommit(True)` raised "Database access not allowed" in 7 of 7 failing jobs and 0 of 23 passing ones.
- No new test: the two quarantined tests already assert the canceled status.
- Not run locally: the batch-exports suite needs Temporal and ClickHouse.

body:
## Problem

- DevEx cannot see which authors the dev loop fails most, because every friction read covers one author, team or PR at a time.
- The red CI split by cause comes from the Python timeline replay, which pages 200 PRs per round of queries.
- A pass over every PR in the repo costs hundreds of queries, so it cannot run on a request.
- This is layer 1 of a stack. Layer 2, #105975, scores authors from this view.

## Changes

- A new managed warehouse view, `engineering_analytics_pr_friction`, holds one row per PR merged in the last 30 days.
- Each row counts what the PR put its author through:
  - red stretches by cause: passed on re-run, master broken, fixed by a push, not provable
  - re-runs that failed again, and CI running time per push
  - the wait for the first approval, and pushes after approval
  - merge-queue time and kickouts
- The view writes the timeline replay as set-based HogQL, so one query covers the whole window.
- A parity test runs seeded PRs through the view and the Python timeline and asserts they agree, the way the cost view is held to the cost model.
- The view counts and does not score. Weights stay a read-time concern in layer 2.
- The view is materialized with a full refresh, so the table only holds PRs inside the window.
- A new organization-level flag, `engineering-analytics-friction`, gates the view. A materialized view spends the team's warehouse compute, and any team with a GitHub source qualifies.
- The product flag targets people, and the view sync runs with no user, so it cannot gate this.
- Timeline fix: two runs of one workflow that start in the same second now break the tie by run id, in Python and in the view. Before, the "latest attempt" depended on row order.
- Each row carries its `source_id`. The view unions every GitHub source of the team, so a read filters on the one source the caller may read.
- A direct query on the materialized view checks access at view level, like the other materialized managed views. SPEC §5 says so.
- A PR whose ready-for-review moment is not observed gets no approval wait, instead of a wait measured from its creation.
- A flag lookup that returns no result keeps the view the team already has. Without that, a flag outage would delete the materialization.
- SPEC §2, §6 and the README narrow the ranking non-goal to performance: output and speed. The view puts authors next to their friction, so the rule change lands with it.
- Mechanical: the source resolver passes the issue events and reviews tables, the provider passes the materialized flag, SPEC §5 documents the view.

> [!NOTE]
> No view appears anywhere until someone creates `engineering-analytics-friction` with an organization condition.

No user-visible UI change.

## How did you test this code?

- `test_pr_friction.py`, parity case: fails when the view and the Python timeline disagree on red, running or queue time.
- `test_pr_friction.py`, values case: fails on wrong re-run, approval, push, kickout, no-run and bot figures, which the parity case does not cover.
- `TestPRTimelineBuilder`, same-second case: fails when the tie depends on row order.
- `test_ci_views.py`, flag case: fails when the view appears without the flag or without the PR snapshot, or when a flag outage drops an existing view.
- `test_pr_friction.py`, values case also fails when an unobserved ready moment yields an approval wait, or a row loses its `source_id`.
- The view also ran read-only against a large real repository through the query API. It stayed within the memory of the heaviest existing product reads.
- Not run: a materialization through the data-modeling workflow, because it needs the flag and a scheduled run.

## Problem

- We want to continue isolating our batch export codebase from the rest of the monorepo.
- [#102172](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/102172) added the batch exports facade, but it moved no caller.
- This PR moves the core platform and billing callers. Two later PRs move the Temporal wiring and the warehouse and CDP callers. A last PR deletes the tach legacy-leaks block.

## Changes

> [!NOTE]
> Four edits change behavior. Everything else in this PR is mechanical.

- **The usage report's `active_batch_exports_in_period` stops counting deleted exports.** Deletion leaves an export unpaused, so the old query counted every export a team ever deleted. The number drops for teams that deleted exports. No in-app surface shows it.
- **`rows_exported_in_period` is `0`, not `None`, for a team whose billable runs recorded no row count.** The report compares the field with `> 0`, which a `None` cannot do.
- **The run-failure email looks up the run within its team.** `send_batch_export_run_failure` takes `team_id`, and the Temporal activity passes `inputs.team_id`.
- **`migrate_team` reports the migrated range from the earliest start of the export's backfills that did not fail.** An export can have several backfills. The old code crashed when it found more than one.
  - A backfill with no start exports all data, so the range then starts at "the start of the team's data".
  - The facade exposes `FAILED_BACKFILL_STATUSES`, built from the model's status enum, so the command does not copy status strings.

Mechanical:

- The integration API, the organization admin count, team deletion, the run-failure email, the usage report and `migrate_team` call `facade.api` instead of the models and the service layer.
- `migrate_team` catches `MultipleBatchExportsError` where it caught `MultipleObjectsReturned`.
- The facade's `get_backfill_for_export` becomes `list_backfills_for_export`, newest first. `migrate_team` is its only caller.
- Team deletion loses `delete_batch_exports` in `posthog/models/team/util.py`. The `delete_teams` activity calls `delete_batch_exports_for_teams`, and #102172's parity test covers that loop.
- The team-deletion tests patch `posthog.temporal.common.client.sync_connect`, because the facade looks the name up there at call time.
- The facade contracts gain `DestinationType`, `BatchExportModel`, `BatchExportRunStatus` and `BatchExportBackfillStatus` as `StrEnum`s, so core names enum values without the model classes. A facade test fails if they differ from the model's `TextChoices`.
- Core tests build their fixtures through `facade.testing`. It gains `integration_id` on `create_batch_export`, and a `get_batch_export` read.
- The activity-logging test moves into the product, because it asserts on the model class. `product_analytics` did the same for insights in [#60001](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/60001).
- `_HasNameOrId.id` in `posthog/api/integration.py` becomes a read-only property, so the frozen `BatchExportRef` contract satisfies it.
- `tach.toml`: the `backend.billing` entry leaves the legacy-leaks block. The `models` and `service` entries stay, because the later PRs still need them.

Look first at `posthog/tasks/usage_report.py` and `posthog/tasks/email.py`. They carry most of the behavior edits.

## How did you test this code?

- After the rebase onto master, these ran locally: the email, usage report, team deletion, facade and activity-logging tests, and `posthog/test/repo_invariants`.
- Two `test_login_from_new_device_notification*` tests in `test_email.py` fail locally because they need GeoIP data. They also fail on master.
- Before the rebase, these also ran: the integration API, HogQL system tables, `delete_teams`, and the batch export API, run-update and service tests.
- New facade test cases:
  - A team whose billable runs recorded no row count gets a total of `0`. It fails if the `Coalesce` goes, which would make the usage report compare `None > 0`.
  - `list_backfills_for_export` returns every backfill newest first, and nothing for another team's id.
- The moved activity-logging test loses docstrings that only repeated the test names. Otherwise the changed tests only swap fixtures. #102172's facade tests cover the other functions these callers now use.
- `test_migrate_team.py` is new and has no database. It covers the range start: failed backfills do not count, a backfill with no start makes the range unbounded, and if every backfill failed the start is unknown.
- Not run: semgrep (not installed locally), and the full backend suite. CI runs the full suite, because `batch_exports` is not isolated yet.

## Problem

- Every budget-steer callback fails before it can queue its analytics event, so the `task run budget steer` event is not recorded at all.
- `BudgetSteerCapture.enqueue` initializes the retained timestamp with `SET key value NX GET EX ttl`. Redis accepts `NX` together with `GET` only from 7.0, and older servers answer `ERR syntax error`.
- The callback raises `redis.exceptions.ResponseError` at that line, which removes the observability needed to confirm the guard behavior shipped in [#105038](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/105038).

<!-- posthog-self-driving-origin:01a0d386-c0ab-751a-8eeb-d39fe08661f9 -->
## Origin

- Scout: a custom scout
- First signal: 2026-09-24
- Inbox report: [open](https://us.posthog.com/project/2/inbox/reports/01a0d386-c0ab-751a-8eeb-d39fe08661f9)
- Task started by: auto-start, after the report was rated P2 and ready to fix
<!-- /posthog-self-driving-origin:01a0d386-c0ab-751a-8eeb-d39fe08661f9 -->

## Changes

- Write the first timestamp with a plain `SET ... NX EX`, then read the key back only when the write finds an existing value. This keeps the first timestamp stable across retries and uses commands every supported Redis version accepts.
- No change to keys, TTL, event UUID, or the dedup behavior.

```diff
-redis.set(key, timestamp, nx=True, get=True, ex=TTL)   # needs Redis >= 7.0
+if not redis.set(key, timestamp, nx=True, ex=TTL):     # works on Redis >= 2.6.12
+    original = redis.get(key)
```

## How did you test this code?

- The agent ran `pytest products/tasks/backend/tests/test_budget_steer.py` only. No manual testing was done.
- `test_replays_preserve_timestamp_across_midnight` now runs its cases against a fake Redis server pinned to 6.2 and to 7.4. The 6.2 cases reproduce the exact `syntax error` the callback raises today, and fail on master. No existing test caught this, because the default fake server speaks the newest command set.
- `products/tasks/backend/tests/test_event_ingest.py` and `test_agent_proxy_callback.py` report the same 23 passed / 72 errors on this branch and on master. Those errors come from infrastructure the sandbox does not provide.

## Problem

- A fork PR that changes a UI shows a green `Visual regression tests pass`, and its snapshot drift first fails in the merge queue.
- The failure kicks every other PR in that queue batch. [This run](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/35999007662/job/107635669522) shows #103522 (a fork) with 20 changed snapshots that its own PR run never compared.
- Fork runs get no `VR_API_TOKEN`, so `Create Visual Review run` and `Complete Visual Review run` skip.
- The gate accepts `skipped` for both jobs, because a PR with no frontend change skips them legitimately. It cannot tell "nothing to check" from "unable to check".

## Changes

- On a fork PR, each Storybook shard now compares its screenshots with the PR's `frontend/snapshots.yml` offline. A mismatch fails the shard, so the gate goes red before the queue.
- The check uses the existing `vr verify` command. The CLI builds from the base branch, so no fork code runs in it.

> [!WARNING]
> This is a fallback. It accepts only an exact pixel hash. It does not know the tolerated hashes or the quarantine of Visual Review, so a flaky story can red a fork PR that changes nothing visible. The step summary and the error annotation say this to the contributor.

- `vr verify --partial` is new. It skips the removed check and accepts a shard with no screenshots, because one shard renders only part of the baseline. No summary job is needed.
- The PR controls `snapshots.yml`, and `verify` cannot check the HMAC offline. So a forged baseline passes this check. The merge queue still catches it, because Visual Review drops entries with a bad signature.
- Internal PRs, merge queue runs and master pushes are unchanged.
- The fork PR handbook page describes the fallback.

## How did you test this code?

- `hogli ci:plan` with stubbed selector outputs: a fork PR builds the CLI and runs the offline step. Internal PR, queue and master runs upload to Visual Review as before and skip it.
- Ran the built CLI locally: `--partial` reports 0 removed. An empty shard passes. A missing baseline fails.
- `hogli lint:workflows` passes, and actionlint reports no new findings. The existing CLI vitest suite passes.
- Not checked: a real fork PR run. That needs a fork PR after this merges.

## Release status

- [ ] This change is behind a feature flag and is not available to users <!-- release-status: behind-feature-flag -->
- [ ] This change makes a previously flagged feature available to everyone <!-- release-status: fully-available -->

## Docs update

Updated `docs/published/handbook/engineering/fork-pull-requests.md`.

## 🤖 Agent context

**Autonomy:** Human-driven (agent-assisted)

**Agent:** Claude Code, Claude Opus 5.5 (`claude-opus-5-5`)

- Came from debugging the merge queue failure linked above. The follow-up option is a trusted `workflow_run` uploader that gives fork PRs a real Visual Review run.
- Skills: `/gh-logs`, `/authoring-ci-workflows`, `/writing-code-comments`, `/reviewing-with-coderabbit`, `/writing-pr-descriptions`.
- CodeRabbit CLI (`--deep`), 2 findings:
  - An empty partial shard skipped baseline validation. Fixed: the CLI now reads the baseline first.
  - "Use the base branch `snapshots.yml` because a fork can forge hashes." Rejected: a maintainer updates the baseline on the fork branch, so the base file would fail every fork that has a legitimate update. The queue still drops forged entries. A workflow comment records the limit.
- PR bot review:
  - ReviewHog: fork test code could flip a job-level env flag through `$GITHUB_ENV` to skip the check. Fixed: the conditions read the event fields.
  - ReviewHog: the drift annotation fired on any failure. Fixed: it shows only on a baseline mismatch.
  - ReviewHog: fork code could put a fake `node` on `$GITHUB_PATH`. Rejected: fork code runs as root in the same job, so no in-job hardening makes the check tamper-proof. The merge queue stays the trusted gate.
  - Codex: no removal detection on fork runs. Rejected: internal selective runs also use `--partial`, and the queue's full run catches removals.
  - CodeRabbit: an old base CLI would lack `--partial`. Withdrawn: the step and the flag land in the same commit.
- No duplicate PR found in the open PR search.

body:
## Problem

A customer tags the PostHog app, and the words of their request never reach the agent. Two shapes:

- The words live in the message's `blocks` or `attachments`, not its `text`. `event["text"]` reads none of them, so a mention sent by a Slack workflow or a rich-text client arrives empty.
- The message has no text of its own, only an attachment. The one record of the request is that message inside the context block, but the block's header and annotations point the agent *past* it, to the prompt slot below the closing tag, which holds only the fallback title.

In both, `_build_posthog_code_task_description` returns its fallback and the agent opens with "I don't see a request in this thread".

## Changes

- A mention whose words are in `blocks` or `attachments` now reaches the agent. The activity reads the event through `extract_message_text`, which merges `text`, `blocks`, and `attachments`, the same extractor the thread and fork paths already use. `event["text"]` was the only path still reading one source.
- A mention with no text of its own keeps its message in the context block. The placeholder that stands in for the initiator's message is used only when the prompt below the divider actually repeats it; with no prompt, the message and its attachment stay in the block instead of being replaced and dropped.
- The block's header, the role annotation, and the request line now point *inside* the tag when there is no initiator text, so the agent reads the message and its file as the ask rather than skipping to the placeholder title.
- No change when the mention has text, which is the overwhelming majority.

Out of scope: a mention that is only `@PostHog` with nothing else still resolves to the fallback, because there is genuinely no request to recover. Answering that case without a sandbox run is a separate follow-up, gated on the untagged-reply routing that keeps a thread live.

## How did you test this code?

- `hogli test posthog/temporal/tests/ai/slack_app/activities/test_task_creation.py` — 41 pass, including the existing case that asserts a genuinely empty thread still returns the bare fallback.
- New unit case: with no initiator text and a screenshot as the whole message, the description must not equal the fallback, must not contain the placeholder, and must keep the attachment note.
- The activity-boundary extraction is covered in `products/slack_app/backend/tests/test_followup_forwarding.py` with a mention whose words live only in `blocks`.
- Not measured: how many of the affected turns this recovers. A sample showed most were bare `@PostHog` mentions, which stay out of scope above.

## Automatic notifications

- [ ] Publish to changelog?

## Docs update

None.

## 🤖 Agent context

**Autonomy:** Human-driven (agent-assisted)

**Agent:** Claude Code, Claude Opus 5 (1M context), plus a PostHog Desktop task run that added the context-header commit on the same branch.

The finding came from reading Slack app traces where the agent's whole user message was the literal string `Task from Slack`. The first commit reads `blocks`/`attachments` and guards the placeholder; a PostHog Desktop task then added the commit that repoints the header and annotations at the in-tag message. This description covers the combined diff.

Skills invoked: `/writing-tests`, `/writing-code-comments`, `/writing-pr-descriptions`, `/reviewing-with-coderabbit`.

CodeRabbit CLI pass: skipped, signed out. `auto_review` posts on open.

No customer data or session content is in this branch. The counts that motivated the fix come from PostHog's own AI observability data.
title: fix(slack): read a mention's blocks and attachments, not only its text

## Problem

- A self-managed CDC source that lags past the critical threshold and also gets its capture paused cannot be resumed from the product.
- The lag sweeper marks its tables `cdc_broken` with reason `critical_lag_self_managed`, and leaves capture running.
- If capture then stops on a non-retryable error, the fix is Resume CDC. Resume refuses any `cdc_broken` marker and points to Repair CDC.
- The lag marker clears only once capture runs and the lag drops. With capture paused, it never clears, so the source stays stuck. Repair CDC would recreate a slot the customer owns and re-sync every table.

## Changes

- Resume CDC now refuses only markers that mean the slot or publication is gone. The self-managed lag marker no longer blocks it.
- Resume still probes the source and refuses when the slot or publication is missing, so an intact slot is still required.
- The facade exports `SELF_MANAGED_LAG_REASON` for the view.

## How did you test this code?

- `test_resume_cdc_with_a_broken_marker` covers a lost slot, a marker with no reason (both refused, no probe), and the self-managed lag marker (resumed). The lag case fails on the old check.
- Ran `TestResumeCDC` and `TestRepairCDC` locally against a disposable Temporal.

## Problem

A failed search in the classic picker can leave an unrelated result on screen without an error or retry action.

## Changes

- Show only remote rows for the current query, preserving the selected form value.
- Keep the existing error and retry state visible after failure. Do not offer a custom event name on failure.
- Offer property expansion only after a successful scoped result for the current query.
- Leave the rebuilt menu unchanged.

Before:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Search[New search] --> Failure[Request fails]
    Failure --> Old[Earlier rows hide the error]
    classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
    classDef phRed fill:#f54e00,stroke:#f54e00,color:#fff;
    classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
    class Search phBlue;
```

## Problem

- About 9% of observation thumbnails show a broken-looking page: raw HTML with no CSS, giant icons, a bare "Skip to content" link.
- Those thumbnails are cut from the first or last seconds of the analysis video, where the recorded page has not applied its CSS yet or is unloading.
- The frame pick only kept 0.5s off the end and nothing off the start, so a pick of 0, an early citation, or a pick past the end landed there.

| Recent prod-us thumbnails (1,500 each) | First 2s | Last 2s |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before #105099 | 3.5% | 5.4% |
| After #105099 | 3.2% | 6.3% |

## Changes

- Every thumbnail pick now lands at least 3 seconds from either end of the analysis video, whatever its source: the model's pick, a citation, a signal, or the 25% fallback. A video of 6 seconds or less takes its midpoint.
- A moment in the first 3 seconds now shows its thumbnail, and seeks the player, at 3s instead.
- The core-turn prompt now asks the model to avoid the last seconds of a recording as well as the first.
- The scan-side `_clamp_thumbnail` is removed. The new margin runs after it with tighter bounds, so it could never change the frame.
- Only activities and the prompt change, so the workflow's command sequence stays the same.

## Problem

- "People" (hundreds of them) who mute PostHog Desktop sounds for a meeting often forget to turn them back on, so later task alerts go unheard.

## Changes

- Notification settings get a "Pause alerts" row with a "Pause for 1 hour" button. While paused, the row shows the end time and a "Resume" button.
- The cmd+k menu has the same control: "Pause notifications for 1 hour", or "Resume notifications" while paused. A toast confirms the change.
- During a pause, alerts make no sound, speak no voice line, and send no system notification, dock badge, or dock bounce.
- Voice lines already queued when a pause starts are dropped. The speech queue checks `enabled` again before each line.
- In-app toasts still show. They are silent and only appear while the app is in use, so error toasts are not lost.
- The pause is one persisted timestamp. It ends when the clock passes it, so it holds across an app restart and needs no timer to turn sound back on.
- The row sends a `setting_changed` event with `setting_name: notifications_paused`, so adoption is visible.

- A new `NotificationsSettings` story renders the settings section in Storybook.

They have no list endpoint of their own, so each one needs the conversation id, and this source gets conversations from the Exports API rather than the paged endpoint. - `conversation_ratings` keys on conversation, rating and rating type. Dixa returns one row per question of a multi-question survey and all of them share a rating id, so the id alone is not unique.

- `conversation_activity_log` is organization-wide and paginated, so it needs no fan-out. It filters incrementally on its own `fromDatetime` parameter.

## Problem

Teams syncing Doppler for access audits cannot answer "who can reach this project, and what does their role let them do?" The source syncs `projects` and `workplace_users` with nothing joining them, and every role reference on a member, invite, or workplace user is an unresolved identifier string.

A second gap sits under change tracking: `activity_logs` records that a config changed, but not which secrets moved. Doppler keeps that per-config history on its own endpoint, which the source never called.

These are long-standing gaps recorded in `COVERAGE_GAPS_APPENDIX.md`, not a new Doppler release.

## Changes

- `project_members` joins projects to workplace users, groups, service accounts, and invites, with each member's project role and environment access.
- `project_roles` and `workplace_roles` resolve the role identifiers carried on members, invites, and workplace users, including the permission slugs each role grants.
- `config_logs` gives the per-config change history: each secret edit and rollback, with the names of the secrets touched and who made the change.
- Secret values never reach the warehouse. Doppler returns the plaintext before and after value of every changed secret in a config log's `diff`, so the source keeps each entry's `name` and reduces `added` and `removed` to booleans. A `diff` of any undocumented shape is dropped rather than passed through.
- A `config_logs` sync also keeps its responses out of HTTP sample capture, whose name-based scrubbers cannot tell a secret under a field called `added` from any other string.
- `config_logs` is the one table left off by default (`should_sync_default=False`). It fans out over every config of every project, and the endpoint takes no time filter to narrow a re-sync, so it is opted into deliberately.
- All four tables are full refresh. None of the four endpoints exposes a server-side timestamp filter, and Doppler documents no ordering guarantee for config logs, so an early-stop cursor could silently skip rows.
- The fan-out helper now walks a list of `(project, config)` parents instead of project slugs only, and the resume bookmark carries the config. A project-only bookmark would restart every config in the bookmarked project after a crash.
- Member rows carry no `project` field, so the fan-out stamps one on. `project` leads that table's primary key, and an unstamped row would collide with the same member in every other project.

## Problem

A PostHog user syncing Drip can see their campaigns and their subscribers, but nothing tells them who is in which campaign. The two tables share no key, so the join that every campaign-performance question starts from cannot be written. Tags and custom field keys, which drive Drip segmentation, do not sync at all.

The endpoint-coverage audit recorded these as long-standing gaps in `COVERAGE_GAPS_APPENDIX.md`. The endpoints have existed for years.

## Changes

- `campaign_subscribers` joins the two existing tables: one row per subscriber per campaign, keyed on `["campaign_id", "id"]`.
- The table covers unsubscribed and removed members, not only current ones. Drip's endpoint filters by a single status and defaults to `active`, so the fan-out runs once per status and tags each row with a `campaign_subscription_status` column. A single-pass table would silently drop everyone who left a campaign, which is the population most churn questions ask about.
- `tags` lists every tag used in the account, one row per tag.
- `custom_field_identifiers` lists every active custom field key on subscriber records, one row per key.
- Both lookups answer with a list of bare strings rather than objects, so each value becomes a single-column row.
- All three tables are full refresh, matching every other Drip table. Drip exposes no server-side update cursor.
- `campaign_subscribers` fans out through the shared `build_dependent_resource` helper. It has no resume support, so that path does not thread the resumable manager.
- Mechanical: `_client_config` extracts the client block the flat and fan-out paths now share. Canonical column descriptions added for the three tables.

`GET /v2/{account_id}/subscribers/{id}/campaign_subscriptions` is skipped. It is real and documented, but it costs one request per subscriber against an account limit of 3,600 requests per hour, so a 100,000-subscriber account would need over a day of continuous requests per sync and would starve every other caller on the same token. `campaign_subscribers` covers the same campaign-to-subscriber relation by fanning out over campaigns instead, which is a few hundred requests. The appendix records the skip and the reason.

## Problem

Anyone syncing Dovetail gets custom field *values* on data entries and docs, but nothing that says what those fields are. A `fields` value carries a field id, a label and a type that only the `/v1/fields` endpoint resolves, so a query over Dovetail custom fields has no lookup table to join against.

The endpoint-coverage audit flagged four Dovetail gaps. Three of them do not need a table, and the reasons are in Changes.

## Changes

- Dovetail sources gain a `Fields` table: one row per custom field definition, carrying the label, the field type, the select options and the owning project.
- The table fans out over `Projects`, because `/v1/fields` requires `filter[project_id]` and has no workspace-wide listing.
- Each project is fetched twice, once per `filter[field_set_type]` value (`data` and `doc`). Dovetail accepts one value per request and offers no "all", so the table is the union of the two passes.
- The passes save no resume checkpoint. `ResumableSourceManager` holds a single checkpoint while each pass paginates on its own, so resuming would restart in the wrong pass. Wrapping the checkpoint in a pass marker was the alternative; it changes the stored state shape for `DocComments` too, and a field-definition table is small enough to redo.
- The primary key is `["project_id", "id"]`. A workspace field group's fields are listed under every project the group is linked to, so the field id alone is not unique table-wide.
- Full refresh only: `/v1/fields` filters on project, workspace field group and field set type, and on no date.
- Three audited endpoints are skipped, because each one duplicates a table the source already syncs through a deprecated path:
  - `GET /v1/notes` — Dovetail renamed notes to data. The reference says new integrations should call `/v1/data`, which the `Data` table already syncs.
  - `GET /v1/insights` — Dovetail renamed insights to docs. The operation is marked `deprecated`, the responses carry a `Deprecation` header, and the `Docs` table already syncs the same records.
  - `GET /v1/insights/{insightId}/comments` — deprecated with the insights resource, and `DocComments` already syncs those comments.
- `COVERAGE_GAPS_APPENDIX.md` ticks `/v1/fields` and records why the other three stay unbuilt.
- Nothing user-visible changes outside the new table in the schema picker. The `fanout_param_variants` field on `DovetailEndpointConfig` is the mechanical part of the diff, along with the switch of that class to the house `@frozen` decorator, which the added field made `prefer-frozen-dataclasses` ask for.

Automated tests only. This sandbox has no Dovetail account, so no request ran against the live API. The endpoint contract came from the vendor's own OpenAPI definition at <https://developers.dovetail.com/reference/get_v1-fields.md>: required filter, `field_set_type` enum, `sort` enum, cursor pagination and the response fields.

- The fan-out issues one request per project and field set type, and the four rows land in one table. This catches a path binding that drops the project filter, and a variant loop that runs one pass instead of two. The framework only binds a resolved param inside the path, so `filter[project_id]` rides in the path string and nothing else checks that it arrives.
- The multi-pass fan-out saves no checkpoint. Passing the resume hook here would checkpoint one pass and resume the other into it.

## Problem

A team syncing DigitalOcean can see their projects, domains and database clusters, but not what is inside them.

- Projects sync as headers only, so spend and inventory cannot be grouped by project. The membership lives behind a per-project endpoint.
- Domains sync as bare zone names, so the DNS records that make up each zone are missing.
- Database clusters sync as current state, so there is no backup inventory and no cluster event history.

These are long-standing gaps recorded in `COVERAGE_GAPS_APPENDIX.md`, not new DigitalOcean endpoints.

## Changes

Four new tables, each a fan-out over a parent endpoint the source already syncs.

| Table | Endpoint | Parent | Primary key |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `project_resources` | `/v2/projects/{project_id}/resources` | `projects` | `project_id`, `urn` |
| `domain_records` | `/v2/domains/{domain_name}/records` | `domains` | `domain_name`, `id` |
| `database_backups` | `/v2/databases/{database_cluster_uuid}/backups` | `databases` | `database_cluster_uuid`, `created_at` |
| `database_events` | `/v2/databases/{database_cluster_uuid}/events` | `databases` | `database_cluster_uuid`, `id` |

- `project_resources` gives the join column that was missing: a resource URN resolves against the id columns already synced on droplets, databases and volumes.
- Every key carries the parent id. DigitalOcean documents a DNS record id as unique per domain and an event id as unique per cluster, and a backup record has no id at all. A key without the parent would collide across parents and multi-match on every merge.
- `database_backups` tolerates a cluster with no backup support. Caching and Valkey clusters return not-found on that endpoint, and the fan-out visits every cluster on the account, so the child treats a 404 as an empty page.
- `database_backups` and `database_events` opt out of HTTP sample capture. Both legs of a fan-out share one session, and their parent leg is `/v2/databases`, whose response embeds live connection URIs and passwords. The child rows themselves project only the cluster id, so no credential reaches the table.
- All four are full refresh, like the rest of the source. DigitalOcean exposes no server-side timestamp filter.
- Curated table and column descriptions are added for each new table, from the public API reference.

Skipped: `/v2/tags/{tag_id}/resources`. The audit listed it as a way to resolve tags to the resources they are applied to, but the [public spec](https://api-engineering.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/spec-ci/DigitalOcean-public.v2.yaml) exposes only `POST` and `DELETE` on that path. There is no `GET` to read tag membership back. The `tags` table already carries per-resource-type counts and a `last_tagged_uri`, which is the closest available data.

Also skipped as redundant: `/v2/projects/default/resources`. It is an alias for whichever project carries `is_default`, and the fan-out over `/v2/projects` already visits that project.

## How did you test this code?

New transport tests cover the fan-out row shaping, since that is where these tables can silently produce useless data:

- `project_resources` and `domain_records` each assert the parent id lands on the child row under the renamed column. Without the rename the join column is absent entirely and the table has no use.
- `domain_records` asserts the record's own `name` (the host part) survives alongside the zone name. Renaming the parent onto `name` would overwrite it.
- `database_backups` and `database_events` assert the cluster uuid reaches every row, and that the parent's `connection` block does not. The parent response holds credentials, so a widened projection would leak them into a queryable table.
- `database_backups` asserts a mixed account still syncs: one Valkey cluster returning 404 next to one PostgreSQL cluster, with the PostgreSQL backups landing.
- The capture-off assertion is extended to both database children, so a future edit cannot put the credential-bearing parent response back into sample capture.

The source-level primary-key test is extended to the four new tables and now asserts the partition key per endpoint rather than assuming `created_at`.

Not run: nothing was verified against a live DigitalOcean account. The endpoint shapes, pagination, response wrappers and available query parameters were read from the vendor's published OpenAPI spec, linked above.

- [ ] Publish to changelog?

The source's docs page renders its table catalog from `get_documented_tables()`, so the four new tables appear there once this lands. No docs file changes here.

**Agent:** Claude Code, Opus 5

Skills invoked: `/implementing-warehouse-sources`, `/reviewing-with-coderabbit`, `/writing-pr-descriptions`, `/writing-tests`.

The bot review that followed raised one finding, on the backup fan-out crossing clusters whose engine supports no backups. Verified against the vendor spec and fixed; the thread is resolved.

Public artifact: the diff draws only on the vendor's public OpenAPI spec and the coverage appendix already in this repository. No session material is committed.

Decisions along the way: the audit's four entries became three tables plus one rejection. ## Problem

A customer who asks PostHog AI a metric question in Slack reads "Governed catalog consulted: no match" in their answer. It is internal bookkeeping and means nothing outside the team.

- `services/mcp/src/templates/sections/metric-discovery.md` tells the agent to state that sentence "in query context".
- `execute-sql` takes `query`, `truncate`, `connectionId` and `sendRawQuery`. There is no `context`, so the reply is the only surface left.
- The eval reads the place the prompt names. `products/data_catalog/evals/scorers.py` builds its judge payload from `call.input.get("context")` on each `execute-sql` call, and tells the judge that a statement there counts as catalog evidence.
- That field never existed, so the evidence path could never fire. The judge graded the final message instead, which rewarded the leak it was meant to prevent.
- The sentence reached roughly one customer reply in thirty over the last two weeks.

## Changes

- `execute-sql` accepts an optional `context` string. It rides beside the query and is never forwarded upstream, so the endpoint's argument list does not change.
- Both prompt variants name the field rather than saying "query context", and say the sentence stays out of the answer.
- No user-visible change on its own. This layer gives the disclosure somewhere to go; the layer above changes what the answer says.
- The regenerated tool-schema and instruction snapshots are mechanical.

The alternative was to drop the requirement and let the disclosure live in the answer in better words. That loses the audit trail and leaves the eval grading prose, which is how the leak started.

## Problem

- Anyone picking up the Devin AI warehouse source sees four endpoints listed as open coverage gaps, and has to re-derive whether each is buildable.
- None of the four is buildable. Two paths do not exist at organization scope, one has no list operation, and one returns a column the `sessions` table already syncs.
- The source stores an organization-level Devin service user key, so every enterprise-scoped listing is out of reach.

## Changes

No tables were added, and nothing changes for a user syncing Devin AI today. This is an appendix update only, verified against the [Devin v3 OpenAPI spec](https://docs.devin.ai/v3-openapi.json) (spec version 3.0.0) rather than the `llms.txt` page index the original sweep used.

Each gap is now ticked with its verdict:

- `/v3/organizations/{org_id}/pr-reviews` exists, but the only GET is a point lookup. It requires a `pr_url` query param and answers with the single latest review for that PR.
- v3 has no list operation for PR reviews at organization or enterprise scope, so there is nothing to enumerate into a table.
- `/v3/organizations/{org_id}/tags` does not exist. The allowed-tags listing sits at `/v3/enterprise/organizations/{org_id}/tags` and needs `ManageEnterpriseSettings`.
- `/v3/organizations/{org_id}/sessions/{devin_id}/tags` does exist, but returns the same `tags` array every synced `sessions` row already carries.
- `/v3/organizations` does not exist. The listing is `/v3/enterprise/organizations` and needs `ViewOrganizations` at enterprise level.
- `/v3/organizations/{org_id}/guardrail-violations` does not exist. The listing is `/v3beta1/enterprise/organizations/{org_id}/guardrail-violations` and needs `ManageEnterpriseSettings` plus `ViewAccountSessions`.

Guardrail violations are recorded as the one endpoint worth revisiting. It carries the standard `items`/`end_cursor` envelope, a `violation_id` key, and server-side `time_after`/`time_before` filters, so it becomes a good table the day this source can hold an enterprise service user.

A fan-out for PR reviews over `sessions.pull_requests` was considered and rejected. That set covers PRs Devin opened rather than PRs it reviewed, costs one request per PR per sync, 404s for most of them, and yields rows with no stable id.

## How did you test this code?

No code changed, so no tests were added or run.

The four verdicts come from the vendor's own reference, not from a live API call. This sandbox holds no Devin credentials, so nothing was curl-tested against `api.devin.ai`.

<details>
<summary>Sources checked</summary>

- [Devin v3 OpenAPI spec](https://docs.devin.ai/v3-openapi.json) — 157 paths, cross-checked against the `v3-openapi-apigee.json` variant, which is identical.
- [Get latest Devin Review status](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/pr-reviews/get-organizations-pr-reviews) — `pr_url` required, `UseReviewManual` permission.
- [Get Organization Allowed Tags](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/tags/organizations-tags) — `ManageEnterpriseSettings`.
- [List Organizations](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/organizations/organizations) — `ViewOrganizations` at enterprise level.
- [List Organization Guardrail Violations](https://docs.devin.ai/api-reference/v3/guardrail-violations/organizations-guardrail-violations) — `ManageEnterpriseSettings` and `ViewAccountSessions` at enterprise level.

</details>

- [ ] Publish to changelog?

None. No user-facing behavior changed, so the Devin AI source doc still matches.

**Autonomy:** Fully autonomous

**Agent:** Claude Code, Opus 5

No duplicate: `gh pr list --state open --search "devin"` and the maintainer's own open PRs were both checked. Nothing open touches the Devin AI source.

## Problem

- A team that stores a config version 2 flag (a person-targeted boolean with ordered rules) gets no value for it from `/flags` or `/decide`: the service rejects every non-v1 row per flag, and the internal cache builders leave such rows out entirely.
- The evaluator for that family already ships (#102982) but nothing calls it, so the reachable behavior for a v2 row is a failed record on every request.

## Changes

- A supported, active v2 flag now evaluates and appears in every response format as a plain boolean: `enabled` is the rule value (a null default reads as `false`), never a variant or a payload.
- Every other non-v1 row keeps today's behavior: a failed record and `errorsWhileComputingFlags` when it reaches the matcher, omission with its dependents in the cache builders.
- Both internal `flags.json` builders (Python and Rust) keep an active v2 row whose document validates, verbatim and without dependencies; inactive, archived, malformed and unsupported-version rows stay omitted.
- The PostgreSQL fallback applies the builders' rule, so a Redis miss serves the flag set the cache would have carried instead of failed records for malformed rows.
- Person properties for v2 rules come from the same override-and-database path v1 conditions use: a predicate key missing from the request overrides triggers the person fetch.

Projection, per evaluator outcome:

| Outcome | `enabled` | `reason.code` | Legacy map (`/flags?v=1`, `/decide?v=3`) | Enabled-only lists (`/decide?v=1`, `v=2`) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Targeting match, value `true` | `true` | `condition_match` | `true` | included |
| Targeting match, value `false` | `false` | `condition_match` | `false` | omitted |
| Terminal rollout miss | flag default, `false` when null | `out_of_rollout_bound` | same boolean | included iff `true` |
| No rule match | flag default, `false` when null | `no_condition_match` | same boolean | included iff `true` |
| Evaluation error (missing context, invalid property or regex, hash) | `false`, `failed: true` | `flag_evaluation_error` | `false`, `errorsWhileComputingFlags` | omitted |

> [!NOTE]
> The evaluator and builder changes are unreachable in production from this PR alone: no write path creates a v2 row yet, and a v2 row cannot exist without one. The PostgreSQL fallback swap is live on ship: on a Redis miss, a team that stores a row the builders omit (a non-object, malformed or unsupported non-v1 document, or an unreadable evaluable v1 document) now gets the flag set its cache entry would carry, so a v1 dependent of such a row is dropped instead of evaluated, and an unsupported row no longer returns a failed record or sets `errorsWhileComputingFlags`. Hash key overrides, device identifiers and experience continuity do not apply to v2 rules; the subject is the request distinct ID. The internal `detailed_analysis` option describes v1 release conditions, so a v2 flag reports an empty `conditions` list; the field stays present because Django's historical `test_evaluation` reads its absence as a rejected internal token.

Rollback: revert. The fallback returns to the plain PostgreSQL read at once (a Redis miss again evaluates dependents of omitted rows and returns failed records for unsupported ones), the builders to omitting every non-v1 row, and the matcher to rejecting every non-v1 flag; stored rows stay readable. A cache entry this builder wrote that still holds a v2 row is served by the reverted reader as a failed record until the next rebuild.

Mechanical: the shared builder fixture flips three expectations (`v2-valid-active` and its two dependents are now kept) and adds one unsupported-family row; the two internal docs describe the new contract.

## How did you test this code?

- `tests/test_rules_v2_evaluation.rs::corpus_cases_project_through_the_matcher_and_the_legacy_formats`: the 122 core cases of the pinned boolean corpus (harness 1.8.0). The 114 complete-context cases run through `evaluate_all_feature_flags` with a stored person, then through the legacy `/flags`, `/decide?v=1` and `/decide?v=2` projections, asserting the value, the reason code and the rule index; the 8 partial and unavailable context cases reach `get_match` directly, since the service reads the person for a missing key and treats an overrides-only request as complete. Catches a matcher branch that changes a value, a reason or an index, adds a variant or payload, or turns an error into `false`. The corpus bytes are unchanged.
- `tests/test_config_format.rs::mixed_team_projects_supported_v2_beside_v1`: v1 on/off, two supported v2 rows, an inactive v2 row, a malformed v2 row with a v1 dependent, and a version-3 row, served from the builder's cache entry and from the PostgreSQL fallback across all six response shapes and a single-key request. Catches the fallback diverging from the cache, or a v2 row leaking a payload or variant.
- `config_dispatch_preserves_siblings_and_wire_errors` now asserts that a supported document in a cache entry evaluates while its rejected siblings keep their failed records, and that the fallback omits the rejected ones.
- The shared fixture `flags_cache_config_formats.json` runs in both builders (Rust `cache_builder` unit test, Python `TestOmitUnsupportedFlags`); Python also checks a supported row is published verbatim and dropped above `MAX_FEATURE_FLAG_FILTER_SIZE_BYTES`.
- Ran locally against isolated databases: the Rust integration suites (`test_flags`, `test_legacy_decide_formats`, `test_rules_v2_v1_contract` with all 74 v1 cases, `test_batch_flag_evaluation`, `test_config_v2`, `test_flag_definitions`, `flags_cache_invalidation_schema`), the `flags::` unit tests, both cache-writer binaries, strict Clippy; Python `test_flags_cache.py`, `test_tasks.py`, `test_legacy_definitions.py`, `test_local_evaluation.py`, `test_facade_references.py`, ruff and mypy.
- A private twelve-request v1 wire recording (`/flags` and proxied `/decide`, protocol versions absent/1/2/3/4/unparsable) is byte-identical between the merge base and this head after normalizing request ids, timestamps and the unordered key list.
- Not run: the real-S3 HyperCache suite and a deployed environment.

- [x] No feature flag controls this change <!-- release-status: no-feature-flag -->
- [ ] This change is behind a feature flag and is not available to users <!-- release-status: behind-feature-flag -->
- [ ] This change makes a previously flagged feature available to everyone <!-- release-status: fully-available -->

**Agent:** Claude Code, Claude Fable 5.1
