- Duplicate check: `gh pr list --state open --search "v2 evaluation"` found no PR wiring the evaluator or admitting v2 rows to the cache.
- Greptile thread (P2, empty `conditions` list for a v2 flag under `detailed_analysis`): first taken by omitting the field; reverted to an empty list in the human review round, because Django's historical `test_evaluation` reads a missing `conditions` key as a rejected internal token and returns 502. V2 rule analysis still belongs to the v3 structured reasons.
- CI round: the whole-repo startup guard caught the validator import on the `django.setup()` path (`posthog.hogql` via `parse_semver`); it is now function-local in the builder.
- Second Greptile round: the row-order thread was refuted on a wrong premise (`published_flag_keys` did not sort; the human review round caught it and the helper sorts now).
- Human review round (14 threads, all taken). Behavior: `only_use_override_person_properties` now yields complete context for a v2 rule set, so a historical `test_evaluation` reads an unset property as not set, as v1 does; `conditions` is an empty list for a v2 flag under `detailed_analysis`. Coverage: v2 reason code and rule index on success, a v2 flag needing preparation only for a missing predicate key, a continuity-flagged v2 flag surviving a hash-key error, and the builder tests again holding an unsupported row. The rest are dispatch order, a dead guard, and doc wording.
- CodeRabbit CLI: ran with `--deep`, four minor findings. Fixed: two stale doc sentences that still called the evaluator dormant, and a dedicated `flag_evaluation_error` code for evaluator failures instead of `internal_error` (metric label and `$feature_flag_reason` stay distinguishable). Rejected: tightening the Python validator's semver check to reject four-component versions. That validator belongs to the writer path, not this PR; a document Python admits and Rust rejects is isolated per flag by the reader's failed record, which the cache-entry case in `config_dispatch_preserves_siblings_and_wire_errors` covers.
- Design decision: the typed v2 outcome reuses the existing `FeatureFlagMatch` shape and reason codes rather than adding v2-specific fields or codes, so every response format and the detailed-analysis path stay untouched; v2 reason codes belong to the later `/flags?v=3` work.
- The request time is now a matcher field (`with_now` for tests), so relative-date rules in one request share one instant and the corpus's fixed clocks can run through the matcher.

## Problem

A pilot engineer cannot create a config version 2 flag, enable one, or disable one during an incident: the closed update path from #102958 admits nothing in any deployed configuration, and the only writer seam is a test-patched module attribute.

- Every deployed configuration still rejects v2 creation with `reserved_config_version` and v2 enabling with `unsupported_config_version`.
- The pilot's incident control (disable, soft delete) must not depend on the same switch that opens creation.

## Changes

- Operators can admit a project's flags to config version 2 writes with two internal feature flags targeted at the `project` group, both off by default: `feature-flag-rules-v2-writes` and `feature-flag-rules-v2-creation`. `facade.config_writes.v2_write_limits(team_id)` and `v2_creation_enabled(team_id)` replace the `V2_UPDATE_LIMITS` attribute and evaluate the flags locally, so an unresolved flag reads as off.
- A project with the writes and creation flags on can `POST` a `filters.version` 2 document: server-owned rule IDs and seeds are allocated, the document is validated strictly and stored exactly, and the row is created disabled. `active: true` on create is rejected with an explicit error, never downgraded. Every other project keeps today's `reserved_config_version` rejection.
- An admitted project can enable and disable a v2 flag as one version-checked `active` toggle on the existing locked update path. Enabling rechecks that the stored document still validates under the current limits and is denied while a flag-write approval policy is enabled; a stale `version` is a 409.
- Disabling (`active: false`) and soft-deleting (`deleted: true`) a stored v2 row work with both flags off, for any project, needing only the current row `version` and no enabled flag-write approval policy (a v2 change that needs approval has nowhere to go, so disable the policy first). Soft-deleting an enabled row disables it in the same locked write. Restore (`deleted: false`) stays rejected.
- `FEATURE_FLAG_RULES_V2_MAX_METADATA_BYTES` bounds one rule's opaque metadata object for the pilot; the deployment filter-size limit bounds the document as for v1.
- Each accepted write saves once, increments `version` once, runs the existing cache invalidation and logs one activity entry through the existing receiver (generic field diff; canonical v2 history is separate work in #104435).
- A submitted value equal to the stored one is an echo, not an operation, so a PUT that must repeat `key` can disable a v2 row outside the allowlist; a changed value is still judged as before.
- Mechanical: the v2 update tests move their lifecycle cases into `test_feature_flag_config_v2_lifecycle.py`; two existing tests that pinned the closed behaviour for stored v2 rows now assert the new contract; `docs/internal/feature-flags/api-writes.md` gains the operation matrix.

> [!NOTE]
> Rollback is turning both flags off. Existing v2 rows stay readable, disableable and deletable; no data is converted. v1 create, update, enable, disable and archive are unchanged.

## How did you test this code?

Automated, on an isolated Postgres database in the Flox environment:

- `test_feature_flag_config_v2_updates.py` and the new `test_feature_flag_config_v2_lifecycle.py` (118 tests). The lifecycle module catches: v2 creation or enabling reaching any entrypoint (HTTP, facade, direct serializer, approval replay) with the writer flags off; a v2 create landing enabled or silently downgraded; disabling or soft-deleting a v2 row needing the allowlist; enabling a stored document that no longer validates; an enabled approval policy leaking a v2 write, including one enabled between validation and the locked create; the writer gate's local-evaluation call and its logged failure branch; and the end-to-end pilot sequence (create, read, enable, replace, stale write, close creation, disable, re-enable, disable, delete) with one activity entry and one version step per write.
- Existing suites: `test_feature_flag.py`, config-version, dependency-format, lifecycle-action, version-history, organization flag, `test_facade*.py`, legacy definitions, local evaluation, flags cache and `products/approvals/backend/tests`: 2213 passed; six tests that asserted the old closed behaviour for stored v2 rows were updated (metadata PATCH now fails on the field list, facade disable now fails only for the missing `version`).
- Rust `test_rules_v2_v1_contract` (v1 corpus) and `test_legacy_decide_formats` (recorded wire formats) pass; `rust/` is unchanged by this PR.
- `mypy` on the changed files, `ruff`, `git diff --check`, `hogli ci:preflight --strict` (0 failures) and `hogli build:openapi` (no generated diff).

Not done: no manual testing against a running stack; repository-wide mypy not run.

## Release status

- [ ] No feature flag controls this change <!-- release-status: no-feature-flag -->
- [x] This change is behind a feature flag and is not available to users <!-- release-status: behind-feature-flag -->
- [ ] This change makes a previously flagged feature available to everyone <!-- release-status: fully-available -->

Both internal flags (`feature-flag-rules-v2-writes`, `feature-flag-rules-v2-creation`) are off, so the behaviour is unreachable until an operator turns them on for a project.

## Automatic notifications

- [ ] Publish to changelog?

## Docs update

Internal doc `docs/internal/feature-flags/api-writes.md` updated in this PR. No public docs change: the public v1 API contract is unchanged and v2 creation is not advertised.

## 🤖 Agent context

**Autonomy:** Human-driven (agent-assisted)

**Agent:** Claude Code, Claude Fable 5.1

- Skills read: `/improving-drf-endpoints`, `/writing-tests`, `/writing-code-comments`, `/splitting-oversized-modules`, `/running-ci-preflight`, `/writing-pr-descriptions`, `/reviewing-with-coderabbit`.
- No duplicate: `gh pr list` and the local worktrees showed no writer-path PR; #104435 (activity history) is related but separate and not stacked on.
- Decisions: a stored v2 row always takes the v2 branch so disable and soft delete never depend on a writer flag, while the allowlist decides which fields the branch accepts; create resolves identity in `validate()` (no stored state to lock) and re-checks the approval policy under the same organization lock `update()` uses; the v1 dependency traversal is skipped for v2 rows because the strict validator admits no cohort, group or flag reference, and enabling revalidates the stored document instead.

## Problem Users whose saved metrics carry per-experiment breakdowns still see their experiment recompute on every first open of the day, even after #105021. On one affected experiment the morning batch published 7 of 9 metrics; the 2 with a breakdown stayed unpublished, and any gap makes the page recompute all metrics. Step by step: 1. The daily job computes each metric and files the result under a hash of the metric's config. 2. For a saved metric, the breakdowns live on the experiment link, not in the saved query itself. 3. The daily discovery hashed the raw saved query, without the breakdowns. Every reader (timeseries sync, cold-start fallback, chart read via the serializer stamp) hashes the config with the breakdowns merged in. 4. Writer and readers use different hashes, so the fresh results are never found. #105021 fixed the empty-breakdowns case of this; this PR fixes the real-breakdowns case. ```mermaid flowchart LR W[daily job
hashes query without breakdowns] -->|files under hash A| S[(results table)] R[sync and chart
hash query with breakdowns] -->|look up hash B| S S -->|nothing under B| X[nothing published,

## Problem

Attribution reports that include today can fall back to slow live queries even after the sessions warmer succeeds.
The report ends at local day-end, while the warmer stops at its current UTC time.
For western timezones, those bounds can require different UTC daily windows.
This is the end-boundary follow-up to #105637.

## Changes

- Warm through the end of each project's current local day, matching the report's date range.
- Reject snapshots built before their window starts once that boundary arrives, even within stale grace.
- Use live attribution until that window is refreshed after its start.
- Opt only marketing sessions into this rule; preserve existing TTL durations, daily chunks, allowlist, and job hashes.

<details>
<summary>Future-window freshness before and after</summary>

Before:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Window starts] --> B[Reuse earlier snapshot until TTL and grace expire]
    classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
    classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
    class A phYellow;
    class B phGray;
```

After:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Window starts] --> B[Reject earlier snapshot]
    B --> C[Use live attribution until refresh]
    C --> D[Use refreshed cache]
    classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
    classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
    classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
    class A phYellow;
    class B,C phBlue;
    class D phGray;
```

</details>

## How did you test this code?

- Extended the existing Dagster test to compare its end with `QueryDateRange`, including both sides of local midnight and DST transition days.
- The extended cases fail against the original warmer and pass with this change.
- Added a ClickHouse regression that warms an empty future window, advances the clock, inserts a session, and checks refreshed data.
- Added executor cases for strict reads, stale grace, and unchanged default behavior.
- Ran the executor, sessions writer, attribution reader, and Dagster suites locally.
- The original calendar fix also passed combined tests with #105636 for revalidation, lazy precompute, and the general warmer.
- Production validation after deployment remains pending. This change does not reduce the cost of queries that already use the cache.

## Problem

- Sales teams in Salesforce cannot see which PostHog Cloud region (US or EU) hosts an Account's organization.
- A restricted picklist on Account and Contact, `Posthog_Org_Region__c` (`US`, `EU`), holds that value. It is deployed in Salesforce.
- Nothing fills it for existing Accounts.
- New organizations take a separate path at signup: the signup flow writes the region on the Contact, and a Salesforce-side change copies it onto the Account. This PR fills existing Accounts and repairs any Account that the signup path misses.

## Changes

- The weekly Salesforce usage enrichment now writes `Posthog_Org_Region__c` on each Account it already updates.
- The region comes from the organization's billing license (`license_id` 1 is EU, 2 is US), read from the duckgres billing tables.
- Any other license, no billing customer, or conflicting customers give no region. The job never defaults one.
- Billing is the source because the job runs on US only, so this instance's `Organization` table cannot name EU organizations.
- Before each 200-record Bulk API update, one SOQL query re-reads the Accounts' `Posthog_Org_ID__c` and region, because the Redis mapping can be hours old.
- Billing is the authoritative source. The job fills an empty region and replaces a different one, such as an interim value copied from Vitally. It logs each replacement and counts it as `regions_replaced`.
- The job writes only when the Account still carries the same `Posthog_Org_ID__c`.
- A describe call skips regions while the field is missing or read-only for the integration user, so a field or permission problem never drops the usage write.
- Salesforce rejects a whole record when one value fails. A rejected record that carries the region goes again without it, so the usage fields still land.
- If that resend raises or Salesforce rejects a record again, the batch keeps the first attempt's counts, and the failure appears in the page's `errors`.
- A replacement is logged only after Salesforce accepts the write.
- A failed billing lookup or a failed re-read skips regions for that page or batch. The usage write continues.
- `regions_filled` and `regions_replaced` appear in the workflow result. The workflow body gains no Temporal commands. The new dataclass fields default to 0.
- Mechanical: two constants, a new `org_regions.py` with `normalize_org_id` and `fetch_org_regions`, and an explicit `frozen=` on the three result dataclasses this PR extends.

> [!NOTE]
> The first run writes every stamped Account whose region is empty or disagrees with billing. Each run adds one SOQL query per 200 Accounts and one describe call per page. It adds no update calls.

> [!WARNING]
> The re-read and the Bulk write are separate calls, and the Bulk API has no conditional update. A restamp between them can receive the old organization's region until the next weekly run replaces it.

## How did you test this code?

- The `decide_org_region` cases catch a missed replacement of a different region, and a write onto an Account restamped or deleted since the cache was built.
- The `fetch_org_regions` case catches a default for an unknown license, acceptance of conflicting licenses, and an unknown license dropped before the conflict check.
- The page-level cases catch a fill or a replacement that is not sent, a region sent to a field Salesforce cannot take, and a billing or re-read failure that blocks the usage write.
- The resend case catches a rejected region value that also drops the usage fields.
- The failed-resend cases (a raised resend and a rejected record) catch lost batch counts, and a resend failure that the page does not report.
- The last-page workflow case catches fill and replacement counts lost across continue-as-new.
- Each new test fails when its guarded line is removed (local mutation check).
- The license-to-region mapping agreed with the US and EU organization tables in a read-only check before this change.
- `fetch_org_regions` ran read-only against the prod-us duckgres. It found `license_id` (integer) and `organization_id` (text), and it sent a 1,000-bind chunk and the statement timeout without error. PostHog's own organization came back as `US`.
- Not checked: a real Bulk API write with the region, because the field is not deployed yet. The first run's `enrich_page_completed` log (`billing_regions`, `region_outcomes`) shows it.

## Release status

- [x] No feature flag controls this change <!-- release-status: no-feature-flag -->
- [ ] This change is behind a feature flag and is not available to users <!-- release-status: behind-feature-flag -->
- [ ] This change makes a previously flagged feature available to everyone <!-- release-status: fully-available -->

## Automatic notifications

- [ ] Publish to changelog?

None. No existing doc covers the Salesforce enrichment.

## 🤖 Agent context

**Autonomy:** Human-driven (agent-assisted)

**Agent:** PostHog Desktop (Claude Code), Claude Opus 5.5 (`claude-opus-5-5`)

- Skills invoked: `/writing-tests`, `/writing-dataclasses`, `/writing-code-comments`, `/reviewing-with-coderabbit`, `/writing-pr-descriptions`.
- Before opening, a code-simplifier pass, an independent code review and a Codex review ran. Applied: the resend without the region, fail-open tests, strict keys on the re-read, UUID-only lookups with a statement timeout, per-page outcome logs, and removal of an unreachable outcome. Declined: a multi-batch freshness test.
- CodeRabbit CLI (`--deep`) found two issues. Fixed: the failure cases now assert that the region key is absent. Rejected: a conditional region write, because the Bulk API has none. The warning above describes the race.
- The first version filled only empty regions. Abhischek chose to replace a different region, so that billing corrects stale interim values and heals the race. This matches the Salesforce field's documented writer policy.
- Abhischek chose billing `license_id` as the source, after a comparison with the organization tables, organization group properties and this instance's own table.
- Review threads on this PR: fixed are Greptile's resend-count and replacement-log comments, and both CodeRabbit resend-report comments. CodeRabbit's request to keep populated regions conflicts with the replace decision above and was not applied.
- Duplicate search: no open PR covers this change.
- Public artifact: the design drew on internal planning notes and read-only production checks. The tests use invented IDs. No session data is committed.

## Problem

- One team's feature flag stored in a config format the v1 readers do not understand could make a job that scans every team's flags rewrite that row, misreport it, or abort the whole run.
- Three such jobs read `filters` as a v1 document with no format check: the payload re-encryption command, the read-only filters audit, and the weekly stale-flags health check. A fourth, the property-type repair command, has no work left and is deleted instead.
- No such rows are stored today; this closes the path before the first one lands, as the internal cache builders (#104427) and the legacy definitions producer (#104948) already did for their paths.

## Changes

- `reencrypt_flag_payloads` skips a flag whose config format is not 1, on the streamed snapshot and again under the row lock, and counts it as skipped with one warning log.
- `fix_invalid_flag_property_types` is deleted rather than guarded. #44130 added it to rewrite `"event"` property types to `"person"`, the API now rejects property types outside the flag set, and a production scan with the command's own predicate on 2026-09-25 found no live rows left: US has 13 `"event"` rows, all on deleted flags, plus 5 `"person_metadata"` rows it has no fix for and the API accepts; EU has none. Its gated-writes baseline line and `ALLOWED_REASONS` entry go with it.
- `audit_flag_filters` no longer judges such flags against the v1 rules; the report carries them as `skipped_unsupported_config_format` instead of as violations.
- The stale-flags health check drops such flags from both candidate queries before reading release conditions, with one log line per flag; the other rows and teams in the batch are unaffected.
- Detection uses `detect_config_format` from the flags facade. Rows in config format 1 are processed exactly as before.
- Skips are per row, not a job-level `try/except`, so an unsupported row never hides a failure on another team's row.
- Inspected and left unchanged because they read only counts, sizes, keys, ids or timestamps: usage report counts, the weekly digest, the last-called sync, the storage-size metrics, the ClickHouse mirror, enriched-analytics discovery, the dev flag sync commands, the replay-key repair and the usage-insight cleanup commands.

- One new test per guarded job: team A holds a config-format-2 row shaped so the job's SQL prefilter still selects it, team B holds a v1 row; the job completes for B and skips A without raising.

body:
## Problem

`posthog-cli-update` has never worked in this monorepo. It resolves versions by walking the GitHub releases API, which stops at 1000 items when unauthenticated while this repo holds over 2000 releases, so it returns:

```
422 Only the first 1000 results are available.
```

Anyone who installed with the script has a broken updater sitting next to their CLI, and it still looks like the way to update.

## Changes

- `posthog-cli update` updates the CLI. It reads `posthog-cli/stable/dist-manifest.json` from the release bucket, so the GitHub API is out of the update path entirely.
- It updates in place **only** for installs made by `install.sh` or `install.ps1`.
- Every other install belongs to a package manager, so it prints what that manager expects instead of fighting it.
- `install-updater = false`, so the broken standalone binary stops shipping, and a successful update deletes one left behind by an earlier install.
- `cli/README.md` documents the command; `cli/RELEASING.md` records why the standalone updater is gone.

| Install | Detected by | Told to run |
| --- | --- | --- |
| install script | receipt's `install_prefix` contains the binary | nothing, it updates here |
| Homebrew | a `Cellar` path component | `brew upgrade posthog-cli` |
| npm | a `node_modules` path component | update through npm, with the path named |
| cargo | parent is `.cargo/bin` | `cargo install posthog-cli --force` |
| anything else | none of the above | the `curl` one-liner |

### Three details that are easy to get wrong

**A receipt is not proof of ownership.** It describes whatever the script installed last, which is often not the binary being run. Before this check a debug build classified as a script install and started self-updating, which would have overwritten `~/.posthog` from a local build. The receipt now only counts when its `install_prefix` contains the running binary.

**Homebrew needs `canonicalize`, not `read_link`.** Brew's symlinks are relative:

```
readlink /opt/homebrew/bin/posthog-cli  →  ../Cellar/posthog-cli/0.18.5/bin/posthog-cli
```

so a single `read_link` never matches an absolute `Cellar` prefix. cargo-dist's own `this_cargo_dist_provided_by_brew` has this bug.

**npm is one case, not several.** A global install, an npx cache and a copy pulled in by a plugin or SDK all live under `node_modules`. Telling the last two to `npm install -g` would install an unrelated copy and leave the one they ran untouched, so all three get the same message with the path named.

## How did you test this code?

- 2 unit tests. `classifies_install_layouts` is one table over `(path, owned_by_script, expected)`, guarding two regressions that have concretely happened here: swapping `canonicalize` back to `read_link`, which breaks Homebrew, and re-splitting the npm branch, which misdirects plugin-SDK users. `only_a_script_install_updates_itself` guards a new variant being added without guidance. They are one table rather than four functions because the path cases were variations of one behavior.
- `cargo clippy --all-targets`: 0 findings. `cargo fmt --check`: clean.
- `hogli ci:preflight` passes.
- Ran the built binary against real layouts on a machine carrying the script, npm and Homebrew installs at once. The debug build reports the curl command; a copy placed under `node_modules` names its own path. That run is what exposed the receipt-ownership bug above, which both unit tests passed before and after.
- Not tested end to end: the self-update path itself, since it runs the real installer over a real install. The version comparison and installer download are exercised only by the paths above.

## Automatic notifications

- [ ] Publish to changelog?

## Docs update

`cli/README.md` and `cli/RELEASING.md` are updated here.

## 🤖 Agent context

**Autonomy:** Human-driven (agent-assisted)

Written by Claude Opus 5 through Claude Code, driven interactively.

Skills invoked: `/writing-tests`, `/writing-pr-descriptions`, `/reviewing-with-coderabbit`.

CodeRabbit CLI pass: **not run**. The CLI is installed but signed out, and sign-in opens a browser, so this PR opens without a local pass.

axoupdater was considered as a library rather than reimplementing the update. It was dropped because its `ReleaseSourceType` is GitHub or Axo only and its install receipt has no field for an API host, so it cannot resolve from our own origin without an environment variable set by every user. Reading the manifest directly is fewer moving parts and uses the bucket the release workflow already publishes.

The version check is equality, not semver ordering, to avoid a new dependency. A local build newer than stable would therefore be offered an update; it reinstalls stable, which is the correct outcome for a released binary and merely odd for a dev build.

`install-updater = false` stops new installs getting the broken binary but cannot reach existing machines, which is why a successful update removes it. That deletion is bounded to one exact filename inside the prefix the receipt owns, and a failure to remove does not fail the update.

Public artifact: nothing here draws on a customer conversation, ticket or log.
title: feat(cli): add posthog-cli update, drop the broken updater

## Problem

A BigQuery source keeps failing and retrying every run once the customer deletes the whole Google Cloud project it syncs against, instead of stopping and telling them why.

BigQuery's rejection names the numeric project id ("Project #123456789 has been deleted."), not the friendly project id, so it doesn't match the existing "Make sure it references valid GCP project" key, which only covers the 404 wording raised when a project id is simply wrong.

## Changes

- Added a `"has been deleted"` key to `BigQuerySource.get_non_retryable_errors()` in `source.py`, so this 403 disables the source with an actionable message instead of retrying indefinitely.
- The wording mirrors what `delete_all_temp_destination_tables` in `bigquery.py` already treats as terminal for the same condition on the temp-table cleanup path — this closes the gap on the main sync path (`_build_source_response`'s `get_table` call).

body:
## Problem

A person who rates a PostHog Slack answer on a Codex run sends a rating that points at nothing, so nobody can open the turn and see what the agent did.

- The Claude CLI mints a `traceparent` per user turn, and [ai-gateway#496](https://github.com/PostHog/ai-gateway/pull/496) taught the gateway to read it, so a Claude turn's generations share one `$ai_trace_id`.
- Codex sends no trace header, so the gateway falls through to stamping a fresh id per request.
- A Codex run's generations therefore each sit alone in a trace of one, and AI observability has no turn to show.

## Changes

- A rating on a Codex turn now resolves to that turn, and the turn's generations appear as one trace.
- The agent-server sets `X-PostHog-Trace-Id` to the run id on the Codex gateway headers.
- The agent-server then reports that run id as the turn's trace id on every path a rating can arrive by: the command result the Slack relay reads, the direct relay, and the turn-complete event the agent-design stream reads.
- The Codex adapter mints its own turn-complete event and reports no trace id, so the server fills it in on the way through.
- Claude keeps its own per-turn ids. That header outranks `traceparent`, so setting it for Claude would replace them with one id for the whole run.
- Nothing changes in the app UI. The effect lands in AI observability and on the rating.

The id is resolved next to the stamp rather than in the Temporal activity that posts the reply. The activity would have to infer it from the run's `runtime_adapter`, and a Codex run with no `AI_GATEWAY_TOKEN` falls back to the Python gateway and carries no stamp, so the inferred id would point a rating at a trace with no generations.

The obvious alternative is a Codex-side per-turn hook mirroring Claude's `traceparent-hook`. Codex accepts gateway headers only at process spawn, through `model_providers.posthog.http_headers`, so it has no per-turn seam. `configureEnvironment` runs once per run, which makes the run the finest granularity available, and the run is the unit a Slack rating already refers to.

## How did you test this code?

- `withTurnTraceId` covers the turn-complete event, 3 cases. It catches the two ways the fallback goes wrong: overwriting a trace id the adapter reported, and naming a run that no header stamped.
- One case in `agent-server.configure-environment.test.ts` covers the header. It catches the header landing on a Claude run, which would replace the CLI's per-turn ids.
- Not run: the desktop Playwright suite. Three cases in `agent-server.test.ts` fail in this sandbox for reasons outside this change: the sandbox git guard blocks the fixture's `git commit`, and the sandbox's own agent instructions reach the built system prompt.

**Agent:** Claude Code, Claude Opus 5 (1M context)

The change came out of reading eight weeks of `slack_app` traces: Codex-adapter runs group at zero while Claude-adapter runs group as intended since ai-gateway#496, which pointed at the missing header rather than at the gateway.

body:
## Problem

- Queries that read a whole property blob under restricted-property access control pay about 4 ms per ClickHouse block to start a new UDF process.
- `JSONDropKeys` is the only utility UDF with type `executable`, so ClickHouse starts the process again for each block.
- The UDF passes its keys as a command-line parameter, and ClickHouse accepts parameters only on `executable` UDFs. An `executable_pool` UDF with a parameter fails to load.
- Small blocks multiply the cost. Each read stream also starts its own processes.

## Changes

- Adds `JSONDropKeysPool(json, keys)`, an `executable_pool` UDF. The JSON comes first and the keys are a per-row `Array(String)` argument, like the built-in JSON functions.
- The function returns the same output as `JSONDropKeys(keys)(json)`, including dotted-key expansion.
- The function uses the existing `json_drop_keys_udf` binary with a new `--row-binary` mode. This mode uses RowBinary with chunk headers, which `decompress` already uses.
- RowBinary lets JSON values contain raw newlines and tabs, which break the old line-based `Raw` format.
- The worker keeps the parsed filter for the most recent key array, so a repeated key array costs one byte comparison per row.
- `JSONDropKeysPool` is unversioned, like the other utility UDFs. It runs the top-level binary, which includes the #97154 optimizations. The printer path uses `JSONDropKeys_v12`, which runs the older v12 build.
- Nothing calls `JSONDropKeysPool` yet. A follow-up PR switches the HogQL printer to it once this config is live on ClickHouse.
- `integration_test.sh` now sets its own `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME`. The repository `.envrc` exports `posthog`, so the script's cleanup removed every container of the local development stack.
- Mechanical: the rebuilt `json_drop_keys_udf_*` binaries, manifest entries in `latest_` and `v12/`, and docs.

Local timings, one thread, 1M small synthetic rows, best of three:

| `max_block_size` | `JSONDropKeys` | `JSONDropKeysPool` |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 65,536 | 0.346 s | 0.26 s |
| 8,192 | 0.873 s | 0.30 s |
| 1,024 | 4.885 s | 0.504 s |

## How did you test this code?

- `TestRunRowBinary` catches a stale filter reused after the keys change, raw newlines that break framing, and multi-chunk flushing. Breaking the filter cache on purpose makes it fail.
- `TestRunRowBinaryErrors` catches truncated chunks, malformed JSON, bad headers, and oversized key arrays that the worker would otherwise accept.
- `integration_test.sh` runs `JSONDropKeysPool` against the existing `JSONDropKeys` fixtures. It also runs a 10,000-row query with keys that change per row across pool chunks.
- On 1M rows, a `countIf` over the output of both functions found zero differences.
- Not checked: production block sizes, concurrent load, and deployment of the manifest to cloud ClickHouse.

body:
## Problem

When a cloud run's sandbox is killed at its memory limit, the run ends with the same "Sandbox stopped" message as a routine stop, so the person reading the task cannot tell their test run ran out of memory.

- Two detectors notice the loss: the credential refresh activity when `sandbox.is_running()` returns false, and the event relay when its stream to the sandbox dies. The relay usually wins, and it is the only detector on runs without GitHub credentials.
- Modal reports the exit code at that moment: 137 for a kill, 124 for a timeout.
- Nothing reads that code, so every loss ends as "Sandbox stopped; resume to continue".

```diff
 refresh_sandbox_credentials():
     if not sandbox.is_running():
-        return Output(sandbox_gone=True)
+        return Output(sandbox_gone=True, sandbox_exit_reason=sandbox.exit_reason())

 run_credential_refresh_loop(..., on_sandbox_gone):
     if result.sandbox_gone:
+        on_sandbox_gone(result.sandbox_exit_reason)
         return SANDBOX_GONE

 _relay_sandbox_events():
     if relay reported sandbox_gone:
+        sandbox_exit_reason_lookup_id = sandbox_id
         sandbox_gone = True

 _mark_sandbox_gone():
+    if no reason yet and patched("tasks-sandbox-exit-reason-on-relay-loss"):
+        sandbox_exit_reason = execute_activity(get_sandbox_exit_reason, sandbox_exit_reason_lookup_id)
-    completion_error = "Sandbox stopped; resume to continue"
+    completion_error = sandbox_gone_error_message(sandbox_exit_reason)
```

Before: the exit code stops at the provider.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Modal[Modal sandbox exits 137] --> Act["refresh activity: sandbox_gone"]
    Act --> Loop{{credential refresh loop}}
    Loop --> Mark["mark sandbox gone"]
    Mark --> Msg(["Sandbox stopped; resume to continue"])
    classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
    classDef phRed fill:#f54e00,stroke:#f54e00,color:#fff;
    classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
    classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
    class Modal phRed;
    class Act,Mark phGray;
    class Loop phBlue;
    class Msg phYellow;
```

After: whichever detector wins carries the exit reason to the run's error.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Modal[Modal sandbox exits 137] --> Act["refresh activity: sandbox_gone + exit reason"]
    Act --> Loop{{credential refresh loop}}
    Loop -->|on_sandbox_gone| Mark["mark sandbox gone"]
    Modal --> Relay{{event relay: sandbox_gone}}
    Relay --> Mark
    Mark --> Lookup["get_sandbox_exit_reason activity"]
    Lookup --> Msg(["Sandbox stopped: killed with exit code 137, usually because it ran out of memory. Resume to continue."])
    classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
    classDef phRed fill:#f54e00,stroke:#f54e00,color:#fff;
    classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
    classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
    class Modal phRed;
    class Act,Lookup,Mark phGray;
    class Loop,Relay phBlue;
    class Msg phYellow;
```

## Changes

- A run that loses its sandbox now says why when the provider reports it:

| Exit code | Run error |
| --- | --- |
| 137 | Sandbox stopped: killed with exit code 137, usually because it ran out of memory. Resume to continue. |
| 124 | Sandbox stopped: timed out. Resume to continue. |
| Other | Sandbox stopped: exited with code N. Resume to continue. |
| Unknown | Sandbox stopped; resume to continue |

- `ModalSandbox.exit_reason()` reads the return code Modal cached on the last status check and polls only when nothing is cached. A poll error is logged and gives no reason.
- A new activity, `get_sandbox_exit_reason`, runs when the event relay reports the loss. It sits behind the Temporal patch `tasks-sandbox-exit-reason-on-relay-loss`. A lookup failure keeps the old message and still ends the run.
- The relay marks the sandbox gone before the lookup runs. The lookup runs from the sandbox-gone completion path, so an inactivity or max-duration timer that fires during it cannot end the run as a timeout instead.
- A completion signal that lands during the lookup wins. A user stop or an agent-reported failure keeps its status and message instead of ending as a sandbox loss.
- The 137 message names the code and hedges the cause. Modal maps its terminated status to 137, which covers an out-of-memory kill and an explicit stop alike, and its timeout status to 124.
- `SandboxBase.exit_reason()` returns `None`, so Docker and other backends keep the old message.
- The refresh activity logs the reason as `sandbox_exit_reason` on both not-running paths.
- `run_credential_refresh_loop` takes an optional `on_sandbox_gone` callback. The execute-sandbox workflow does not pass it and is unchanged.
- The sandbox-gone state marker and completion status are unchanged.
- The refresh path needs no patch: the new output field decodes as `None` in older histories, and no command changes there.
- `RefreshSandboxCredentialsOutput` is now `@frozen`. Every caller already built it with keyword arguments, and the semgrep rule `prefer-frozen-dataclasses` blocks a bare `@dataclass` whose body changes.
- Out of scope: a run that streams events through sandbox event ingest and has no GitHub credentials has no loss detector at all, so it still ends on the inactivity timeout.
title: fix(tasks): report why the sandbox stopped when a run ends on sandbox loss

## Problem

On the PostHog mobile app, the execution mode a user picks in the new-task composer (plan, auto, accept-edits, bypass-permissions) was lost when the backend activated a pre-warmed cloud task.
Mobile fires a warm request while the user is still typing to shorten sandbox startup.

body:
## Problem

- The MCP tool-calls scout computes per-category failure rate, struggle share, p95 duration and problem-tool counts every run, then throws them away. They survive only as report prose, so nobody can trend a category, alert on one, or see when it stepped.
- A quiet run leaves no trace at all, so a healthy category is indistinguishable from one nobody measured.
- The scout's four lenses are all failure-shaped, so a tool that starts being called reflexively in most agent sessions after a prompt change is invisible — every call succeeds.
- No canonical scout could ship a default record schema: `structured_output_schema` lived only on the per-team config row, so turning the channel on meant someone pasting JSON into the API for every project.

Closes #105812

<!-- posthog-self-driving-origin:01a0d2fb-42c3-7d18-9619-077ad25d41f8 -->
## Origin

- Scout: a custom scout
- First signal: 2026-09-24
- Inbox report: [open](https://us.posthog.com/project/2/inbox/reports/01a0d2fb-42c3-7d18-9619-077ad25d41f8)
- Task started by: auto-start, after the report was rated P2 and ready to fix
<!-- /posthog-self-driving-origin:01a0d2fb-42c3-7d18-9619-077ad25d41f8 -->

## Changes

**Canonical scouts can ship a record contract.** A new `scout-structured-output-schema` frontmatter key names a bundled JSON Schema file. The harness validates it at discovery — a broken schema fails the sync once instead of every run on every team — stamps it on a canonical config row at creation, and backfills rows whose schema is null. A schema a team set is never overwritten, the same rule the display name follows.

The schema file must name a bundled file under `references/` or `scripts/`, so it is read once, carries the same size and path caps as every other bundled file, and rides the existing content hash. That is the one deviation from the issue's sketch of a top-level sibling file.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> A canonical schema is effectively fixed per team once seeded. The config column is what the record endpoint enforces, and nothing overwrites it, so editing a shipped schema refreshes each team's copy of the *file* and leaves already-seeded configs on the schema they were given. Changing a schema teams already run needs a migration, not a frontmatter edit. Both docstrings and the skills guide say so.

**The MCP scout records two kinds every run.** One `category_rollup` per category with traffic, healthy ones and the project-wide `all` baseline included, carrying volume, reach, rates with their denominators, and `mcp_report_action` — what the scout did. Then `tool_session_share` rows for the top tools per source. Recording happens after Decide and before close-out, so the action is the outcome of the report call rather than a plan, and a run that files nothing still leaves the series intact. A new cookbook query 11 produces the category-grain numbers: distinct sessions and users from the raw calls after the tool-to-category join, p95 over the category's calls, and struggle share on the category's sessions, for every category rather than only the ones with failure candidates. Field names are `mcp_`-prefixed because `output_<key>` is shared across every scout in a project.

**A team cannot clear a shipped schema to null.** Null is what the reconcile reads as "never seeded", so a clear on a canonical scout would be undone within one tick and recording would come back on. The config API refuses that clear and names the switches that stick: the dry-run setting withholds the channel, and disabling the scout stops the runs. A team can still replace the schema with its own, and a null patch over a column that is already null is a no-op rather than a refusal. Wildcard-enrolled teams skip the per-tick reconcile by design, so they pick the schema up when their configs are next created or synced, the same as the display name.

**A "called too much" lens.** Lens 10 and cookbook query 10 rank each tool by the share of its source's sessions that called it, current window against the prior one. The limit is per source, bare `exec` is excluded from the ranking but kept in the denominators, the prior share is null below 20 prior sessions, and distinct users ride along so one developer's twenty sessions do not pass the reach bar. The step change is the finding, not the level. Decide carries a session-share bar, a qualifying tool counts in its category's problem tools, and the fix-loop metric names the share. The fix hypothesis points at prompt or tool-description wording rather than the handler. Deterministic — no judge.

**A consumption surface.** `references/metrics-dashboard.md` carries the HogQL for rate-per-category over time, session share per tool with a step-change alert recipe, and problem-tool count next to the scout's decisions. It states two traps explicitly: plot the recorded rate, never a count of records, and take the latest snapshot per day rather than summing the hourly seven-day windows. The step-change alert computes the share delta in SQL with the prior share present.

**Also:** the intent lens is no longer described as sparse and opt-in — on the hono regime its coverage is high, so it is a default lens with the coverage probe kept. `exploring-scouts` and `working-with-scouts` now point at this scout as the shipped example of a recorded series.

Rollout follows the existing `signals-scout` flag enrollment; no new gate.

## How did you test this code?

Automated, in `products/signals/backend/test/test_scout_harness_lazy_seed.py`:

- **Frontmatter parsing** — a valid declaration yields the schema and leaves the file in the bundle (the bundle assertion is the regression: drop it and a schema edit silently stops reaching teams). Eight malformed declarations each fail the parse: a non-string value, a path outside the bundle dirs, a traversal, a missing file, invalid JSON, a non-object root, a regex keyword, and the key on a companion skill.
- **Seeding, against the real on-disk fleet** — the schema lands on the MCP scout's config and not on a scout that ships none; the reconcile fills a null column and then loses to a team-set schema on the next tick.
- **The shipped schema's contract** — one record of each kind validates, and three near-misses do not: a stray field, a payload satisfying both `oneOf` branches, and an out-of-enum `mcp_report_action`. The record shape is spread across the schema, the skill body and the dashboard recipe, so this is what catches a field renamed in one and not the others.

- **The config API refuses to clear a shipped schema** — three parameterized cases in `test_scout_harness_api.py`: a custom scout's null PATCH clears the schema, the canonical MCP scout's null PATCH is a 400 with the schema unchanged, and a null PATCH over an already-null column is a 200. The regression is the reconcile turning recording back on after a clear the API accepted.

Queries 10 and 11 were run against real `$mcp_tool_call` telemetry before they went in the cookbook. Query 10 surfaced a real step change of the kind the lens exists for, and its per-source limit was confirmed to keep every source in the result. Query 11's category-grain counts were checked against the per-tool leaderboards.

Live dogfood: the shipped schema is set on the MCP scout's config in one PostHog project, so its hourly runs are shown the schema before this body lands. The first such run recorded a `category_rollup` for every category plus the `all` baseline, and `has_structured_output` flipped on the run row. With the previous body it summed per-tool session and user counts, so one category showed more sessions than the whole project. That is the failure mode query 11 exists to prevent, and the dashboard recipe's first query runs on the records as written.

Not verified end to end in the sandbox: a scout run recording against the live channel with this body.

## Problem

- An author who adds the `stamphog` label waits about 2.5 minutes (median) for a verdict, and the LLM uses under 45 seconds of that.
- A PR that fails a hard gate, such as a workflow file or an oversized diff, still waits about 2 minutes (median) for a refusal. The verdict was known after the context fetch.
- The rest is sandbox setup: a full-history clone and checkout, a blame prefetch, a cold `uv` install, and a blocking teardown.
- Gates run inside the sandbox, so a deny pays for every step above and then asks Sonnet to word a verdict it cannot change.

## Changes

Expected effect, estimated from local measurements (not yet seen in prod):

| Path | Before (median) | After (estimate) |
|---|---|---|
| Hard gate deny | ~2 min, p90 ~5 min | ~15–30 s |
| Full T1 review | ~2.5 min | ~70–90 s |

- **Final gate denies post right away.** The worker runs the engine's own gate pre-check (`review_local.py --pregate`) in a child process after the context fetch.
  - A deny the sandbox cannot overturn skips the reviewer-bot wait and the sandbox.
  - One tool-less Sonnet call words the refusal; the gate messages stand in when it fails.
  - Anything not final, or any error, falls through to the full review. So the fast path can miss a deny, but never approves.
  - The workflow branch sits behind `workflow.patched("stamphog-pre-gates")`.
- **Author familiarity comes from GitHub GraphQL on the server.** Blame and path history run beside the other context reads, capped at 15 s. The sandbox no longer needs git history.
  - Matching uses the commit author login first, then the `(#N)` PR number. GitHub blame follows renames, so the band can shift slightly. `stamphog_review_completed` now carries the band and its source for recalibration.
- **The sandbox fetches only the PR head (depth 1) and the merge-base trees.** Locally on this repo: ~26 s instead of ~44.5 s, same changed-file list. The engine diffs `merge_base..head` when the context carries the merge base.
  - Commit trailers for provenance come from the PR commits API, so the fast path reports them too.
- **The sandbox boots from a new `STAMPHOG_REVIEW` image** with the engine's dependencies already in the uv cache. The pins still come from the `review_local.py` header. Install drops from ~11 s to ~1 s.
- **Sandbox teardown runs on a background thread**, so the verdict no longer waits ~10 s for it.
- Mechanical: lockfiles leave the blame set, per-step timings land in `run.output["timings_ms"]`, and the engine version moves to 2.1.0.

> [!NOTE]
> Riskiest parts: the clone rework in `_clone_pr` (auth on every fetch, private repos) and the pre-check child process on the worker. The rest is plumbing and tests.

Before:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Fetch context]:::phYellow --> B[Wait for reviewer bots]
  B --> C[Sandbox: full-history clone, blame prefetch, uv install]:::phGray
  C --> D[Gates]
  D --> E{{Sonnet review}}:::phBlue
  E --> F[Teardown]:::phGray
  F --> G[Post verdict]:::phYellow
  classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
  classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
  classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
```

After:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Fetch context + familiarity]:::phYellow --> P[Gate pre-check on worker]
  P -- final deny --> R{{Tool-less refusal summary}}:::phBlue --> G[Post verdict]:::phYellow
  P -- otherwise --> B[Wait for reviewer bots]
  B --> C[Sandbox: depth-1 head, warm uv cache]:::phGray
  C --> D[Gates]
  D --> E{{Sonnet review}}:::phBlue
  E --> G
  E -.-> T[Teardown in background]:::phGray
  classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
  classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
  classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
```

## How did you test this code?

- New tests pin each regression this could introduce:
  - A pre-check deny the full review would not reach.
  - A fast deny that still makes a sandbox.
  - A fetch without the auth header.
  - A diff on the shallow checkout that differs from the three-dot diff.
  - Familiarity from facts that differs from the git path.
  - Provenance from the API that differs from `git log`.
- Local run of the new clone sequence on PostHog/posthog PRs: same file list, numstat and `manifest_script_changes` result as a full clone.
- Private-repo check against a private PostHog repo with credential helpers off: the sequence works, and removing the prefetch makes it fail, so the check catches the case.
- The uv warm path in the Docker image: 0.9 s offline vs 5.2 s cold.
- Not tested:
  - The Modal image build. The first review after deploy pays a one-time layer build.
  - A real Temporal replay of the patched workflow.
  - A fork PR.
  - A PR with more than 250 commits, where provenance is left out.

**Agent:** Claude Code, Claude Opus 5.5 (orchestrator and one subagent per commit)

## Problem

- An alert snoozed in the logs product still fires a delivery on the shared alerts platform.
- The backfill copies configuration fields into the platform, but not `snooze_until`. Every platform alert starts unsnoozed.
- Seen on dev: a snoozed test alert produced a fire preview on the first evaluation after a backfill.

## Changes

- Each backfill run now copies the logs alert's snooze onto its `PlatformAlert` row. A snoozed alert stays silent, and an alert unsnoozed since the last run is unsnoozed on the platform too.
- The copy sets the `snoozed` state as well as `snooze_until`. Logs-style evaluation honors `snooze_until` only while the state is `snoozed`, as the logs snooze API does. Clearing a snooze returns the alert to `not_firing`.
- The configuration write and the snooze write run in one transaction, so a check that is due during a backfill never reads the new configuration with the old snooze.
- Snooze goes on the alert row, not the configuration, because the platform keeps snooze with the alert state.
- The backfill is still a seed, not a sync. A snooze changed between runs reaches the platform on the next run. `docs/internal/alerts-platform-temporal.md` says so.
- Nothing user-visible outside dev: the platform path runs only in the dev deployment.

## How did you test this code?

- `test_a_copied_snooze_reaches_the_check_and_a_later_unsnooze_clears_it` in `products/alerts/backend/test/test_platform_lifecycle.py` catches the backfill dropping the snooze state or timestamp, and a re-run failing to clear them. It fails with either write removed.
- Suppression of a `snoozed` alert on a breached check is already covered by the `SNOOZED` cases in `products/alerts/backend/test/test_state_machine.py`.
- Not run: the backfill against dev after this change.

## Problem

- A Replay Vision observation hid its recording behind a collapsed bar, so the evidence for a result took an extra click to see.
- The verdict was a small tag next to rows of lifecycle and config metadata, and the rating form took a large bordered block.
- An observation outlives its recording, and once the recording expired the page showed a generic "Recording not found" screen.

## Changes

- **Layout:** the result sits on the left and the player on the right, visible on load and pinned while scrolling. The columns split 1:2 and stack on narrow screens, where a citation click scrolls the player into view.
- **Question, answer, explanation:** a finished scan leads with its prompt in a clipped box with a "Show full prompt" modal, shared with the scanner Configuration card. In-progress, failed and not-scanned observations skip the prompt.
- **Result headline:** a monitor verdict is a large green or red pill, a score is colored on a red to green scale, assigned categories are large pills, and a summary title is large text. A freeform category explains itself on hover.
- **Rating:** "Did the scanner get this right?" is one line in its own strip. A thumb opens an optional note popover, the note saves when the popover closes, and the strip disappears once rated. Ratings stay editable in the Calibration tab.
- **Facts:** Person, Scanned, Status, Triggered by, Confidence and Scanner (a link back to the scanner), then pinned properties as a single list in the same card.
- **Details:** a collapsed section holds the observation ID, session link, observation event link (succeeded scans only), timings and model.
- **Failed and not-scanned scans:** a red or grey headline with the reason and Retry.
- **Expired recordings:** once the recording's metadata returns 404, the player's place shows the frame saved at scan time, says the recording passed its retention period, and links to the retention setting. The result stays readable and rateable.
- **Shortcuts:** `j` and `k` move to the next and previous observation, and `y` and `n` answer the rating question while it shows.
- **Removed:**
  - The page no longer shows "Signals emitted (N)" or linked inbox reports.
  - The `signal_reports` endpoint stays, since the MCP tool enabled in #106247 reads it.
  - The Lifecycle and Configuration cards.
  - The `vision-observation-recording-toggle` and `vision-observation-open-signal-report` data-attrs, whose elements no longer exist.
- **Mechanical:** new stories for every scanner type and state.

body:
## Problem

- Every logged-in page downloads and parses 1,422 KiB of CSS before its first render. About half of it (686 KiB) belongs to lazily loaded features such as the Monaco editor, maps and notebooks.
- esbuild puts the CSS of every chunk, lazy ones included, into the entry stylesheet. It has no CSS code splitting.
- One stylesheet also means any CSS edit renames all of it, so returning users download it all again after most deploys. That undoes the cache stability #105531 gives the JS.

## Changes

This only affects browsers opted in to the stable build (`?stable_chunks=1`, from #105531). The default build is unchanged.

- A second esbuild pass (`frontend/bin/stableCss.mjs`) builds the same CSS as groups, using the app's own Sass, Tailwind and PostCSS plugins. Each group's file is named by its own content.
  - **Eager layers** hold the CSS that the boot chain (entry, App, bootApp, AuthenticatedShell) imports statically: Tailwind, global styles and app components.
  - **Lazy groups** hold the rest. Each group is a run of adjacent files imported by the same JS chunks, so every group keeps its rules in the entry stylesheet's order.
  - Every group lists its files in the entry stylesheet's order. The build fails if the boot stylesheets stop being in layer order, rather than reorder rules silently.
- The stable page links the eager layers instead of the full stylesheet, and preloads them.
- Each lazy entry chunk starts with one line, `await window.ESBUILD_LOAD_CSS([...])`, for the groups its static imports need. The chunk runs only once its styles apply, so nothing renders unstyled.
  - Group URLs come from the import map (`@css/<group>`, read with `import.meta.resolve`). JS chunks therefore name their CSS by identity, and a CSS edit does not rename the chunks that load it.
  - Only lazy entry chunks get the line, never shared chunks, which keeps top-level await out of import cycles. The copied source map shifts down one line.
- The loader inserts each lazy stylesheet by its rank in the entry stylesheet, so the cascade among lazy stylesheets does not depend on the order scenes load in.
- If a split stylesheet fails or stalls, the page loads the full stylesheet through the existing `cssLoaderScript`, with its retries and failure reports, and loads no split stylesheet after it. If even that fails, the chunk throws a `ChunkLoadError`, so the app's chunk-load recovery reloads the page. The failed group is forgotten so a different chunk that needs the same group can still retry it.
- A browser without `import.meta.resolve` (Chromium 89 to 104) gets the full stylesheet instead of a prelude that throws.

| Opted-in page | Today | Split |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CSS before first render | 1,422 KiB, 1 file | 736 KiB: Tailwind 332, global 244, app 160 |
| Lazy CSS | none, all in the entry | 686 KiB in 165 files, loaded with their chunks |
| After editing one lazy component's SCSS | everything renamed | that stylesheet and its own JS chunk renamed |

> [!NOTE]
> Lazy stylesheets load after the eager layers, where the single stylesheet interleaved them. Only three selectors appear in both a lazy group and an eager layer, and none sets a different value for the same property. Rules with different selectors of equal specificity cannot be checked statically, which is what the opt-in testing is for.

## How did you test this code?

- `stableCssPlan.test.ts`:
  - The boot chain's CSS forms ordered eager layers.
  - A lazy entry also waits for the CSS of the shared chunks it imports. Without that, part of a scene would render unstyled.
  - Out-of-order boot stylesheets fail the build.
- `cssLoader.test.ts` covers the stable loader: ready once every split stylesheet applies, and the full stylesheet when one fails. `stableChunkNames.test.ts` covers the prelude sitting on its own first line.
- `test_stable_chunks.py` parses `eagerCss` from the manifest and rejects a malformed list.
- Headless Chromium with the real build and manifest:
  - The eager layers apply in order.
  - A lazy scene's stylesheet loads before its module resolves.
  - A lazy stylesheet returning 404 falls back to the full one.
  - All 225 chunks that wait on CSS settle, and none hangs. 9 throw "Team ID is not known", which is app code running without a Django page.
- Two builds of the same source are byte-identical. After a one-line lazy SCSS edit, 2 of 2,023 import-map entries change: the stylesheet, and its component's JS chunk, which esbuild re-minifies.
- Not checked: a real logged-in session, Safari and Firefox, and the CDN `js_url` path. The opt-in test in production covers these, as for #105531.

## Problem

- On the pending-deletion screen, "Cancel project deletion" can fail with a 404. The project then stays queued for deletion.
- The request goes to `/api/organizations/undefined/projects/<id>/cancel-deletion/`.
- `cancelProjectDeletion` reads `currentProject.organization_id`, but `api/projects/@current` returns `organization` and not `organization_id`.
- After `loadCurrentProject` runs, `currentProject` has no `organization_id`, so every cancel attempt 404s.
- The regression came in with #99317.

## Changes

- The cancel request now takes the organization id from `organizationLogic.currentOrganizationId`. The user sees the cancel button work again.
- `currentOrganizationId` falls back to `@current` when the organization is not loaded yet. The org-scoped route accepts that value.
- Nothing looks different on the screen, so this PR has no screenshots.

## How did you test this code?

- New kea logic test in `projectLogic.test.ts`. It loads a project without `organization_id`, cancels, and asserts that the request uses the current organization id.
- Without the fix the test fails, because the request goes to `/organizations/undefined/`.
- Not checked: a manual run against a local stack.

## Problem

Slack API metrics cannot say which feature a call or a 429 came from.

- Every flow that gets its client from `SlackIntegration` records under `source="integration"`.
- So `slack_api_requests_total` puts the calls and 429s of error tracking alerts, subscriptions, the Stamphog digest and a scout delivery into one series.
- Per-flow volume and rate-limit data are needed before any of these flows move onto shared alert delivery.

## Changes

- Each outbound notification flow now records its Slack calls under its own `source` label: `error_tracking_alerts`, `subscriptions`, `signals_inbox`, `signals_scout`, `stamphog`, `visual_review`, `loop_notifications`, `eval_reports`, `customer_analytics_event_stream`.
- `SlackIntegration` takes an optional `source` keyword and passes it to the sync and async clients it builds.
- The default stays `integration`, so the Slack app and every other caller keep their current label.
- The `Retry-After` gauge keeps its per-bucket labels. Slack applies one limit per workspace, app and method, so all flows wait on the same reset.
- `fetch_channel_map` now requires `source`, so the channel listing that each digest makes carries the same label as its posts.
- Mechanical: the Stamphog test fake accepts the new keyword, and the Slack egress README documents the label.

> [!NOTE]
> A query that filters on `source="integration"` loses the series of the flows above. No file in this repository queries the metric by `source`. Dashboards outside the repository were not checked.

No user-visible change.

## Problem

- Anyone changing an error tracking issue filter works in a 97-line method that no test pins, so a review cannot tell a semantics change from a rewrite.
- `_issue_property_to_ast` routed the filter key to a field and then ran eleven inline operator cases in one body.
- Ruff scored it C901 20 and PLR0912 16 branches, against a repository limit of 10.
- The module changed 12 times in 90 days, so that review cost repeats.

<!-- posthog-self-driving-origin:01a0d2ee-5146-777c-a547-38415c9e8879 -->
## Origin

- Scout: a custom scout
- First signal: 2026-09-24
- Inbox report: [open](https://us.posthog.com/project/2/inbox/reports/01a0d2ee-5146-777c-a547-38415c9e8879)
- Task started by: auto-start, after the report was rated P2 and ready to fix
<!-- /posthog-self-driving-origin:01a0d2ee-5146-777c-a547-38415c9e8879 -->

## Changes

- Nothing user-visible changes. The built HogQL is identical for every operator, key and value shape.
- Four module-level tables replace the operator chain, one per operator family: membership, pattern, range, nullability.
- The field table carries the value constructor, so the `first_seen` date cast is declared next to the field rather than tested at the call site.
- The `issue_description` key alias is a table entry, so the inline rename is gone.
- `_issue_property_to_ast` keeps only the coordination: resolve the field, dispatch on the tables.
- A new parameterized test pins the HogQL each supported operator produces.

Tables beat a dispatch method per family here. An operator maps to operators and templates, not to behavior, so a table states the whole mapping on one screen and a reader checks it by reading down a column.

> [!NOTE]
> These tables are a holding pattern, not the end state. `posthog/hogql/property.py::_expr_to_compare_op` is the house mechanism for the same job, and this local copy has drifted from it: no `multiSearchAnyCaseInsensitive` for multi-value `ICONTAINS`, no relative date resolution, no `REGEX` or `BETWEEN`. Adopting it would change the built query, so it does not belong in a behavior-neutral PR. The general fix is to make the issue fields resolvable in a HogQL scope so `property_to_expr` handles them like every other filter, and this block deletes.

> [!NOTE]
> `_where_exprs_legacy` still scores 11 in the same file. It is untouched, pre-existing, and a flat accumulator rather than an operator chain, so it stays out of this diff.

## How did you test this code?

- `hogli test products/error_tracking/backend/hogql_queries/test/test_error_tracking_query_runner.py` passes, including the ClickHouse query snapshots.
- Equivalence was checked by dumping `_issue_property_to_ast(...).to_hogql()` for every `PropertyOperator`, every supported and unsupported filter key, and list, scalar, empty, `None`, float and bool values, on both master and this branch. The 1560 outputs match exactly.
- The new test was confirmed to bite: inverting the `ENDS_WITH` pattern template fails `test_issue_filter_operator_mapping_08_ends_with` and nothing else.
- The new test catches a regression no existing test did. The runner tests exercise `EXACT`, `IS_SET`, `IS_NOT_SET` and the `first_seen` range operators against data. They never assert the HogQL for `ICONTAINS`, the four prefix and suffix operators, the `issue_description` key alias, or the three paths that return no expression.
- Not checked manually: no UI is involved, and no behavior changes.
- `ruff check --select C901,PLR0912,PLR0915,PLR1702 --preview` reports nothing for `_issue_property_to_ast`.

- Draft by default: open new PRs as drafts (`gh pr create --draft`) — drafts run only a narrow CI subset and save runner credits. Fix CI and run affected tests locally before marking ready for review.
- Labels: apply `skip-agent-review` for trivial/chore PRs that don't need Copilot or Greptile review.
- When a human directed the work, the PR must be attributable to that person, even if agent-assisted.
- If a human directed this work, assign them as the PR assignee (the DRI) — actually set the assignee, don't just name them here. Leave a PR unassigned only when it is fully autonomous with no human driver (set Autonomy to "Fully autonomous").
- Never write a GitHub @mention or username you have not verified this session. Resolve a real handle from `gh api user` (current user) or the PR's actual author/assignee via `gh pr view --json author,assignees` — never infer a handle from a display name.
- Do not add a human Co-authored-by just for the sake of attribution — if no human was involved in the changes, own it as agent-authored.
- Agent-authored PRs always require human review — do not self-merge or auto-approve.
- Do NOT claim manual testing you haven't done.
- Shape and style: invoke the `/writing-pr-descriptions` skill before writing this body. In short: lead with the effect a person sees rather than the code path behind it, make the body stand alone for a reader who opens no files, size it to the change, link evidence rather than asserting what CI already reports, then hold what's left to one fact per bullet in under 25 words. A body that got longer as bullets was not cut.
-->

## Problem

- The first goal-space setup run in production published the context page and nothing else: no tracker canvas, no loops, and it reported 403s for `canvas:write` and `hog_flow:write`. Three causes, all in the merged setup path.
- The MCP session hid `workflows-schedule-create` and `workflows-test-run`. They require `person:read` and `group:read` beside `hog_flow:write`, and the least-privilege list `SPACE_SETUP_SCOPES` omitted both, so the run could not schedule or test a loop through MCP.
- The setup task was created without its repository. The start call derived it and put it in the prompt, but never passed it to the task, so the sandbox had no checkout.
- The token in the sandbox environment (`POSTHOG_PERSONAL_API_KEY`) is minted at provisioning by four activities that pass no scopes, so it takes the `read_only` default while the MCP session carries the run's grant. Any shell or REST fallback then fails with the 403s the run reported.

## Changes

- A goal-space setup run can now schedule and test its loops through MCP: `SPACE_SETUP_SCOPES` gains `person:read`, `group:read`, and `integration:read` for the repository reachability check the loops skill performs.
- The setup task now carries its repository, so the sandbox clones it. A team that cannot reach a private repository through a GitHub integration gets the existing recoverable setup error and message instead of a 500.
- Shell and REST fallbacks in a sandbox now hold the same grant as the MCP session, for every run, not only setup.
- A run with no recorded dispatch, such as one started by the API or bootstrap, gets the same run-source policy dispatch applies rather than `read_only`. That policy now lives once, in `dispatched_run_scopes`, and the reconciler uses it too.
- A recorded scope value that does not parse fails closed to `read_only`. That covers a list holding a non-string, and a workflow snapshot that does not parse now narrows instead of dropping the intersection.
- `create_oauth_access_token_for_run` defaults `scopes` to what `pending_dispatch` recorded at run creation, the same value the launch activities receive on their input. A caller that passes scopes is unchanged.
- `read_only` stays the floor for a run whose state predates `pending_dispatch`, and the workflow snapshot intersection and loop-run stripping still apply after the default resolves.
- Mechanical: the state-value parser `_workflow_run_scopes` used inline is now a shared helper.

## How did you test this code?

- `products/tasks/backend/logic/services/test_space_setup.py`: one test extracts every MCP tool the setup steps name and checks its required scopes against `SPACE_SETUP_SCOPES`, reading the generated `tool-definitions-all.json` so both sides share one source. It fails today on `person:read` and `group:read`, and it catches the next reviewer who narrows the list past a tool the prompt instructs.
- `products/tasks/backend/tests/test_channel_extras.py`: the setup-start test now asserts the task's repository, and a new case checks that a private repository with no GitHub integration returns the recoverable 503 with no task created, instead of the 500 attaching the repository made reachable.
- `products/tasks/backend/temporal/tests/test_oauth.py`: nine parameterized cases on `create_oauth_access_token_for_run` with no explicit scopes. They catch a provisioning mint returning `read_only` for a run dispatched as `full` or a list, a malformed recorded value being coerced instead of failing closed, an explicit `read_only` request being widened, and a run with no recorded dispatch losing the policy dispatch applied to it, across the user-created, agent-sourced, loop, and scout cases. No existing test called the function without scopes.
- Also ran the provisioning and launch activity tests. Three failures in `test_inject_fresh_tokens_on_resume.py` and `test_provision_sandbox.py` reproduce on clean master in this sandbox (a missing `SANDBOX_JWT_PRIVATE_KEY` setting) and are unrelated.
- Not run: a live sandbox run. The diagnosis comes from the stored summary and state of a production setup run: the two 403s on the environment credential, and a task with no repository.

body:
## Problem

A self-driving cloud run whose agent has gone quiet stays open for hours instead of ending after its inactivity timeout, because a periodic quota recheck restarts the timer every 5 minutes.

- `_wait_for_event` creates a fresh `_wait_for_inactivity` timer on every pass of the loop.
- `_wait_for_inactivity` sleeps the full timeout from the moment it starts.
- Signal-report runs that open a PR also wake the loop every 5 minutes for a quota recheck.
- A 30-minute timeout never elapses, so the sandbox keeps running until something else kills it.
- `_wait_for_ci_follow_up` already anchors on `_last_active_time`. The inactivity timer did not.

```diff
 async def _wait_for_inactivity(timeout):
-    sleep(timeout)
+    if patched("tasks-inactivity-anchored-on-last-activity"):
+        last_active_time = last_active_time or now
+        remaining = timeout - (now - last_active_time)
+        if remaining > 0:
+            sleep(remaining)
+    else:
+        sleep(timeout)
     return TIMEOUT_REACHED
```

Before: every quota recheck restarts the idle clock.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Start([Loop pass]) --> Wait{{wait for first event}}
    Wait --> Sig[External signal]
    Wait --> Idle["Inactivity sleep: full 30m"]
    Wait --> Quota["Quota recheck: 5m"]
    Quota -->|fires first, every time| Start
    Idle -.->|never reached| End([Run ends])
    classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
    classDef phRed fill:#f54e00,stroke:#f54e00,color:#fff;
    classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
    classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
    class Start,End phYellow;
    class Wait phBlue;
    class Sig,Quota phRed;
    class Idle phGray;
```

After: the idle clock counts from the last activity, so a recheck wake keeps the remaining time.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Start([Loop pass]) --> Wait{{wait for first event}}
    Wait --> Sig[External signal]
    Wait --> Idle["Inactivity sleep: timeout minus idle so far"]
    Wait --> Quota["Quota recheck: 5m"]
    Quota -->|re-arms, idle time kept| Start
    Idle -->|fires 30m after last activity| End([Run ends])
    classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff;
    classDef phRed fill:#f54e00,stroke:#f54e00,color:#fff;
    classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000;
    classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000;
    class Start,End phYellow;
    class Wait phBlue;
    class Sig,Quota phRed;
    class Idle phGray;
```

## Changes

- An idle run now ends one inactivity timeout after its last activity, whatever else wakes the loop
- The timer sleeps only the time left since `_last_active_time`, and fires at once when none is left
- Every event that is real activity already writes `_last_active_time`: an active heartbeat, client activity, a follow-up dispatch, a permission response, and a CI dispatch or skip. Those keep the same behavior
- A run with no recorded activity anchors on its first wait, so a recheck cannot restart that timer either
- A queued signal now wins over an overdue timeout when both complete in the same pass. A follow-up that arrived during a slow CI check is delivered instead of dropped
title: fix(tasks): anchor the inactivity timeout on the last activity time

## Problem

Support staff on a read-only impersonation session cannot size a workflow audience: the count never loads and the request fails with `403 impersonation_read_only`. That is every audience-sizing read in the workflow builder while impersonating.

- `ImpersonationReadOnlyMiddleware` blocks every non-idempotent method during a read-only session.
- `POST hog_flows/user_blast_radius` carries its filters in the body, because they are too large for a query string.
- The middleware rejects it before it reaches the viewset, so the endpoint's own permissions never run.

## Changes

- The audience count now loads during read-only impersonation, through one entry in `READ_ONLY_IMPERSONATION_ALLOWLISTED_PATHS`.
- The regex names the single action, so the writing actions under the same `hog_flows/` prefix stay blocked.
- Nothing about the endpoint changes, and no other surface changes.

The action is safe to allowlist because it only reads. It counts matching persons or groups, reads the team's batch trigger limit, and returns a `TimestampSigner` signature as the confirm token. The audience helpers under `products/workflows/backend/services/` hold no write. The endpoints that spend the confirm token (`run`, `batch_jobs`) stay blocked, so a read-only session still cannot dispatch a send.

The alternative was to declare read-only actions on the viewset and have the middleware consult that. The allowlist is deliberately fail-closed and security-reviewed, so a platform change to how "read-only" is decided belongs in its own PR, not behind a support fix.

No visual change: the fix restores a count that already has its own UI.

## How did you test this code?

- Added one case to the existing `test_read_only_impersonation_allows_allowlisted_post` list, rather than a new test.
- The case catches the regression where an edit to the allowlist regex stops matching this path and support sessions get the 403 again. It failed with the entry removed and passed with it in place.
- Added two cases to `test_read_only_impersonation_blocks_mutating_siblings`: `hog_flows/<id>/publish/` and `hog_flows/bulk_delete/`.
- Those two catch the opposite regression: a later edit widening the regex to the `hog_flows/` prefix would hand a read-only session a workflow write.
- Checked directly that the committed regex matches the audience path with and without the trailing slash, and rejects `publish`, `bulk_delete`, and the bare prefix.
- Not run: pytest after the master merge. The local virtualenv has protobuf runtime 5.29.6 against gencode 6.31.1, so Django cannot import, and the machine has too little disk to rebuild the environment. The allowed-path case did run before the merge, and failed with the allowlist entry removed. CI runs the suite.

None. The allowlist is internal and carries its own comment.
